Immersing yourself in Cronos: The New Dawn isn't just playing a game; it's embarking on a journey to another world! From the very first moments, I was struck by the incredible atmosphere, meticulously crafted by the creators down to the smallest details. Every corner of this world, every ray of light, every melody – everything works in concert to make you feel like you're part of this story. The storyline is so captivating and multi-layered that it's impossible to tear yourself away. The constantly arising questions and mysteries keep you on edge and compel you to move forward, exploring every inch of this wondrous world in search of answers. And be prepared, because Cronos: The New Dawn will definitely make you sweat a bit! Intense moments are cleverly interspersed with moments of quiet sadness. And the notes found in the ruins… Some of them are so imbued with despair that you can practically feel the hopelessness of this world. But there are also those that can bring a smile to your face, reminding you that even in the darkest of times, there is room for hope.

Without a doubt, I highly recommend experiencing Cronos: The New Dawn!

This game is so far an awesome entry if you like survival horror akin to Dead Space 1 or 2. While not as good as either of those games this is still an easy recommendation. Some very light spoiler (e.g. the existence of an nth thing) filled specifics include:

[h1] Enemies: 7/10 [/h1]

While not really bringing anything too new or innovative on the enemies front they are still satisfying and fun to fight and the encounters are varied enough where they don't get too repetitive. The main enemy gimick in this game isn't too impactfull though unless you aren't paying attention. It is very powerful if they get it off but at the same time I would have  preferred for it to happen more often and more easily and it been less strong than the current version. Having defeated the third boss I've only experienced jank with the enemies twice, once where a bigger enemy bugged out and just stood there (I was out of ammo so I didn't complain) and the 3rd boss falling on top of me locking me inside him until he attacked which moved our models and let me out. 

[h1] Atmosphere: 9/10 [/h1]

Arguably one of the most important aspects for this kind of game and this one nails it. The visuals and ambient noises mesh nicely to keep you on the edge and until you really start to know what to listen for make it so you're never 100% sure whether there is an enemy nearby or not. IMO the jump scares are mainly used after some tension has been built so they don't feel cheap. At the same time they don't occur every time tension is built so they don't feel overused either. In addition, the use of "yellow paint" type indicators seems to be unobtrusive enough to not interfere with the vibes while also making sure you're not just swinging at random objects and trying to navigate to places you can't.

[h1] Combat/Weapons: 7/10 [/h1]

So far the guns feel good to use and they each seem to have an at least semi creative trick to them. Combat is tense and sufficiently drains your resources to make sure you need to be scrounging for more without feeling unfair.

[h1] Visuals: 7/10 [/h1]

I would give this a higher rating as the environments do look awesome and do what they need to do but for some reason the facial expressions are just... weird. Not sure if this was a stylistic choice or what but 80% of the characters just really like showing off their teeth and it ruins the immersion of the cut scenes. I'm not a history expert though so maybe these are actually historically accurate expressions for people in 1981 Poland.

[h1] Story: 7/10 [/h1]

So far the lore seems interesting enough and is staying consistent and the story has me wanting to keep playing to find out what happens next and what some characters are going to do. The pacing of the game has been nice as well with each section not seeming to drag on too long before getting to the next story beat. There is exactly one section where I think they messed this up and that is on a certain stairwell where you use an "infinite" resource to clear 3 separate blockers. The problem is that the pacing is ruined as you have to go all the way back down to get another use of the resource then walk back up to use it. This could be improved by simply putting a guaranteed usage behind each obstacle or only having one of the three in place.

All in all, if you like survival horror then get this game!

I was very skeptical going into Cronos, especially with all the games that come out in Sep and Oct. Reviews were all over the place, and I honestly thought it’d be another forgettable horror game. But after the first chapter, I realized I was way off. The story feels like 12 Monkeys — time travel, outbreaks, and a world falling apart. It’s messy, weird, and somehow it all works.

The devs clearly drew inspiration from The Thing and Aliens. Environments are gross in the best way: twisted biomass, mutated bodies, and little touches like how enemies react when one of their own goes down. With Reshade and HDR on, it looks incredible — easily one of the best-looking horror games I’ve played, above Dead Space. The Callisto Protocol tried this vibe and failed.

Level design is stellar. Each area — the church, hospital, factory, and even the starting zone — is crafted like a mini-movie. Every chapter feels unique, with its own pacing, atmosphere, and challenges.

I wasn’t sure Bloober Team could carry survival horror forward, especially after Silent Hill 2 Remake, but Cronos proves they can. I’m genuinely hyped for their Silent Hill 1 remake.

Gameplay mixes Dead Space, Resident Evil, and a bit of Silent Hill. The main character has a Bioshock-style vibe, fitting the time-travel theme perfectly. Controls are tight, movement is smooth, and upgrades make combat flow well. Boss fights are clever — more about using the environment than dumping ammo.

Difficulty is balanced. It keeps you alert without being brutal. Enemy variety isn’t massive, but the merging mechanic keeps even basic enemies dangerous.

Atmosphere is incredible. The world is brutal yet beautiful, puzzles break up the pace, and the music is haunting. One of my favourite moments was in a safe room with a cathedral-like track playing — I literally stood there for ten minutes just listening.

One thing I really want to praise is how Cronos handles New Game Plus. The game doesn’t have traditional difficulty settings, but once you start New Game Plus, you can choose to play harder or easier while keeping your upgrades from the first run. This is brilliant. Too often, games like Resident Evil 4 only reward players with things like unlimited ammo after completing the hardest difficulty — which feels pointless. In Cronos, New Game Plus lets you enjoy tougher enemies while keeping your fully upgraded favorite weapons, making the experience twice as enjoyable. I wish more developers adopted Bloober Team’s approach to  replayability.

That said, it’s not perfect. Some room layouts can make you a bit nauseous, a few animations feel stiff, and inventory/upgrade limitations can feel punishing. And unskippable cutscenes?  Bad idea - they should add an option to skip them in the next patch, especially since I’ll play this multiple times.

Performance is top-notch. With frame generation on, I ran 4K max settings at 120 FPS, stable and smooth, with no major bugs. And it shipped without Denuvo, which is a huge plus in my book.

I’m going out on a limb: Cronos is easily in my top 5 horror games of all time. Creepy moments, solid combat, upgrades, enemy mechanics, cinematic level design, eerie atmosphere, replayability — it hits all the right notes. Sure, some might prefer Silent Hill F for story or replay value, but for me, Cronos nails it. In movie terms, I’d rank it alongside the first Blade Runner - Classic!

CRONOS: The New Dawn is a survival action horror game harkening to Dead Space, The Evil Within and to an extent, Signalis.  You play as a mysterious protagonist who is a rigid member of a group called ‘The Collective’. You are tasked with diving back in time to Poland in the 80s to discover why a deadly outbreak has occurred.

Cronos is captivating at first, but to me, scuffed its alluring polish the longer the game played out.

[h2] [b] Why is the first half so good? [/b] [/h2]
The atmosphere of Cronos is top tier.  Its haunted crumbling Poland, combined with a dark synth soundtrack led to goosebumps as I started playing the game.  The tense mechanics of survival horror feel elevated in this world, where ammo is scarce and the horrors are unknown.  The sense of discovery and the tense nature of being murdered in your clunky suit make for a truly captivating environment.

As you progress a campaign begins to unfold.  The mystery of this world and who you are, keep you thinking and guessing as the game plays out.  Adventure to a new location, try to find a dive point and jump back in time to learn more about the outbreak.  It’s a compelling loop at first.

The merge mechanic, while being a large part of the early trailers.  Is a small but cool mechanic that keeps you micro managing enemies during combat.  I enjoyed this element of the game

Additionally, the game looks like a movie.  The visuals are stellar.

[h2] [b] Why is the second half so tedious? [/b] [/h2]
This part will have some spoilers, so be aware.  Cronos runs into a problem where there are very few enemy types.  Most enemies are ‘Zombies with a tentacle arm’ (of varying sizes) and most of the bosses are ‘Big Tentacle Dog’ (of varying health).  After ~6 hours of going through similarly haunted tunnels and encountering the same jump scares again, the enemy variety grows tedious.

There are text documents scattered in the world you can read.  At a certain point, they all just end up saying the same thing in another way and there is little point in reading them.

[b] The FOV is super narrow. [/b] If this was able to be expanded, it would lead to a much more enjoyable gaming experience.  I got motion sickness on some of the gravboot sequences.

The power fantasy that Dead Space mastered is not met.  Where in dead space towards the end you are still fragile, but have a sonic shotgun that rips the skin from your foes.  In Cronos, the weapons are largely lack luster.

Lastly, the story ends up falling apart.  The game shines while the narrative remains somewhat aloof.  But as you reach the end, the game over explains itself[spoiler]and all becomes an allegory for a toxic relationship. This is a real bummer of an ending. [/spoiler]

[h2] [b] TL;DR  [/b] [/h2]
It’s a cool game, with great audio and visuals that overstays its welcome.  If you haven’t played the Deadspace remake, play that first.  If you want something that has more intrigue but less satisfying combat, hop on the Cronos wagon.  All of this said, I still look on the game fondly.

Where "Dead Space" is to "Resident Evil 4", as "Cronos: The New Dawn" is to "Dead Space".

This game isn't terrible. The setting and story are unique. The voice acting is also very cool, as I enjoy the Traveler's cold and almost automated sounding reactions to the world around her.

However, I will say that this game feels almost like a direct carbon copy of "Dead Space". You have designated buttons for punching and stomping melee attacks. Enemies are grotesque and strange. Only major difference is the overall setting and consumable/ammo crafting system.

Only gripes I have against this game so far is:
- Random Frame-rate Drops/Stuttering (Should be fixed in future patches)
- Combat feels ineffective. Enemies take multiple shots to take down and ammunition is scarce. Melee combat is lacking and attacks feel very under-powered. Wouldn't be much of an issue if a dodge mechanic was implemented, but melee is a death sentence if you are facing multiple enemies.
- Not enough checkpoints. I've found myself replaying significant chunks of gameplay due to deaths.
- Clunky and annoying inventory management. (May be better as game progresses and you unlock upgrades.)

I still recommend this game, but not at the current $60 price tag. It is worth buying if it goes on sale. I only picked this up because I had some interest in the title and I had a few spare Steam Cards laying around.

The game very obviously walks in the footsteps of Dead Space and makes no apologies about it. Combat, inventory management, enemies, even major story elements all borrow heavily. However, that's not necessarily a bad thing. Dead Space hasn't really had any spiritual successors to speak of and it remains to this day such a functionally solid experience that even a game copying mostly 1:1 is destined to be good. The game runs well, has a banger soundtrack, spooky vibes, and cool weapons. In general it's just a very well put together experience.

My largest criticism is that for all it does to live up to the legacy of the games that came before it, the game and its story don't do much to try to genuinely stand apart. It spends so much time trying to be the next Dead Space that it doesn't manage to be anything but a game trying to be the next Dead Space. The story is serviceable, but nothing special. The enemies are good up to a point, but eventually become a bit predictable. The environments are mostly unique but only really cover classic horror story tropes (the spooky hospital, the industrial wasteland, the haunted church, etc.) For a game that markets itself as "a new breed of horror," it doesn't really do anything new, even with its great premise.

Where Cronos does stand out is the aesthetic. The game's protagonist, the Traveler, is just too freaking cool. From her bulky diving suit to her clipped and stoic dialogue, she radiates simultaneous calm and menace in every second she interacts with other characters. The technology of other Travelers, from their weapons to their time travel "anchors" to the breadcrumbs of ammo caches and anti-grav platforms seeded through the world, stand out from their Soviet-era surroundings in the absolute best way. It's just cool, and doesn't need any deeper justification than that.

All in all, a very solid (if flawed) title from Bloober Team. I very much enjoyed it and if scifi survival horror is your jam, you will too.

This game got strangely middling reviews for something I think is a near masterpiece of world building and story telling.  The gameplay loop isn't revolutionary but I don't need my survival horror mechanics revolutionary.  I need them competent and well designed.

Cronos gives you a slower dead space as far as gameplay goes but with a much heavier focus on resource management.  Progression is slow but significant.  Inventory slots are almost comically restrictive which makes combat extremely tense.

But none of that matter much because the gameplay is just a competent coat of paint on the core brilliance of the game.  Cronos is one of those rare games that feels like it's actually FROM somewhere.  It feels like it's made by people from Poland.  It's drenched in late soviet themes and environments.  But it blends that with a player character who is truly unique.  The purpose of your mission, the organization that created it and the "people" who carry it out are a fantastic mystery.  All of the world building is fascinating and compelling.

I have not been a fan of Bloobers games.  I very much disliked the medium.  It was only the excellent SH2 remake that had me interested in this game.  But Bloober has finally done what they needed to.  Combine they're absolutely riveting world building and story telling with gameplay good enough to never get in the way.

This is a well thought out and competently designed survival horror game.  It leans far more to the survival parts than the action parts.  And all of that stuff is ultimately in service of what this game does better than almost any other game in the genre.  Create a world that drives you to explore it and understand it.

A stunning achievement for Bloober.

Think of this game as a slower and more methodical Dead Space, with some elements borrowed from Resident Evil (tight inventory management etc.) and a bizarre story that is more in line with something you would find in Silent Hill, but with more sci-fi mixed in. An excellent action-survival horror game by Bloober Team. If you liked the 1st Dead Space, you'll probably like this game. Skill expression in Cronos comes in the form of tight inventory and resource management, and in my opinion is done well by Bloober. In Dead Space, the gimmick was you had to shoot monsters limbs instead of their heads. In Cronos, the gimmick is you have to prevent monsters from merging with dead corpses. If you allow them to absorb a dead body, they become faster, stronger and gain new abilities in some cases. It's a fun mechanic. Kill an enemy, lure another to attempt to merge with it's corpse, then use your fireproof suits' flamethrower to burn the corpse and stun the monsters at the same time. It's all about resource efficiency in Cronos. Every scrap and every round is precious and you'll find yourself coming up with creative ways to save inventory space and conserve ammo. Cronos The New Dawn is one of my favorite games this year. Highly recommended!

Pros:
+Nice graphics and effects. Bloober seems to be getting more proficient with using Unreal Engine 5 and Cronos looks great with detailed environments and a dark, moody atmosphere with grand set-pieces. Nothing like a derelict commie block infested with hideous mutants to set the horror atmosphere. 

+Satisfying game-play loop. Explore, find secrets and goodies, kill baddies, take their stuff, burn their corpses, and for the love of God, don't let them merge! The gameplay is challenging and fun in Cronos, demanding that you consider how to efficiently expend your resources and kill enemies with as little ammo as possible. Set fire traps, lure enemies in and burn 'em. Allowing monsters to merge with corpses will quickly turn an easy fight with low level enemies into an impossible obstacle with buffed monsters that spit acid, have chitinous armor and take way too much precious ammo to kill. Plan your attacks carefully. 

+Good sound effects. The ambiance is creepy and the music is kind of 80's synth sci-fi and moody. The weapons all sound meaty and powerful. 

Cons:
-There are dispensers that recharge your flamethrower but only dispense one unit of ammo at a time. I found myself backtracking to these A LOT to make sure I burned all the corpses in certain areas using the free ammo instead of precious crafting resources. It borders on tedious.

-The voice acting ranges from decent to terrible. Some of the characters sound like they're just reading their lines off a script with comical inflection that doesn't match what's going on in the story. 

-There were a couple glitches so far where my character got stuck on invisible geometry and I had to jimmy her around to get myself free. 

-Even if you're at full health, you can still accidentally push Q and waste a health pack. Also, for some reason pushing Q causes your character to use the largest health pack in your inventory instead of using the smaller ones up first. 

-There are a couple "gotcha!" moments where monsters burst out right on top of you and grab you. Jump scares are a lazy horror mechanic if not done very sparingly and carefully. I don't appreciate being forced to take damage in a game where resources are so scarce. 

Overall, Cronos The New Dawn is a well done game with fun, fresh survival horror elements and a cool Slavic-retro-NASA-punk aesthetic. I'd give it an 8/10 so far. Go play it!

The current survival horror market is obsessed with remakes, sequels and remasters. Cronos is a creative breath of fresh air in a stagnant genre.

The story is pretty good. It's well paced, with a great main character and decent side characters. It's a great flavour of post-apocalypse. I do think it didn't make as much use of its premise as it could have though. You're a time travelling diving suit sent to extract the memories of significant people, but you never time travel to any interesting points in the story. It's either before everything went to shit, or after it went to shit. Missed opportunity for some zombie apocalypse type events where the outbreak is currently happening. Overall I liked the narrative, though it leaves a lot unexplained. I like that, but if you don't be warned. 
The protagonist, the Traveller, has excellent voice acting. She pulls off this incredible alien vibe, where she's stilted, and awkward, but still emotes. She sounds like a robot trying to emote, or perhaps a human trying not to. It really works for the character, and as the game progresses you pick up more on her subtle tics that betray her feelings, as well as her becoming more human. 

This is the flavour of survival horror where combat and resource management is the focus, and the fear comes from running out of resources in the middle of a fight. Cronos has executed this quite well. Combat is absolutely fantastic! It is slow and you need to be very precise. Weapons have slow charge times and your character moves quite slowly, so you need to keep your distance and aim carefully, lest you waste one of your precious, precious bullets. That sounds boring, but the sound and animations of these weapons really sells it. Even your starting pistol is excellent. The charging noise is crisp, the firing sound is meaty, and it kicks with a super satisfying weightiness. All the other weapons that aren't the SMG are great. The shotgun sounds like God slamming a car door, the grenades feel appropriately forceful and even the melee manages to strike the right balance between feeling like a last resort while still being situationally useful. It even almost (but not quite) manages to be a survival horror game without a shitty final boss! 

The "don't let them merge" tagline is true, you really don't want to let those fuckers merge. I made the mistake of leaving a tanky enemy alive as I picked off half a dozen other creatures, and he merged with a bunch of corpses to become nigh on unkillable. I used every bullet I have, and had to resort to running back to a safe area to collect flamethrower ammo so I could stun him and kill him with melee. It was awesome. When you see an enemy going for a merge it becomes the biggest threat in the room. Switching away from whatever you were doing to prioritising that target adds a great ebb and flow to combat that keeps you on your toes. 

It can be a bit heavy handed at times with the dynamic difficulty, generously giving you new resources once combat is over. It does encourage you to use the fun stuff because you know the game will spawn in some more ammo for you on the road ahead, but I feel like the tension takes a hit because of it.

Level design is meh. It's aggressively linear with few to no secrets to uncover. I was hoping for something like the police station from the Resident Evil 2 remake where your curiosity is often rewarded, but alas. The best you get secrets-wise is the occasional door that you need bolt cutters to open, so you just... keep the bolt cutters on you. Wow. 

Visuals are another huge win. It has the kind of "anomaly" aesthetic that games like STALKER or Pacific Drive have, with the addition of horrifying flesh creatures. It is immersive and really sucks you into the story, and to figuring out what happened here. Although it definitely plays its cards too early, and has nothing new to show you as it goes along. The horrible flesh creatures and their horrible nests never really change, and I found myself lost mostly because every intricately detailed drab brutalist corridoor starts looking the same after a while. 

Performance is ok. I have a Radeon 9070 and a 5800X3D and ran the game on high at 1440p, 80-100 FPS with FSR set to quality. Turning on ray tracing cut off about 30 frames and I could not for the life of me see any difference so I just left it off. I think that the demo represents overall performance quite well so give that a go.

Overall, very good. It also has a demo, so this review is pointless because you can just try it for yourself :)

I gave a thumbs up because I honestly think with this new IP, Team Bloober is onto something, yet I honestly can't say it's totally worth it's full price. I would honestly wait for a sale.

The pacing stats off actually pretty good, easing you into it's style of gameplay and preparing you for later encounters. The atmosphere is fantastic, I truly love the idea of going through an anomaly ridden post apocalyptic area with no idea what is around any corner, and it's also a different country to what I've seen over and over (being USA.) Enemy design is pretty fantastic, and I love the idea that if you do not kill monsters fast enough or leave flesh bodies around, that they can absorb them to become stronger. The upgrade system for weapons is essentially just RE4's, but it's done pretty well here. Each weapon upgrade truly does give it so much more usefulness as you'd expect. Not making it too overpowered, but just strong enough to deal with everything you encounter and feel just perfect.

Though my problems with the game are vast. Your inventory is small, even after maxing out the slots which you can do over the course of the game, it's much to slow and the space needed for trying to carry everything is still too small, and the final upgrade for inventory space is near the end of the game. The slow pacing at the beginning of the game continues into the late game, which then feels more like it's dragging on for anything story and is slowly drip fed to you, and is honestly confusing until late game. The worst of which are the audio tapes and the spheres that give conversations of characters, you're essentially forced to stand still so as to concentrate on listening lest you lose track of what's going on, already slowing down the already slow pace. The game provides you with a low ammo count, hinting that you have to be smart with your ammo, lead enemies into traps, bunch them together for group kills, and charging your shots for maximum damage. Which at times is aggravating, but you're provided with enough ammo through the various areas and material to craft them, that it's actually not too much of a problem. Yet it leads back to it's issues with inventory space, as if you really wanted to grab everything, you'd be running back and fourth to the item box to store everything, which leads to so much backtracking that it becomes such a huge chore. Bosses all felt the same, at least for me. Just bullet sponges with the same sort of area, lead them here, use trap, shoot weak spot that shows up, which honestly just had each boss showing no real unique property with an exception of a couple of them. The game is also very linear, but has big areas you can easily get lost in. The game would honestly have been so much better if it simply had a map, which with the supposed technology in lore that you have, is actually a baffling feature to not have.

Team Bloober has something special, and this attempt is fairly middling, but if they can take from this and improve on it on their future games, then they can have something truly great. I REALLY wanted to love this game, I really did, but it's not quite there on the scale they wanted it. I personally feel this game is the definition of a 7/10, and that's being fairly generous.

Cronos: The New Dawn stands tall as an entry to the sci-fi genre, but falters slightly as a horror game.

Cronos, like many horror games, isn't scary but rather tense and atmospheric. Like with the Silent Hill 2 remake, Bloober succeeds in crafting a tangible atmosphere through great sound and level design, accentuated by the slow-burn pacing. However, the game never generates anything more than a slight feeling of unease. The idea of enemies merging with corpses and taking on their attributes is great but it should've been capitalized on more. Instead, the mechanic lacked any noticeable impact, limited by the lack of enemy variety and subpar AI. Enemies simply waltz towards you with little variation in their behavior. It retains the frustrating inventory management system and the lack of mobility of classic horror games, but lacks any in-depth puzzles standard to the genre. 

Otherwise, Cronos is a great game. The gunplay is slower than average, but the charging and fire mechanics makes it methodical and satisfying. Combined with the aforementioned tense atmosphere, it is always fun exploring the world and gunning down Orphans (thats what they're called I swear). 

The story hooks you in right away due to wanting to know more about how the world practically ended and the nature of The Vocation. The game does so well to establish the interesting time travel technology and lore without revealing too much all at once. Cronos excels with its art design, with the Traveler suits and relics being standouts. While Cronos is solid with caveats gameplay wise, it's creative design and gripping story allows it to stand along side it's inspirations as a a unique piece of sci-fi media. 

Overall, Cronos: The New Dawn is fun and deeply interesting. I'd say it is close to a must play for sci-fi fans and a decent recommendation for [i]patient[/i] horror fans.

Fans of Dead Space might wonder why no other studios have successfully replicated it, after all this time. Wonder no more. Cronos: The New Dawn is the best Dead Space imitation yet and a genuine spiritual successor. It is almost as good as Isaac Clarke’s first encounter with necromorphs but not a mere copy. It blends many themes together, from sci-fi movies to Bloober’s own games, and crafts a unique atmosphere and story that make it easy to recommend.

The game begins with you undergoing questioning inside a pod, ala the baseline tests in Blade Runner. After this, you enter a post-apocalyptic ash-covered wasteland that looks like The Upside Down in Stranger Things; a virus decimated humanity long ago and your mission, as a Traveler, is to enter time rifts and extract the minds of key people from the past to change the future, which draws comparisons to 12 Monkeys. You upload these minds and chat to them to find your next target. Like in Bloober’s [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1386900/Observer_System_Redux/]Observer[/url], these mind dives are interesting but could have been more prominent in the back half. Standing in your way are Orphans: mutated humans that shamble and slash, and try their best to merge with fellow corpses to become even tougher foes.

It has many intriguing story elements. The time rifts allow you to revisit the outbreak’s beginning, and you cross paths with characters trying to survive. There is an opportunity to discover more about your role, as you will come across voice logs by fallen Travelers. Some of your predecessors left traces in the form of outposts where you can save, store items, and buy supplies. One blemish of the narrative is that it has a lot of bland flavor text, especially early, but this becomes more appealing as it goes.

Players explore four main areas, including an apartment block, steelworks, and a hospital. All are awesome, with nice detail and side areas to search. The best is probably the hospital, which also has an element of anticipation. While not a unique setting, it is nicely crafted, suitably dangerous, and the perfect size. Like other areas, it has a central outpost you can return to as desired to take a breather, re-equip, or store items. Not that the game needs the player to control the pace, as the encounters, scares, puzzles, and narrative pieces blend wonderfully.

The atmosphere is one of the best and most consistent features. The mood is sublime, whether you are roaming across the barren future landscape, looking up at buildings torn apart by time rifts, or diving into an underground metro covered with pulsing biomass. One particular foe hangs in this biomass and will pull you in, but slowing down to carefully listen gives you a tactical edge. With the HUD disappearing when out of combat, it is easy to appreciate the setting. There are scares now and then too, which are a strength of Bloober following their [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1029890/Layers_of_Fear_2_2019/]Layers of Fear[/url] franchise, and some are definitely effective. It is also great that the game runs smoothly at near max settings, albeit with high quality upscaling enabled.

There is nothing crazy about the action; it is a solid experience that emphasizes many elements of the genre, such as limited inventory space, scarce resources, positioning, accuracy, and preparation via crafting, upgrades, and exploration. The weapons are reliable but a little boring, with a pistol, shotgun, and multi-shot carbine doing most of the killing. Some survival-horror genre tropes remain annoying, like not being able to collect bullets for the near-empty weapon you’re holding when the inventory is full. But item and resource management was usually not an annoyance.

The action sets itself apart with minor but crucial tweaks. The Orphans ability to merge, with ‘Don’t let them merge’ packing almost as much punch as ‘Cut off their limbs,’ does change how to play. You mentally note corpses, and keep track during battle to prevent any from getting stronger. Another slight tweak is that many weapons have charged modes which increases damage but takes time. Finally, an area-of-effect torch attack will burn corpses and stun Orphans, giving time to reload or run. Put this all together and the combat remains entertaining over the respectable 14 hour story.

Even though the Dead Space franchise is on an indefinite hiatus, we are lucky that Bloober have cooked up something quite similar with their latest release. It is the best game from the studio and the most gamey of all of their titles. With an intriguing story, solid combat, amazing atmosphere, and great pacing, it offers plenty. Some might see Cronos: The New Dawn as a mere blend of things that came before, but ignore such a merger at your peril.

[h1]Cronos: New Dawn – Review[/h1]
[b]“Dead Space walked so Cronos could traumatize me all over again.”[/b]

Pardon my French, but this is one F*****-up ride, in the best possible way. [i]Cronos: New Dawn[/i] feels like the long-lost cousin of Dead Space: less cold vacuum, more rust and dust, but even with a touch of screwed up gravity.

The fighting is deliberately slow, setting a grim, deliberate pace. The fact that you [i]don’t[/i] run by default feels like a statement, it's a bloody marathon it is. Movement and melee attacks took me straight back to Dead Space territory, and honestly, there’s no shame in stealing with pride. Every swing, reload, and stomp feels heavy and mean, like you’re punishing the floor for existing. It’s got that same grim satisfaction as turning Necromorphs into intergalactic stew.

Monster design is delightful in its depravity. Twitching limbs, wrong-way faces, exploding gas babies — because of course there are. It’s not subtle, but it is gloriously gory, and whats with the excessive amount of arms.

The story starts out confusing, but somewhere between the screams and too many arms, a red thread starts to appear. The sound design is what stands out for me.  The creaks, the hissing, the quiet breathing when you thought you were alone… it’s an anxiety symphony. Not innovative, but brilliantly executed. As a self-proclaimed horror connoisseur, I’ll admit: I jumped. More than once.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Highlights[/h2]
→ The slow, weighty combat perfectly fits the horror — every hit matters, every miss hurts.
→ The sound design is phenomenal, not just immersive, but downright cruel.
→ Puzzles give you just enough to add variation in the game play.
→ Weapon design is standard (maybe not a highlight), but upgrading them feels rewarding.
→ Linearity works in its favor, forward momentum keeps the tension alive. This is not an exploration game.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]But...[/h2]
• Inventory management is unnecessary annoying, like paperwork in purgatory.
• The story occasionally wanders off before it remembers where it was going.
• The inspirations are a little too obvious, sometimes it feels like Dead Space without the space.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
Cronos: New Dawn doesn’t reinvent horror, but it absolutely understands it. It’s tense, cruel, and relentlessly atmospheric, a grounded, blood-soaked echo of its spiritual predecessors. It won’t blow you away; it’ll drag you through the dark, kicking, swearing, and after the initial mental comparison you might even end up loving it.

After Silent Hill 2 Remake I was looking forward to this new IP, though I was also a bit skeptical about Bloober’s ability to deliver a strong original game. Their stories are usually well written, but the gameplay often ends up feeling flat or uninspired.

I’m happy to say that I’m really enjoying Cronos: The New Dawn. The setting is fascinating: it takes place in Nowa Huta (New Steelworks), a real district in Kraków with a rich history tied to the socialist dream, years of neglect, and periods of unrest. Pairing that backdrop with the quarantine caused by the disease immediately struck a chord with me, since it echoes the feelings many of us had during the COVID lockdowns. The tension between wanting to break free and being confronted with the aftermath of the outbreak makes the story especially engaging.

On top of that, the mystery of who you are and what your true goals are is well written, and I’m genuinely curious to see how it unfolds. The combat is fun too: it’s straightforward, but the mechanic where enemies can grow stronger by absorbing corpses adds real tension. Every encounter ends up feeling like a mini hardpoint defense, where smart positioning matters if you don’t want to get overwhelmed by an OP enemy.

PLAY THIS GAME! This game fucken rips! It's so under-appreciated! Do not understand why it's not more well-reviewed.

Especially play this game if you loved: Signalis, the original Resident Evil games, the RE2 remake, Silent Hill 2 remake, The Evil Within 2, or Alien Isolation. In other words, this is one of those rare slow, tense, survival horror games about careful resource management. 

On top of that, this game has OBSCENELY good environmental art, low-key some amazing voice acting, and some excellent writing. Some people don't connect with the plot, but if you like mysteries-within-mysteries and meditative sci-fi about big themes this is for you. The plot stumbles a bit at the end, but it's still worth it all-told.

The quick TLDR is: it's a solid, but somewhat bland, horror, third-person shooter. A quick score would put it at a 6.5/10 (above average - good). 
If you like Survival Horror/Horror Action (it has difficulties picking which one it wants to be), then it's still worth a playthrough if you're hungering for a game and it's on sale. 

I did enjoy my time with it, but in my playthrough I was wishing it was better than actually it is, since the core movement and shooting felt great. The visuals are great. The enemies are basic, but felt nice to shoot. However in the end the overall package was just kinda by-the-numbers bland. 

This left me somewhat disappointed because it does the basics pretty damn well, but there's nothing too special to make it stand out from the other, more better acclaimed games in the genre. 
Also I had plenty of resources throughout the entire game. I've seen other people complain about the ammo count, but I basically had a small armoury throughout. No idea if the devs made the game easier or I'm just too used to these kind of games.

The real issue I have with the game is that the level design is incredibly linear, but the slower paced gameplay feels like it needs a more open/Resident Evil 1 type level design. 
Especially since it has a limited inventory, which does nothing other than be annoying. You're not making any meaningful decisions on route planning, or what items to take because the game is a line bar the odd optional offshoot for items. So it's restricting you just for the sake of it. There's nothing stopping you (most of the time) to run back down the line you ran up to put stuff away. It just adds needless travel time if you care about loot.

The shooting is your basic third-person style seen in many other modern survival horror games, but at a slower, more deliberate pace, with nothing else going for it outside of the focus on charged shots (the charged shots are quite nice, I do like them). 
Which is fine, I like the slower pace, but the game turns into a shooting gallery with explosive barrels galore, so what's the point of trying for the slower gameplay if you're constantly locking me into combat arenas with explosives everywhere?

The game seems to have an identity crisis on what kind of horror game it wanted to be. Survival horror, or action horror. And currently it sits in this awkward middle ground where it satisfies neither too well. This is where my disappointment comes from. 

The story is fine, it starts interesting but it did lose me as it went on. I feel like it tried too much and by the end I stopped caring. Interesting ideas, but the execution didn't fully land for me. 

Overall like I said at the start, if you're a horror fan it's worth a try on a good sale, and I do wish Bloober Team luck on their future projects. They had the basics down, but Cronos: The New Dawn wasn't quite there in closing it out.

What a banger of a game.

I didn't expect much when I first started it, but I really liked it and found myself at work looking forward to getting home to continue. You can tell it took inspiration from both Dead Space and Resident Evil games, which are still some of the best survival horrors to this day, while doing its own thing.
Starting with the gameplay: It has the same feel as the tank controls in earlier Resident Evil games. You're slow, yeah, but so are the enemies. It makes sense since you're a lass wearing 300+ lbs of pure steel armor and a goofy iron dome helmet. You gotta play ahead, if you know what I mean. Avoiding attacks is about telegraphing and paying attention to enemy animations before you pull the trigger. When you shoot, you hit hard! This comes through with charged shots, screen shake, sound, and controller vibration—it all feels just right. A well-placed shot stuns enemies, letting you follow up with melee attacks. Flame blasts and pyre grenades are also tools to stun a horde surrounding you. There are plenty of ways to become a force to be reckoned with in this game.

Encounters feel handcrafted, no RNG in levels, and you can tell. Surviving an ambush by blasting through a bunch of monsters and slaughtering them into a gory pile on the floor had me like, "Goddamn! I clutched it." That made me look forward to encounters because it felt so good to survive them when done right.

And to do that preparation is key. Resources are limited, especially early on, and inventory space is tight. There were moments of tough decisions: to progress, you need key items, and key items take up inventory space. Drop ammo? Let go of a pyre grenade or a flame canister? It's hard because you might need them, and you will need them. Backtracking became an annoying thing in this game. You store important items to grab a key, and running back and forth between a locked door and a checkpoint to get a key or bolt cutter I stored—because I wasn’t using it—became a common chore. But that’s just me, and you may not mind it. Checkpoints are mercifully placed and well-paced throughout the game. When I felt I was struggling, seeing doors with green lights was a relief. A moment to catch my bearings, restock, upgrade, and move on.

There are plenty of hidden doors, rooms, and secrets. If you explore, you get nice trinkets as rewards; not just useless stuff, but actual optional weapons and upgrades to existing weapons that will make your job easier.
As for the story, I wasn’t super interested at first, but with each log, document, and audio recording I found, it started to get intriguing. Who am I? What’s going on? Who are the travelers? Are they human? Some nice twists at the end and a few different endings made the story enjoyable overall.

Performance-wise, it ran really well. It’s surprising to see an UE5 game run so smoothly; this game is well-optimized. I could enjoy it from beginning to end without stopping to tweak graphics settings due to frame drops. It actually ran much better than Silent Hill 2, the previous game from Bloober Team.

I highly recommend this game. It’s interesting, with strong gameplay, excellent level design, a great story, beautiful visuals, and overall a solid survival horror experience.

Really solid survival horror entry from Bloober. It doesn't necessarily innovate much with combat and gameplay mechanics, taking a lot from Resident Evil, which is actually fine. What distinguishes it from the rest is definitely the setting and locations chosen - those are very strong and for the majority of the game they ramp up in all the right ways. As someone who is familiar with the real life places the action happens (and you can find at least 4 of the main inspirations in Cracow - the home city of Bloober) the locations visited in game added a lot of extra atmosphere and fun. But even without that aspect, the world crafted from an amalgamation of body/space horror and 1981-1988 Cracow presents a very strong reason to play the game.

From the technical standpoint it's impressive for an AA game and some of the use of lighting is top notch and RTX gives some bang for your buck - however I had to enable DLSS to have smoother framerate as it sometimes chops, like a lot of UE5 games. Also, unless you are really good with shooting using controller, I would strongly recommend keyboard and mouse.

Briefly on difficulty/gameplay - the game has decent variety in arsenal and passives to choose from, although acquisition of both is quite stretched out throughout all the game chapters - to really have fun with the variety you will have to touch NG+. The balance of resources/ammo scarcity is quite impressive and very well fine tuned - it was always never too much, never too little. The game is challenging and there is no easy mode, but from my experience not to the extent that would cross into annoying or tedious.

As far as the story goes, at some point it seemingly pivots into an unexpected direction, but by the end once you think about what happened and piece it all together it does make sense. Very much similar to movie [spoiler]12 Monkeys[/spoiler]. Overall it is intriguing and keeps you going smoothly.

Now, some negatives. I think most of them are down to this being an AA game that punches above its weight at Resident Evils and alike. Something you will notice is that after about halfway of the game there is less "new" monsters - altered versions of some you've seen before but by that point you should be familiar with most types. 
The worst part of the game are bossfights - the game reuses same/very similar a boss and a mechanic upwards of 4 times and another boss you will run into two times. There is only one "real" unique boss in the game, quite far into the playtime.

Overall, worth a recommendation - the locations, setting, lore and exploration are very fun and the game is worth the money asked in my eyes. A must if you are a fan of survival shooters or live in Nowa Huta :D

[h1]Hopefully the Dawn of a New Horror Franchise[/h1]
What a thrill ride this was. Bloober have outdone themselves with what is not only the best original game they’ve ever made, but the most exciting new horror IP since the original Dead Space. Part John Carpenter’s The Thing, part 12 Monkeys, this title is full of creativity and incredible game design. If you call yourself a fan of horror in any capacity, you need to buy this game ASAP.

You play as The Traveler, an agent of a mysterious and seemingly alien entity known as “The Collective”. You are sent to Poland after a horrifying outbreak has turned seemingly all of humanity into assimilated biomass with the only remaining things that resemble people being these incredibly hostile fleshy zombie abominations that hate fire. Throughout the games handful of “dungeons”, let’s just call them for the sake of this review, you will eventually time travel to the beginnings of the infection that turned Poland into US Outpost 31. Here you will retrace your steps through areas you just explored, and see them full of life again. The Collective sends you to these points in time to “extract” a human target that is useful for them gaining knowledge about the disease. This element of the game remained fresh and captivating all the way up until the finale. What caused the outbreak? Who is your character? What is The Collective and why do they want these targets extracted? It may take a few play throughs to fully piece together all its mysteries, but it’s a very rewarding plot line to follow that delivers in big ways during the rare moments of narrative or character development. I also want to give a shoutout to the lead actress who played The Traveler, she did a phenomenal job. However, this isn’t a game you’ll be primarily playing for the story, you’re going to be playing it for the incredibly rich level design and horror combat sandbox.

Cronos immediately gets mad props for bringing back the corpse burning mechanic from Resident Evil Remake. The Crimson Head system from RE1 Remake is one of the most genius ideas ever developed in a horror game and practically no game recycles it. Or if they do, they do it in a context that’s not interesting. Cronos has enemies that will consume the corpses of their fallen brethren and this will morph them into far deadlier versions of what you fought before. They’ll gain armor and health, do more damage, and become far more aggressive. To avoid this you have to burn corpses of fallen enemies, but you have nowhere near enough to do this to all of them so you have to be aware of enemies trying to merge with each other. Not only does this add to the believability of these mutated beings merging into one biomass, but it also adds a wicked level of tension to every encounter. Torches are scarce so using one for I-frames as a mini boss is attacking you or burning bodies of fallen foes is an important decision to make constantly. This decision wouldn't be interesting if the game flooded you with ammo and supplies and thankfully it doesn’t. Cronos is more action packed than the old Resident Evil titles, but it is far more reserved than something like Resident Evil 4. The strategy in a lot of survival horror games is to run past enemies to avoid wasting ammo on fodder enemies. In this game, roughly 80% of enemies and enemy encounters really are mandatory unless you perfect the movement for a speedrun or something. This isn’t a game where enemies will let you run by them. They chase you and lunge at you and constantly appear. So you’re going to be doing a lot of shooting and you have to make your shots count. You do this by charging up your guns for high damage before firing them, and also by taking advantage of explosive canisters. And because this is a game with time travel, some red barrels can be rewound in time to before you shot them so you can use them again. So cool!

What backs this up is some terrific level design. Again, not as sprawling or as maze like as classic Resident Evil, but far more detailed than something like most action horror games. Many times I would have to do the walk of shame back to the item box to dump stuff off from my insanely small inventory and grab a pair of bolt cutters to open a chained door I just found. Half the time I wouldn’t be able to carry everything in the locked room in one visit because… again, the inventory is so small. Keys take up as much space as ammo which take up as much space as each individual weapon in your arsenal. Some are annoyed by this but I love it for that old school horror rush. Gaining shortcuts in this game that led back to save rooms gave me euphoria I haven’t felt since the early Souls game by Fromsoftware. By the end of the title, I felt like I had truly conquered this game, both its enemies and its level design.

The game looks pretty damn good even at low or medium settings and ran flawlessly on my steam deck. Had two crashes on my gaming rig ironically, but I was able to jump right back in afterwards. The game is sadly an Unreal Engine product, so performance problems are inevitable, but a team of this size likely isn't going to be using an in house engine so I’m just grateful the game ran with fewer bugs than most games that are twice the budget of this one. Nice job guys 👍 

My only complaint is that once you finish the game, you unlock New Game + and hard mode. NG+ is pretty much the same game but with all your guns and upgrades, and Hard mode is just increased damage to you from enemies with fewer auto saves. Shame there wasn't a Hardcore or Madhouse style mode that changed up enemies and added traps and stuff.

Overall this is a must play for horror fans. Really solid atmosphere and gameplay that keeps the tension high.

-----
*Since someone asked me why I felt the gameplay was similar to RE2, here it is:

[list]
[*]Slow paced, horror oriented gameplay - you're put in these creepy, nerve racking locations. The tension slowly builds while you expect an enemy just around the corner. I personally found Cronos to be scarier than RE2.
[*]Circular style of unlocking areas - when you first enter a new location you encounter multiple locked doors you cannot enter immediately. You basically end up with one path you can visit that circles back around to where you started, but on the way you find the items/keys/number codes that now allow you to unlock the previously locked areas. This sometimes also creates shortcuts to make traversal faster.
[*]Combat - different kind of weapons to use for different situations/enemies, the health system is very similar. After clearing an area you generally don't need to clear it again (there's some exceptions just like in RE2). Cronos has a charge weapon system which makes it a bit different, and of course the enemies merge to become stronger, but other than that the combat feels similar to that of RE2.
[*]Inventory systems - you need to decide what to bring with you, how much ammo and what to leave behind in the safe room chest, which btw works exactly like in RE2. You can also upgrade your inventory space as you progress through the game.
[*]Crafting systems - you pick up crafting items and you have multiple recipes you can use, depending on how you want to play or the situation at hand.
[*]Puzzles to some extent - they're much more basic in Cronos, and this kind of puzzles where you examine items doesn't exist. Still, it's somewhat reminiscent.
[/list]

Sort of scratches the itch if you're looking for something similar to Dead Space.  Main VA did a phenomenal job, aesthetic of the game is extremely cold, mechanical, and harsh.  Fun to play.  Bloober Team still has not learned how to tell their own story without a horrific over-reliance on tropes - especially EVERYONE writing EVERYTHING on notes.  Bloober, seriously, if you take anything from this game, learn to do environmental storytelling.  Letters and notes CAN be interesting but not when they feel so artificial and inauthentic as this.  Get it on sale, $40 and below is reasonable for this.

+ You can pet cats and they give you gifts in return and then they all hang out in your safe room!

+ Visually, the game impresses with accomplished use of UE5's core rendering features. There is copious small-scale detail everywhere, lighting and shadows paint a moody, creepy post-apocalypse and volumetric fog abounds to enhance the atmosphere even more. The art direction for the environments is superb with the communist influence on the architecture perfectly meshing with sci-fi desolation.

- I wish the Orphans had a more unique design though, they look very much like the sort of merged bio-mass mutants you encounter in sci-fi horror everywhere. They're too safe visually, too lacking in design features that stretch the imagination.

+ The initial parts of the story deal mainly with cryptic world-building and larger scale elements like the Collective, the Change and the Travellers, typical "The Noun" story-telling tropes, but that happen to actually be interesting.

- The latter bits take a surprising turn to a much more personal, intimate story, but one that I also feel is very tired and out of place. It also allows the writers' more "orthodox" views on mental health, suicidal ideation and abuse to rear their heads just a bit, probably not enough to break the story since most people won't even notice them, but enough to dissapoint me at least.

+ Easily the best part of the game is the combat though. It's slow, yet precise and very tactical; it requires constant positional and situational awareness from you, so you can use the various explosive barrels scattered throughout the levels to your advantage. And if you meet the combat and encounter design half-way, you'll have a much easier time managing ammo, resources and inventory, the game not actually being that scarce with them. Weapons feel good to use and there's a solid upgrade system in place that by the end make you feel pretty powerful. 

+ Complementing the combat is some really good level-design. The game is linear, sure, but the paths you traverse are neatly intertwined and shortcuts are always fun to discover, which makes exploration quite engaging. On top of that, environments still feel like believable places, relics and ruins of Poland before the end of the world. Some elements, like the gravity defying sections might be a tiny bit out of place, but at least traversing them is pretty fun. Exploration is also rewarding, with plenty of resources to fuel your upgrades to be found, new weapons and a lot of lore collectables.

+ The score features some really appropriate eerie synth tunes that fit the environments and some of the cut-scenes very nicely.

* The game runs reasonably well, some frame-rate dips when the game streams data during traversal, but combat and tense moments remain unaffected. 

- Voice acting is pretty poor overall and fails to sell dramatic moments. Significant dip in quality compared to Silent Hill 2 Remake.

While the sight of a small inventory where ammo, weapons, and key items took up space all the same had me intrigued at first, in practice you aren't going to be doing ''Resident Evil'' much in this game. The areas are fairly small, mostly linear with 1 or 2 diverting paths that usually leads to some bonus resources.

The combat is neat, I liked the weapon design. Basically the tri-fecta of Pistol, Shotgun and Rifle and each having 2 variants, one based on charging shots and another trading the charge mechanic for a quicker approach.
The enemies however leave a bit to be desired. Given their supposed origin in the plot, it's rather disappointing that they are visually indistinct. A humanoid mutant with a tentacle arm. Sometimes they are fat or spit acid, but the silhouette remains similiar. There are some that fall out outside of it but they are too infrequent imo. Some enemies are also armored on certain bodyparts but the colour palette of pale grey flesh and slightly more grey scales doesn't communicate it well.

Now the one mechanic that kind of let me down the most, one which they even advertise as a unique feature on their store page. ''Merging''. Enemies can use the corpses of others to merge with them, basically leveling up in their enemy class, which is why you are given a fire sidearm that lets you burn corpses and set enemies on fire which burns their corpse  automatically should you kill them during the burn phase.
It sounds like a neat idea on paper, but in practice I almost never had to use this. Enemies signal when they are going to merge and basically tunnel vision to the nearest corpse and ignore you in the meantime. ANY damage can knock them out of that state and they virtually never try again to merge. When a new Bloober games comes out, I will jump on it as close to day 1 as I can. I really enjoyed The Medium and Silent Hill 2 Remake. Cronos delivered for me in some aspects, but failed in some others. 

What I liked: 
* It's horror. Definitely horror. It's so atmospheric and scary. 
* The story is compelling. The lore is really well-delivered through documents and voice recordings. Voice acting is great. 
* Exploration is fun. I like to try to see if I can find all items (while playing blind). This time around it's cats. It's such a relief to hear a sweet miauw instead of a scary boo. 
* The enemies merging is a fun mechanic. It's not as nerve-wrecking towards the middle of the game as it is in the beginning. 
* The music is really creepy and fits the game perfectly. 
* Ultimately, the question the game poses I really liked. The final decision really made me think. I don't know if I went for the best option, but it felt right. 

What I didn't like: 
* There are some cheap "grab this item and get grabbed and hurt by an enemy" moments. 
* It's survival horror alright. I ran out of ammo many times. I'm not a very expert shooter, but I feel I did pretty well. Credits (to buy stuff) are everywhere but ammo and healing not so much. 
* Weapons take up inventory space, so you can't really carry a full loadout.
* No dodge. No quick turn. Just clompy stomping, which makes avoiding enemy attacks really hard.
* There are a few encounters that felt really frustrating to me with the combat limitations the game presents. Overall it was doable, but especially the final boss battle left me shaking. I retried it (only) three times, but it felt frustrating because you'd want your character to be able to do more. 

Overall, I really like that they created a new game with a new story. They built a compelling Soviet Poland, which wasn't necessarily "fun" to explore but it was enticing. I can't wait for Bloober's next game. Even though it wasn't a game of the year for me, I really do enjoy their storytelling.

After 15.8 hours I have completed my playthrough of Cronos The New Dawn and I must say, this game surprised me! I had an amazing adventure through the world of Cronos that was filled with a bunch of pros and cons, so lets go over them.

PROS:

Graphics - Cronos is gorgeous. Literally, every aspect of this game is incredible looking. From the locations, to the enemies, to the player characters and NPC's, everything is highly detailed, fits the world and is truly fantastic to look at. I kept taking screenshots as I was playing through the game because I couldn't believe how good it looked. 

Level Design - This game features fantastic level design. Truly so much to explore, shortcuts to find, vertical leveling with the gravity boots, it has it all. As you explore the areas and find secret rooms, collectibles (theres alot) etc, multiple weapons. Truly great design.

Sound Design - This game features fantastic sound design which is extremely neccessary for a horror game. The simple yet detailed sounds that keep you on edge as you explore the world are fantastic. The music is great as well (think stranger things style music) and overall its done beautifully.

Gameplay - Cronos features fantastic gameplay. It truly brings survival horror to the forefront. This is not an action game in the slightest. It has moments where it can "feel" action, but you are barely given any ammo, have limited weaponry and must strategize almost every encounter. The enemies who are living will absorb other enemies who are dead or killed turning them into super enemies if you allow them to, so you must always be on edge. A great upgrade system for your weapons and suit, similiar to dead space. Fantastic bosses that are fun and challenging (especially the last two). The enviornment also plays a huge factor in this game and how you approach enemies. Overall the gameplay is solid and I enjoyed it.

Enemy Design - As mentioned in gameplay, Cronos features some pretty fun badass enemies. They are admittingly limited in scope, but thats because they can transform if you dont play effectively. Theres enough enemies here in variety to make it super fun without getting dull. 

Weapon Design - The weapons in the game are super fun. They have 2 modes of fire each usually, resulting in different strategies you can use with them. You wont be able to upgrade every weapon in one playthrough, so choose your upgrades wisely. 

Story - Cronos has a very interesting, very ambigious story that will keep you hooked all the way to the end. You can make choices in the game that will effect your outcome, so this is a narrative experience that can be played multiple times for different endings which increases replayability. 

CONS:

Inventory System - So this game is a true survival horror, it has limited inventory, limited resources. Nothing wrong with this at all. Whats wrong is how extreme it goes with it at the start of the game, almost forcing you to choose inventory space upgrade with your suit cores first over anything else. It removes the choice from the player because otherwise, you will be extremely limited. Also, the game has valuables you can sell that you pick up through the world, but you can only sell it at the save areas. The problem with is, by the time you reach the save area, you will probably have had to get rid of the valuable to make space for something more important to your gameplay before reaching the station. It can be pretty dam annoying at the start of the game, almost too annoying. I managed to get through it with relative ease, but I felt like my choices as a player was made for me, instead of the other way around if that makes sense. 

Horrible Turn Speed - So the main character is obviously in a heavy suit of armor, i get this. Shes going to be very slow. The problem is shes extremely slow, even with maximum mouse turn speed, she is turning slower than anything ive ever seen. Even in dead space it was not this bad and I never had to up my mouse turn to max for that game. This game I am at maximum turn and it feels like i didnt change anything. If you are trying to sell the idea of a tanky slow main character fine, but its frustrating as a mouse and keyboard player to feel that level of slowness when you have an option to increase it and it barely does anything. 

The map system - The GPS system in this game tries to be similiar to dead space, but it doesnt give you a blue trajectory line. It actually doesnt give you anything other than the mark at the top of the compass showing you a general direction. The system is pretty bad to be honest, i would rather there be almost no system because it really doesnt help you much in the game. There is no actual map, so i just personally wish they went all in on a no map style game. Regardless, small con. 

Over reliance on horror tropes: So after having played a couple of games from Blooper, i can confidently say they overly rely on jump scares and horror tropes. This game didnt feel scary at all very much. It was super predictable in every aspect of the horror and more so felt like a psychological thriller than anything else. This game and their jump scares is freaking ridiculous. Towards the end they start spamming it and im just sitting here like...dude stop it thats dumb and predictable. Blooper NAILS the setting, the music, the atmosphere but when it comes to the horror, they play it safe, no risks and very little real fear. 

Overall Cronos is still an incredible game and a fun experience that I might want to do one more play through of just to get a little more. I highly recommend it based on the above pros and cons in its current form at the time of the review.

What I Loved (Pros):

Atmosphere is Stunning: This is the absolute highlight. The world is incredibly dense, oppressive, and immersive. It's worth playing for the mood alone.

Smart Ammo Scarcity: No mindless shooting here. You are forced to search everything, which makes exploration tense and rewarding.

Story Makes You Think: The lore is super cryptic and constantly throws questions at you. You have to piece a lot together yourself, but the twists and turns are genuinely compelling.

Weapons Feel Great: The guns have a satisfying punch, and the alternate fire modes or charged shots bring a refreshing new dynamic to the gameplay.

Performance: Running with DLSS was super solid. Hardly any stutters; it ran smoothly almost all the time.

What Was Just Okay (Neutrals):

Heavy Reading: If you truly want to understand the lore, you'll have to read an extensive amount. It got a bit tedious at times.

Slow Pace: The game is quite deliberate and slow. It's probably not for adrenaline junkies. You have to be in the mood for it.

The "Merging" Feature: It was a cool idea, but used way too little. A lot of potential was left on the table here.

What Annoyed Me (Cons):

Low Variety: The level structures and enemies sadly repeat too often. After a while, it starts to feel like "the same thing, just in a different room."

The level structure also lets you too often predict what happens next e.g. boss rooms, horde rooms, or this freakin wall spitters are easily spottable and often will not surprise you.

Wasted Polish Setting: You barely notice you're in Poland. No cool, distinctly Polish vibes. The setting just doesn't shine through.

Verdict:

I still had a lot of fun despite the issues. The fantastic atmosphere and the story completely sucked me in. It's not an absolute must-buy, but definitely a solid choice for anyone who loves deep lore and thick atmosphere.

For a sequel, my wishlist is: More Merging! And please, please, more enemy variety!

Mechanically, the game is quite simple, and the combat even more so: aim and shoot. But it quickly becomes more engaging thanks to the variety of weapons you can find. Each one has its own personality and almost all of them feature a charged shot that adds a bit even more variety to combat. The atmosphere is, without a doubt, one of the strongest aspects of the game. Narrow corridors keep you tense and on edge, while some larger open areas filled with item crates clearly signal that a fight is about to happen. The sound design also deserves special mention — unsettling in the best way possible, reinforcing the game’s horror tone. The story is mysterious and layered. It doesn’t hand you everything on a silver platter, instead encouraging you to piece together the narrative through audiologs, letters, and flashbacks. [spoiler] (Yes, it’s all about time travel and paradoxes — and it’s fantastic). [/spoiler]

Exploring the world of Cronos is rewarding. Beyond resources like ammo and crafting materials, you’ll also find energy (the game’s currency) and valuable items to sell. And despite the heavy tension, exploring never feels like a chore — it just pulls you in deeper.

I wrapped up my first playthrough in just over 15 hours, and I’m already itching to dive into NG+ to chase down the collectibles and achievements I missed. All in all, Cronos is a solid game. Fun, properly challenging, and if you enjoy titles like Dead Space, you’ll almost certainly enjoy this one too.

Cronos: The New Dawn feels like Bloober's most ambitious project, seeping with confidence and being a testament to their dedication for the survival horror genre. After years of criticism and repulsiveness this studio has endured, this is the game that shows what they’ve learned from both their past mistakes and also the pressure, expectations, and eventually successes from their Silent Hill 2 Remake. Of course, older titles such as The Medium or The Observer gave them all the right directions, and all of that dedication led us here.

You play as The Traveler. An unknown, menacingly looking resemblance of a human, yet unsure of what lies beyond the suit. Set in socialist Poland in the 1980s, a very unique setting that's fairly unexplored in the genre, you'll be given plenty of retro-futuristic vibes, a perfect blend of eras that somehow just works like it was always meant to be. The cold and industrial environment will make you uncomfortable, unsure of what lies behind the next corner. It's a breath of fresh air compared to the usual locations within the genre, like mansions or prisons, but this alone isn't enough to shape the game's identity.

The game starts very slow and sluggish, before any actual action happens. The action will keep ramping up, though, but once the game reaches its peak, it stays in that one spot. It never drops in quality, but there also isn't anything new to push the game higher. This "safe space" leads to feeling of repetitiveness and slow burn, because there’s only so much that the survival horror genre can offer in its runtime, so making games longer than they should’ve been with barely anything new to spice it up leads to some rather dull moments.

The Traveler’s knowledge creates an early disconnect between the protagonist and the player. The character knows more than you do, which raises a lot of questions, and when you seem to catch up to The Traveler and start discovering things together, the game throws at you more hidden knowledge, so you never feel like you belong there in a sense as a player, because you're constantly being kept in the dark. 

Still, when it works, it really works. Notes are written excellently, each one unique, and exciting to read, providing meaningful worldbuilding that gives you glimpses of what the world used to be before and during the disease. The environmental storytelling is equally as strong. Gameplay itself feels like an amalgamation of Resident Evil 4 and Dead Space. I'd even argue this is a better spiritual successor to Dead Space than The Callisto Protocol ever was. Resource management is one of the best I’ve ever seen in the genre. Every shot counts, every decision matters, and there are no difficulty options. You deal with what you’re given. It's all very reminiscent of RE: Code Veronica, and I mean this as a compliment. Monster design is fantastic. They're disturbing, grotesque, and often being made of multiple body parts that creates unnerving body horror. Unfortunately, the variety doesn't hold up for long. The first few hours put all cards on table, and by the halfway point you’ve seen it all. The merging mechanic where enemies combine into something bigger sounds terrifying on paper, but it rarely feels like a threat. It's very easy to prevent them from doing that if you play as you're expected, meaning being cautious and managing your resources properly. It only becomes dangerous when you're careless and let it happen too often, to the point when the enemies basically become bulletproof with only a small weak point. Exploration is fun but occasionally tedious. Compared to other games, there isn't any real backtracking, other than the bolt cutters. This is by far the biggest rigamarole in the game. They take up precious inventory space, so you’ll find yourself wasting time running back and forth just to take them out of your safehouse and immediately put back in, and it feels like almost an necessary action, as those secret spots provide much needed resources. Things such as sections with gravity shoes don’t expand the game’s dynamics, they just add simple platforming, never doing anything creative with it like Dead Space’s zero-gravity encounters. The upgrade system is pretty good and straightforward but lacks any visual sense of progression which is a little disappointing. Your armor and weapons look the same from start to finish, minus the story-based attachments you find along the way.

Environment isn't reactive at all either, there's barely any interaction with objects, everything is made of static props, which is somehow very common in modern games and it's extremely lazy. It's disconnecting players from the game and breaking immersion that used to be a norm many years ago. Squeeze-through passages, that once used to load areas, are now placed randomly and most of the time serve zero purpose. Compared to their Silent Hill 2 Remake, there are things that Cronos adapted and fleshed out, but more things were downgraded, and one of the biggest issues is character animations. They are very puppet-like, stiff and exaggerated, and cannot be taken seriously. Those little details and body language of SH2R are nowhere to be found, because all the characters feel cartoonish. Unreal Engine 5 once again proves to be both a blessing and a curse. Crashes, inconsistent framerate, weird stutters, even on a 4090 it struggles to maintain stable framerate, and relying on framegen to make the game playable should be objectively unacceptable. The game doesn't recognize localized keyboard buttons for weapon swapping, and there's incredibly weird and sluggishly slow mouse acceleration, even on maxed out sensitivity in game, both problems that were NOT present in SH2R.

Overall, I'm happy for Bloober trying again, they really put their motto "Horror is in our blood" to practice, which is true. They know and understand the genre like the back of their hand, they know what survival horror means to players, and they respect the inspirations. But they're not good writers and not very good at making original IPs. I don't want to say they can't come up with original ideas, because that's not necessarily true, but they're bad at evolving these mechanics beyond their original use. This is one of their biggest weaknesses, how they'd rather stay in a safe space with mechanics that worked for other games, rather than evolving those ideas and making them their own.

I do hope this game is successful enough to get a prequel or sequel, because there is a lot ofambiguity in the story set up for something bigger. Timelines, The Collective, essences and origin of the virus, there are a lot of things to be resolved, but all Cronos does is that it leaves those unanswered questions lingering in the air. Hopefully Bloober listens to fan feedback and Cronos 2 will be better, because there is a lot of potential. The path is paved, all they need to do is grow more confident with their decisions, rather than *merging* ideas.

Such is our calling.
