Ghosts in the Machine is perhaps the most fitting synopsis of Cronos: The New Dawn, which follows a mysterious being known as ND-3476, The Traveler, who awakens with a core mission objective to seek out and extract historical figures of significance to The Collective. A best hits album of sorts to the survival horror genre, Cronos: The New Dawn has influences clearly on display from Resident Evil, Silent Hill, and Dead Space, while still managing to have an identity entirely its own. 


The narrative of Cronos: The New Dawn is as compelling as it is cryptic, as The Traveler is awakes in a strange location known as The Terminal, which exists to store the "essences" of people of significance to The Collective's mission. At some point in the far past, a virus or similarly strange mutation began to spread throughout humanity. While its origin was unknown, its symptoms were always fatal, characterized by a highly malleable cellular structures, which would fuse with other organic life. At some point in the far future, technology is developed which is capable of sending Travelers back in time, to extract the minds of significant figures, to join a sort of hybrid collective consciousness. Cronos: The New Dawn draws a lot of parables to communism, with the outbreak taking place in a similar environment to communist regimes of the 1980's, much of which is conveyed through journal entries. The Traveler is but one "Vocation" assigned to beings spread throughout time, and so The Traveler soon encounters The Warden, who is tasked with repairing The Terminal. The two work together with the ambition of saving humanity, one essence at a time. 


There is an overarching theme at play of determinism, both in the roles assigned to people, and the control (or lack thereof) on fate. The Traveler delivers her lines with a cool robotic cadence, which elevates the experience of assuming the role of a being wholly driven by their mission. One aspect that is particularly interesting is that as The Traveler collects the essences of past humans, they begin to be influenced by their consciousnesses, sometimes hallucinating imagery or voices. In my brief experience, it seemed to be that these hallucinations varied from essence to essence, depending on which were collected throughout the course of the game, with some of them relating to one another in interesting ways, only evidenced through environmental story telling.


The gameplay of Cronos: The New Dawn feels most mechanically similar to Resident Evil 2 & 3 Remakes, with The Traveler beginning their journey with only a humble pistol. As The Traveler progresses, they can find new weaponry, most of which have a primary and secondary mode of firing. In combat, enemies, Orphans, shamble about, though a few are fast moving, or climb across the walls, leading to enjoyable gameplay moments when The Traveler is frantically running around an area, dodging and shooting Orphans. Cronos: The New Dawn, rewards skilled gameplay, with advanced enemies being partially armored, making aiming more important. Orphans have an interesting mechanic, wherein they can fuse with the corpses of their fallen comrades, to become even stronger. However, similar to early Resident Evil games, burning the corpses will prevent them from becoming fused. 

There are many satisfying ways this comes together in combat, as enemies become vulnerable during attempted fusions, which can occasionally provide a strategic incentive towards baiting them into a trap. Fire is also a powerful offensive element, causing enemies to stop in their tracks, providing an ideal moment for targeting weak points, or taking out a hoard at once. Resource management feels very fulfilling, with Cronos: The New Dawn being a bit sparing with ammo drops early in the game, incentivizing The Traveler to craft their own ammo, and avoid situations which would let them take damage. However, late game the tables turn, as The Traveler enhances their equipment, and suit, eventually becoming a walking death machine.

Cronos: The New Dawn, was a very enjoyable survival horror experience, which is an easy recommend to survival horror enthusiasts. Among all the great games that sprouted in 2025, this one stands out as a true gem, carefully crafted by a small team, without chasing current trends. Having no expectations whatsoever, I was able to fully enjoy every aspect that shapes its world and the experience within. And for those complaining that it’s too hard: planning and making the careful decisions is all you need to get the most out of the gameplay, regardless of the difficulty.

Before you even launch the game, take a step back: make sure you have enough time, the right conditions, headphones, and the proper mood. There are moments full of tension and combat, but also quieter stages when everything slows down and you can truly appreciate the sound details that build the entire atmosphere. It’s also worth taking a moment to admire the beautifully modelled environments.

The game’s linearity still allows for partial exploration and secret hunting. Whether you decide to spend some extra time finding additional resources will ultimately define your own difficulty level. Without upgrades, every fight will take longer, consume more ammo, and relying solely on melee attacks can become frustrating. Each encounter is a challenge: sometimes you must trust your intuition, while other times you’ll need to use the environment wisely and plan your approach before the fight even begins.

The story and lore blend nicely with the gameplay, encouraging you to read notes and discover the world through environmental storytelling. It may not be the strongest point of the game, but it’s original and unfolds at a satisfying pace.
Despite a few rough edges, this is still a solid, well-crafted, and complete experience - something that’s becoming increasingly rare these days.

[h1]The gist of it:[/h1]
Bloober Team has had its ups and downs over their history of horror games, but I can appreciate the fact that they're keeping the genre alive as best as they can. Cronos: The New Dawn is another creation of theirs, and it's quite a good horror game, but with some annoying flaws. 

👍 [u]The good parts:[/u]
+Depressing Eastern European atmosphere
+Hardcore gameplay mechanics

👎[u]The bad parts:[/u]
-Boring level design

[h1]Story[/h1]
Not much can be said about its story, it's not good or bad, and as the name implies, it deals with time travel. Time travel stories can be a bit tricky, and if you've seen one, you've seen them all. The game tries to keep things mysterious all the way, but as is the nature of time travel, you'll figure out the ending quite soon if you've seen other games/movies/shows about it. 

Without spoiling much, it is the same old adage: no matter what you do, you can't change the past, but in the case of time travel, you can try, but not without consequences. The entire story is kinda depressing, which was to be expected considering it is a horror game, but it is the atmosphere that truly makes it shine, and being also Eastern European, it felt somewhat nostalgic.

Story rating: 7.5/10

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
A generic survival horror third-person shooter is the best way to describe it. It does nothing new in the genre, but nothing worse either. It's what I would label a "safe product", no risk. I do appreciate that it is not casual or friendly at all. Resources are super scarce, inventory management is limited hell, and not dying is quite hard. 

You shoot infected humans just like any other Resident Evil, you have limited inventory space where you cannot carry every weapon or items which means you have to decide what to keep and you may end up with no ammo and lots of enemies. It is hardcore in that sense, and it requires some thinking instead of just closing your eyes and spray shooting everything. It has the classic nature of games in its DNA, which I loved. 

Aside from the shooting stuff, it does bring some basic new mechanics, such as gravity and pulling/clearing paths, but they're super basic and just meant for clearing your super linear path. Exploration was not as fun or rewarding as I hoped it would be. 

Gameplay rating: 8/10

[h1]Audio[/h1]
The audio design is pretty good overall, which is very important for a horror game. Voice acting is pretty good for all the characters you meet, including yours, the soundtrack is just there, nothing remarkable, and the sound effects are fantastic, which helped in making the atmosphere depressing. 

Audio rating: 8/10

[h1]Graphics, performance and tech analysis[/h1]
It's an Unreal Engine 5 game which will run ok at best, though considering the linearity and small spaces you are playing in, the game should be running at 200 FPS instead of below 100 on a high-end PC, but alas that is UE5 for ya, a tragedy of an engine. As long as you do not use ray-tracing the game is stutter-free. 

Level design is disappointing, unfortunately, considering the genre. There are very few places you can explore freely, and you are 90% of the time going in one direction. The atmosphere is great though, the feeling of post-apocalyptic Eastern European is nice, though I wish I could've explored the entire apartment building just like in SH2, instead of nothing...

Graphics, performance, and tech analysis score: 7.5/10

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Overall, Cronos is a fine game, not great, not bad, a safe product that you should buy if you're a fan of the genre, but probably on sale. 

[h1]Final score: 7.7/10[/h1]

A Haunting Journey Through a Ruined Future

Cronos: The New Dawn is a masterclass in atmospheric horror that goes far beyond a simple narrative. It’s a game that doesn't just immerse you; it haunts you. From the moment you step into its world, the game’s atmosphere is palpable, a thick blanket of melancholic dread. The journey through ruined, sprawling cities is given a unique and unsettling edge by its 80s-inspired synthwave score. This musical choice, while reminiscent of the classic sci-fi of Blade Runner, transforms into something truly chilling, providing a perfect counterpoint to the desolate environments and creating a horror experience unlike any other.

What makes Cronos truly special is its chillingly effective social commentary. The game's 1980s setting, particularly its nods to Eastern Europe at the time, is no mere aesthetic choice; it’s the perfect backdrop for a story about the horrors of communism. The game's brilliant narrative explores the horrific outcome of a humanity that has merged into a collective consciousness, leaving behind those who resisted, who are referred to as the "Orphans." This serves as a powerful allegory for the loss of individuality under a totalitarian system and the terrifying fate of those who refuse to join. This theme is brilliantly woven into the very design of the enemies, who terrifyingly merge to become more powerful and all-consuming if left unchecked—a visceral, horrifying metaphor for the collective swallowing up the individual. It's a unique and resonant take on a subject that feels perpetually relevant.

Underpinning the entire experience is the game's clever use of time travel, a genre element that the game embraces fully. This sci-fi subgenre, which so often serves as a simple plot device, is used here to create a profound sense of mystery. As you navigate different eras, the game slowly unfolds its secrets, revealing the history behind the ruined world and its inhabitants. The narrative unfolds at a deliberate pace, leaving you to piece together the events of a long-gone past, a puzzle that lingers in your mind long after the credits have rolled.

Cronos: The New Dawn isn't just a horror game; it's a thoughtful, atmospheric, and unforgettable journey that marries compelling storytelling with a unique aesthetic. It delivers on multiple levels, making it a standout title for anyone looking for an experience that is as intelligent as it is terrifying.

It's been a little long since I finished the game, but generally I actually quite liked it. I wish I remembered more about the specifics to go on about them.

The one thing I've got right now is that I actually quite liked how the Traveler "feels" as a character. She is disembodied from the environment, feeling nearly apathetic to her circumstances beyond the needs of the Collective, but her perspective shifts into a somewhat warmer state as the game progresses, influenced by the inherent nature of her mission and those she ultimately is exposed to in the process. There are several points where the player is presented with choices that reflect this divergence, and while most of them are for the sake of flavor, a particular scenario midway through the game I feel best illustrates this, even though this, too, is primarily flavor text.

A small detail, but I found the game very appropriately difficult in my first playthrough: difficult enough that misjudging my position or misfiring my gun causes problems, but not so difficult that I felt like each encounter was a struggle. In fact, most encounters feel more like "puzzles" rather than "engagements", but there are a few scenes where if you aren't amply prepared, you'll probably have to reload your save. That said, most combat scenarios you can get through with relative ease if you consistently use the charging system taught to you at the very beginning of the game.

The biggest problem I actually have with this game lies in a single item: the bolt cutters. You find them pretty early on, and they stick with you basically for the rest of the game if you have any interest in the optional paths and loot. They will nearly-always occupy one of your inventory slots, because putting them in your item box might cause you to stumble upon a chain to cut just to waltz all the way back to your nearest safe-house and back. Steam has long needed to make its review system more diverse, because the difference between a positive review for Chronos and pure enthusiasm for Silent Hill 2 is massive.
In fact, it’s not enough anymore for Steam to just add a “mixed” or “yellow” review type; what’s really needed is a 5, 10, or even 100-point rating scale. It’s a shame they’re not in a hurry to implement something like that.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3594742848
Chronos is a solid B-tier survival horror game. I’ve played all of Bloober Team’s titles, and while I wouldn’t call myself a fan, I have a generally positive attitude toward their work. I like most of their games and genuinely enjoy watching their progress — the difference between The Medium (which, by the way, had a great concept but somewhat flawed execution) and Chronos is truly impressive.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3591106476
That said, the miracle hasn’t happened yet. Chronos feels like an arthouse film with all the pros and cons that come with that. It’s not for everyone: the pursuit of originality often overshadows execution. You can also really feel the game’s budget constraints, with simplistic textures and, for much of the experience, rather mediocre level design. It’s obvious the developers tried to make a large-scale game, but at the same time, they were cutting costs almost everywhere.

The team did manage to find a certain balance thanks in part to lessons from Silent Hill, in how to guide the player through small, enclosed spaces while still providing dopamine hits without constantly introducing new assets or textures. However, in my opinion, this balance doesn’t quite work here, mostly because Silent Hill had a bigger budget and, to me, a more appealing atmosphere. A ruined post-apocalyptic Warsaw is certainly an original setting, but not necessarily an attractive one.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3595197126
The story didn’t surprise me, but it didn’t disappoint either. Overall, Chronos has enough ideas to feel original, but not enough budget to appeal to everyone. I think it will mostly resonate with fans of survival horror. If you’re not into the genre, you won’t be missing much by skipping it.
I hope Bloober Team continues to get bigger budgets, as they’ve proven that under a major publisher’s wing, they’re capable of great things. Unfortunately, on their own, they still haven’t quite managed to break free from making solid but undeniably B-tier games.

Cronos the New Dawn opens with a solid, intriguing premise that becomes more muddied and confusing the further along you progress. Any story that involves time travel is bound to become entangled in its own plot devices, and this game is no different. I frequently found myself wondering WHEN I was, WHEN we were going, and WHEN the game ultimately ended up. 

You find yourself in a post-apocalyptic scenario overrun by Dead Space-ish monsters. Traversal is tense and enemies are fun to encounter and fight. Charging up a powerful shot is very satisfying when it connects with a monster's face. The added mechanic of enemies being able to merge with dead monsters and become more powerful adds to the frantic panic of combat in a fun way. This is a survival horror in which you must gather and manage scarce resources, including a limited inventory similar to Resident Evil. I really enjoyed these aspects of the game.

What I didn't enjoy as much was...everything else. The idea of exploring a ruined, 1980s eastern Europe is interesting on paper, but I don't feel like they pulled it off. Environments are largely the same. Long outdoor corridors littered with brown, grey, and rusty red objects and goo, and indoor hallways littered with brown, grey, and rusty red objects and goo. I found the environments to be very basic and boring. Everything is the same dull color. Nothing stands out as interesting or worthy of further examination. I fell hook, line, and sinker for the hype leading up to this due to the excellent SH2 remake, and I'm glad to say it didn't disappoint. In fact, I didn't expect such a unique experience. I would have been just as happy with the Dead Space/Resident Evil 4 clone I expected from the trailers, but instead I was greeted with a unique and unforgettable campaign. While the game is undeniably influenced by those aforementioned games, the tight resource management and combat loop really set it apart. In fact, given Bloober's emphasis on story rather than gameplay, I was surprised to find myself being more invested in the tight combat and action-oriented gameplay offered here. This is especially impressive considering that the SH2 remake, often considered their greatest game, also did not have much depth of combat. They really honed their skills with this one.

The story is admittedly obtuse. Without spoiling anything, I think the existential ideas they were trying to tell could have used better means of exposition. The cut-scene dialogue especially seems off. Compared to the self-aware camp of Resident Evil or the uncanny performances in Silent Hill, the dialogue between characters seems a bit too forced and unnatural...and not on purpose. It's not necessarily "bad"...just not realistic enough to warrant investment. I suspect this is mainly a translation issue and could have probably used some slightly better localization. Not only this, but the game uses WAY too many found notes - unfortunately not enough environmental story-telling. It's a shame, because the levels themselves are well-designed. However, barring a few  memorable sequences, I think there was plenty of lost opportunities to world-build through gameplay and level design, rather than long, un-skippable cut-scenes and ubiquitous found notes. Again, weird and unnatural translations don't help the delivery here. 

That being said, repeated play-throughs help the convoluted story become clearer. And in the end, I was invested. I became addicted to the tight inventory limitations, weapon hunting, and resource management - all of which dictated how I approached enemy encounters. I couldn't help but be immersed in the world Bloober built, as the well-crafted gameplay forced me to stay in it. In fact, I made sure to replay 3 times in order to get everything I could out of the experience, which in the end, is the mark of a great survival horror.

Other than story, my other complaints are trivial. I wish there were harder difficulty modes, and I found the campaign a bit too short. I'd love to see more! Hopefully there is a sequel and/or some DLC on the way. But regardless, I'm excited to see whatever Bloober has in store next.

I’ve always appreciated the way Bloober Team approaches their narratives. Whether they always stick the landing is another question, but they’re consistently engaging — dark, spooky, and unsettling in all the right ways. Cronos: The New Dawn is no exception.

Set in an alternate 1980s Poland, the game builds a wonderfully strange and tense atmosphere, supported by eerie synth tones that give it a retro-horror vibe. Some reviewers have said that the game doesn’t really do anything new, and while that might be true mechanically, I think the narrative is novel enough to stand out.

That said, I do wish the gameplay had one extra layer of flexibility — something as simple as a dodge could completely change the feel of combat. Without it, the controls can feel stiff and clunky in that old-school survival horror way. Once you get used to that rhythm, though, it really works.

Inventory and resource management are highlights. You need to think carefully about what to craft — bullets or heals — because you’ll die multiple times learning how to handle different encounters. It has that Soulslike loop of dying, learning, and improving, and much of the challenge comes from the surprise of each scenario: how many enemies there are, which directions they come from, and how much ammo you’ve got to spare.

Technically, it’s more than just a mild improvement over Bloober’s Silent Hill 2 remake. There’s still some stuttering, but it’s far less frequent, and the game often runs smoothly for long stretches. Apart from the rare and frankly bizarre instance where the frame rate dropped below 60 FPS — most noticeably in one of the small save rooms — performance was excellent overall. I was playing at 4K resolution with ray tracing on, everything maxed out, using DLSS Performance mode and Frame Generation. Frame rates typically hovered between the high 70s and 144 FPS (my monitor’s refresh rate), averaging comfortably around the 100–110 FPS mark.

Texture quality can be a bit soft, even when using the Ultra Plus mod to sharpen things up — it’s still a little muddy at times — but overall, it’s a great-looking game that really pushes Unreal Engine 5.

Gripes and Frustrations
Combat would really benefit from a dodge or sidestep mechanic; it sometimes feels like your only defensive option is to backpedal and pray.
The jump scares are overused. One or two is great, but when you rely on them this often, it starts to feel like Horror for Dummies was the creative guide. These moments are supposed to be used sparingly to increase their effectiveness, not thrown at the player every twenty minutes.
The Eliza boss fight is a frustrating encounter that took me several attempts. The final phase especially — with waves of enemies swarming you in a tight space while you’re forced to shoot into the distance — feels overly punishing. I can easily imagine a lot of players giving up here.

Final Thoughts

I started this review by saying that Bloober doesn’t always stick the landing when it comes to their endings. Without giving anything away, I can honestly say that this time, while they haven’t created anything truly amazing, the finale does leave things open for another entry in the franchise. Much like the slight technical improvement over Silent Hill 2, it shows that Bloober are moving in the right direction — both in terms of performance and narrative closure.

Bloober continues to surprise, between The Medium, SH2 and now Cronos their catalog keeps getting better! Cronos wears its inspirations boldly on its sleeve and certainly isn't re-inventing the genre, but what it lacks in innovation it more than makes up for in an entertaining and consistent game play loop with a compelling story that had more than a few genuine surprises. Its settings benefit massively from the "temporal" nature of the plot, and seems to know just when to switch things up after being in an area for a while. The combat feels rewarding and seemed to favor a slower approach, as supplies (while not bone dry) are just limited enough to keep the tension up. A missed shot in a few of the more challenging sections can really sting, which is exactly what I want from a Survival Horror game. Its economy, crafting system (ammo/supplies ect.) and upgrade systems are very basic (with the genre staple "safe zones" for purchasing equipment and upgrades) but with its very limited inventory size and focus on careful timing with shots, I found myself engaged with its systems through-out. These mechanics in addition with items that take inventory space but don't provide an immediate combat need (sellables, keys, ect.) made inventory balancing land in a great spot for my tastes. 

Cronos is not the scariest game ever made and certainly won't keep you up at night if you enjoy this genre - but it had more than a few great segments that get the blood pumping. If you go in with the expectation of hair raising, sweat inducing segments like seen in the SH2 Remake and you may be let down. That being said, when it hits it really hits and got more than a few well timed jumps out of me without feeling cheap. The scripted sections are all eerie and have a great surreal quality, often making you think twice about if what you are seeing is what it seems. The enemy variety is for sure a weaker point, and I would have liked to have seen one or two more designs, but overall the look and sound of the enemies really grew on me as the game progressed. The merging mechanic is also excellent at making you snap from cautious defensive game play to a more aggressive approach, putting you in control of the difficulty during combat depending on resources and quick thinking. The boss encounters were also well done, but outside of one in particular a bit underwhelming. (*Minor Story Spoiler*) The way your "targets interact with you after you find them was a great boost to the psychological horror aspects, but this game is certainly tipping the scale more towards "combat" than "scary moments".

If you are a fan of Dead Space, RE4, The Evil Within or any of its contemporaries, Cronos is absolutely worth your time and a great addition to the genre. It is confident in its direction and commits to its theme fully, has excellent environmental story telling with an interesting and compelling plot, with some lightly designed but interesting game play gimmicks, and really solid overall foundations that made it a great ride from start to finish! Really excited to see what Bloober does next, they are a team to keep your eye on for sure!

43 Hours | 100% Achievements (The True Dawn)

Let me be clear: Cronos: The New Dawn is a superb survival horror experience, but it’s one that demands mastery and respect for its core mechanics. Hitting the 100% achievement mark felt like earning a degree in resource management and strategic combat, and if you’re looking for a title that rewards deep commitment, this is it.

The Atmosphere and World (10/10)
Bloober Team knocked the atmosphere out of the park. The grim, brutalist architecture of 1980s post-apocalypse Poland combined with the unsettling sci-fi aesthetic is truly unique. Exploring the ravaged wasteland as the Traveler, jumping between time periods to unravel the mystery of "The Change," is constantly intriguing. I spent hours hunting down every audio log and text file, and the lore here is dense, disturbing, and genuinely compelling.

Strategic Combat and the Merging Mechanic
This is where the game earns its survival horror stripes, and why the "Mixed" reviews don't understand the depth. Cronos isn't a fast-paced action game; it’s a constant tactical exercise.

    Charged Shots are King: Learning to prioritize charged blasts and headshots for ammo efficiency is essential. Normal shots are a waste of precious resources.

    The Merging Mechanic: This is the genius layer of difficulty. Every encounter is a puzzle: Do I spend my precious Pyre fuel to burn the corpse now, or risk a nearby Orphan merging with it to become a heavily armored, acid-spitting abomination? When you get deep into the game, failing to burn a body quickly means an immediate, terrifying difficulty spike, which is what made the hardest encounters so satisfying to overcome.

The 100% Journey
My 43 hours weren't just running through the story. Achieving all the cores, finding every collectible, and unlocking all the suit upgrades is a massive undertaking. The 37 Cores are expertly hidden, forcing you to use the time manipulation puzzles and Gravity Boots to fully explore every corner. If you are an achievement hunter, this game is perfectly paced to push you to the brink of your resources while rewarding your exploration with meaningful power progression.

Final Verdict
If you love strategic survival horror games like the modern Resident Evil remakes and Dead Space, and appreciate a punishing difficulty that you can eventually conquer through mastery and resourcefulness, buy this game. It is a slow, tense, and incredibly rewarding journey to the "New Dawn."

TL;DR: Strategic survival horror masterclass with fantastic atmosphere and lore. The merging mechanic ensures every fight is tense, and the collectibles/upgrades are essential for the full experience. A must-buy for genre fans.

Came for the demo, stayed for the story. 

I'd strongly encourage you to give the demo a spin. If you don't like the gameplay, worldbuilding or mysterious story then buying the full game's probably a waste of money. 

For those who wanna know what you're getting into before downloading the demo, this one's somewhere between Resident Evil and Dead Space in terms of gameplay. Your character has limited mobility (thanks to the huge environmental suit) so you'll be relying on carefully timed sidesteps for evasion, melee attacks to give yourself a bit of breathing room and the inarguably effective strategy of "shoot it in the face" to solve problems. 

Inventory management is gonna be a primary concern in your first run-through (yes, there is a New Game +) and a much lesser concern in the second since you'll have access to all the inventory upgrades. Ammunition is limited but you generally have enough to get the job done if you're careful about how you use it. Your weapons take up a slot in your inventory each, so you'll wanna find which ones work for you and stick to them. Healing items are usually worth having around, but never more than one stack. It's a much better strategy to stack ammo and just no get hit. 

The weapons all have their own unique personality. Handguns have balanced stats, hit reasonably hard and have plentiful ammo. Shotguns benefit from fantastic penetration, a wide cone of fire and high damage in exchange for extremely limited ammunition. Coming hot off the heels of Bloober’s fantastic Silent Hill 2 remake stands a new IP — Cronos: The New Dawn. I was eager to see what Bloober could do with a fresh property and what learnings, if any, they could take from their work on SH2. I’m pleased to say that, for the survival horror fan, Cronos delivers an A+ performance.

First things first, this game is a true, blue survival horror experience — the combat is tough, resources are scarce, and the horrors are never-ending. You’re thrown into the deep end pretty quickly and are expected to understand fast or die trying. Despite the initial difficulty on display here, I have no doubt that survival horror regulars will excel. What starts off as tricky quickly changes as you learn how best to dispatch your foes, maintain your resources, and exploit the environment.

The storyline is gripping, if not a little vague at times. It certainly leaves you wanting a bit more by the end and leaves you with a few lingering question even when the credits roll on the "true ending".

I’d love to see another game in this universe from Bloober, with a few quality-of-life improvements — namely, an in-game map. While I only found myself lost a few times, backtracking through areas without a dedicated map can sometimes be a bit of a pain. The addition of a dodge button also wouldn’t go amiss; I can see why the devs opted to exclude it. Still, combat might feel a little less clunky with its inclusion.

Overall, Cronos is a fantastic survival horror game. Its atmosphere bleeds Dead Space 1, and its cryptic story sinks its hooks in deep.

It took me around 32 hours to fully 100% the game, including a New Game+ hard mode run. For any budding survival horror fan, it’s well worth a pickup — though if you’re not used to the genre, your mileage may vary!

Cronos The New Dawn is an original IP from Bloober Team, but it wears its influences on its sleeve, drawing heavily from the original Dead Space (2008) and Resident Evil 4 (2005). The weighty movement and enemy design feel very Dead Space, while the shooting, inventory management, and even some of the lore mechanics play like a mash-up of both classics.

But if you’re looking for a truly modern take on that formula, this isn’t the game for you. Yes, it introduces a few new mechanics, but many of them feel like rehashed ideas from the titles I mentioned above. Still, much like the original games it borrows from, if you enjoyed those classics, chances are you’ll have a good time with this one too.

The story is all over the place at first and has only a slim chance of keeping you hooked until almost the midpoint of the game. The saving grace is the scenery and environment: I love me some slavjank, or eurojank if you prefer, and this bleak, broken, post-apocalyptic version of Poland really hit the spot for me.

Where the game really falls short and right on its face - is replayability. Doing multiple runs just to chase an S rank, only to be rewarded with a single achievement and no meaningful unlocks—no special suit, no secret weapon, no infinite-ammo variant—feels like a completely pointless feature. The same goes for NG+: yes, beating the game unlocks Hard Mode and that does shake things up a bit, but again, you only get an achievement for finishing it. Woohoo. How exciting. The phylactery system has the same problem: finishing the game with specific extraction combinations also just gives you an achievement and nothing more. For me, this is the game’s biggest flaw—after beating it and writing this review, I honestly don’t feel any desire to go through the whole thing again just for a “better” ending, different extractions, and an S rank, when none of it offers anything meaningfully rewarding in return.

This is especially disappointing for someone like me, because Resident Evil is one of my favorite franchises of all time: when you beat those games and earn that sweet S rank without dying or saving, under a tight time limit, you at least get something in return to make your next run more worthwhile and more fun. Does this game offer that? Nope.

The game has some other flaws as well. There’s no quick-turn like in its predecessors, the inventory management is clunky, and you can’t delete items or sort your stash or inventory in any meaningful way. Performance is also pretty rough; it runs on Unreal Engine, and I had abysmal performance issues, with horrible 0.1% lows whenever I Alt-Tabbed out of the game in fullscreen or clicked outside it in windowed or borderless and then came back. If you’re the kind of person who expects things to run smoothly without a hitch, you’ll have to turn a blind eye to the performance.

So, would I recommend this game despite its shortcomings? Absolutely—but only if you’re specifically looking for a classic experience in the vein of the original Dead Space or Resident Evil 4, and only if you can get it at a discount. Wait for a sale, grab the game, and have fun.

I was able to play the demo on low graphics settings, so I bought the whole thing. It’s a Dead Space (2008) clone. Everyone knows that. You even have a stomp, but without the dismemberment mechanic it serves no purpose.

Living enemies can absorb the bodies of dead enemies, so you must torch the dead, which feels like The Evil Within, how you had to drop a match on fallen enemies you didn’t kill with a headshot or they might get back up again. The stomp in Dead Space severed the limbs of the dead so a certain enemy couldn’t transform them into new enemies. Cronos doesn’t let you do that. In fact, your torch is so limited it barely exists, though at least your melee attacks deal damage and [i]can[/i] kill enemies.

In terms of gameplay, Cronos has little going for it. Without the ability to dismember enemies, there is no visual confirmation you’re doing damage to them. The limited ammo for the torch means dead bodies will be everywhere, so you’re under pressure to kill these things before they find fallen comrades to merge with. That’s kind of cool, but ammo is so scarce I have to wonder why the Collective doesn’t just ditch projectile weapons and invest in flamethrowers. When enemies do merge, it doesn’t have much of an impact on gameplay. In fact, the few times it happened, it meant game over because I didn’t have enough ammo to defeat these stronger foes.

The limits in Dead Space felt natural as part of the environment. The limits in Cronos feel arbitrary. Running out of ammo is so easy, but with careful observation and strategy and lots and lots of inventory management, you can get through any section despite the lack of resources.

Everything here has been done before, to greater effect, but Cronos has one thing going for it: the story.

That makes the experience.

I’ve played multiple clones that did it just as good or better. Corridor 7 as a clone of Wolfenstein 3D. Alida as a clone of Riven. Dante’s Inferno as a clone of God of War. And now Cronos as a clone of Dead Space, if for no other reason than to find out what the hell is going on here.

Once it drops its big revelation, Cronos becomes cinematic and suspenseful. Not to mention terrifying. It’s psychological horror done right, as the game casts the player in a unique role who has an unusual point of view. Is the Traveler’s POV the only one that matters, or is there a bigger picture to consider? The player must make a choice, and there seems to be no correct, moral solution. No heroes. No villains. Could all of this suffering be worthwhile? I don’t know, but the game sure made me question what I consider justice.

The story makes Cronos worthwhile. Check it out.

Cronos: The New Dawn surprised me in all the right ways. The atmosphere is easily the strongest part of the game. The retro futuristic Eastern European setting feels cold, eerie, and completely unique. The brutalist architecture, strange biology, and heavy synth soundtrack come together to create a world that is both unsettling and fascinating.

The story is a big step above what most survival horror games try to do. The time travel concept, the Essences, and the Orphans make the world feel layered and intentional. It stays interesting from start to finish and gives you plenty to think about.

The gameplay is classic survival horror. Ammo matters, every fight has weight, and you have to plan ahead. The combat is not perfect and melee can feel stiff, but the tension it creates actually works with the tone of the game. Fire becomes an important tool since it prevents enemies from merging into stronger forms, which adds a nice bit of strategy.

The pacing has a little backtracking, but the atmosphere is strong enough that it never feels boring. The world is worth exploring and the environments never feel copy pasted. Multiple endings give it solid replay value.

Overall, Cronos: The New Dawn is a standout survival horror experience that does more right than wrong. The atmosphere and storytelling carry it hard, and the gameplay supports it well enough to make the whole package feel worthwhile.

A dark, haunting, and memorable journey that easily earns a place in my top 5 of the year.

After having unlocked all achievements here’s my review: 

Cronos is definitely not a Silent Hill, Resident Evil, or Dead Space clone, but it does have obvious inspirations from all three, especially from Dead Space. My first playthrough took me over 15 hours, and it was a blind run and aiming for full completionist. NG+ for 100% took me 8 hours. It’s not a short or a fast paced one, it’s a slow burn, designed to keep you tense for most of it.

Performance in this game is yet another somewhat weak entry for Bloober team, SH2 had sub-par performance because of the mist (defeating the whole purpose of it in the original) among other factors, and here it’s no different. It has great detail but with how claustrophobic the scenery sometimes is, I don’t see how I’m not getting more frames. Upscaling is an unfortunate must here.

The first playthrough is basically split into two parts. The first part (about 40%) is classic Dead Space: it’s slow, and introduces you to a lot of mechanics little by little that you’ll carry through the rest of the game. The second half (around 60%) feels more like Resident Evil 4 or the lab section of RE2. It’s not horror anymore, it still has some cheap jumpscares and the environment might say otherwise, but it leans way more into the survival side. More fights, more enemies, more chaos.

The most stressful thing in this game like any good survival horror is the inventory. You always feel like you don’t have enough space. The storage chest is super annoying because it doesn’t really let you organize or sort it in any meaningful way, so good luck finding what you need quickly (especially in NG+). It should’ve been a grid pattern and not a list with few items on display at any given moment.

Weapons feel pretty decent. The best part is you can respec them from the start, so when you find a better weapon, you don’t just waste all your earlier investment. Unto aiming, especially with the starter pistol and it’s kind of a pain, but that’s the way it’s intended as it makes shots more tense, and in a panic, you will miss more often than not. It has a sway that never goes away, it just decreases as you upgrade the weapon, especially when you charge the shot.
 
The enemy death-absorption mechanic is very interesting and unique and you can’t forget about it, because it can turn a very simple encounter into a game over if you don’t keep it in mind. I finished my NG+ with 0 absorptions (it’s a tracked metric for your run rank, like in RE). It’s easy to avoid but punishes you if you let it slip. I died once in my blind playthrough because I didn't keep it in check.

I played on K&M and it was pretty responsive except for one mechanic that you only do three times per playthrough. Out of the six times I had to do it, I plugged in a controller 4/6 times because it’s just way harder for no reason on K&M.

Lore-wise? Super confusing. The game wants to have 3–4 main story beats, but it focuses hard on what I thought was the least interesting one. The narrative (or lack thereof) starts the game off great; it grabs your attention and makes you want to keep going to find out more, but then it takes some twists that aren’t worth it and ruin what was a strong beginning with excellent potential, turning it into something pretty underwhelming and confusing story.

TL:DR: Do I recommend it? Yes, it’s a good game despite its flaws (which aren't many, and that alone makes it a good game with great legs to stand on by itself). 
Is it worth buying at full price? Maybe. It’s not Dead Space, Silent Hill 2, or RE, and it’s nowhere near their quality in mechanics and narrative. I would recommend to wait for it on sale, you will get your money’s worth at full price, but at a discount, it’ll be a greater value.
Would I pick Cronos over DS Remake, SH2 Remake or RE? Absolutely not. It’s more of a Dead Space Lite (which isn’t a bad thing, but I'd recoommend DS Remake over Cronos), and the closest thing we’ll get to a spiritual successor. At least until EA (hopefully) decides to remaster DS2.

Since their remake of Silent Hill 2, Bloober Team has shown they can do more than their usual horror walking sims — and with Cronos: The New Dawn, they’ve proven they can do more than just remakes.
The story is great. The lore felt well-established with all its unique terminologies. I really loved the design behind the travelers' tech: their suits, weapons, the way they speak; there's something really unique to it.
The sound design is excellent. The main character’s suit, weapons, and gadgets all sound authentic. The synth soundtrack worked surprisingly well for a game of this genre.
Visually, the game is stunning. When it comes to environment design and lighting, Bloober is among the best in the industry. More than once, I caught myself just appreciating how beautiful everything looked.
My biggest complaint is the optimization. DLSS was the only thing that allowed me to enjoy this game on high settings.
The gameplay is solid. The survival horror aspect was done really well; ammo and resources felt well balanced, and inventory management is crucial. While mostly linear, the game rewards exploration and backtracking. The guns were generally fun to use, though I didn’t really care much for a few of them. The enemy merging mechanic is cool; it encourages smart resource management.
I think the game would’ve benefited from a wider variety of combat mechanics. Too often, combat comes down to shooting unarmored spots or baiting enemies near red/orange barrels, which sometimes made some encounters easier than what the devs seemingly intended. The bosses could've been more unique too — most of them felt like tankier versions of regular enemies. 
I definitely recommend this to any Resident Evil or Dead Space fan. I think this is Bloober’s best game yet, and I hope to see more survival horror from them.

Cronos: The New Dawn has become a very pleasant discovery for me this year.
The gameplay is deeply engaging and strongly reminds me of the best Resident Evil titles — the remakes of 2 and 4, as well as parts RE7 and RE8. Just like in those games, progressing through the story, upgrading your character, and uncovering the world’s mysteries  and what has happened was incredibly rewarding.

I especially loved the switch between perspectives — exploring the ruined future after the catastrophe and then jumping back into the past to see what the world looked like before it all went wrong. This contrast gives a unique perspective on the events.

It’s rare to encounter such intricate stories where, at first, you have no idea what’s happening — but piece by piece it all starts to make sense. Here it’s done very well.

I’d also like to highlight the presence of New Game+ — in the best Resident Evil traditions. After finishing the game, you can start over while keeping your stats and weapons, allowing you to max out upgrades and go for the remaining achievements. That’s a huge plus. 

The story and the way monsters merge reminded me of the iconic movies The Thing — the original from 1982 and the 2011 prequel. I’m sure I’m not the only one who noticed this.

Final verdict: if you enjoy Resident Evil–style gameplay, intricate stories, and horror with a touch of mystery, this game will absolutely pull you in. Highly recommended — you won’t regret it.

Cronos: The New Dawn is a good horror experience with fantastic combat/gameplay and a let down of a story. First 3/4 of the game the story is intriguing despite the - very predictable in my opinion (called it in the first 2 hours of gameplay) - plot twist and very questionable plot points. Then it's just... I don't even know how one can ruin an ending like that!

SPOILERS AHEAD -  click on text only if you don't care

So basically [spoiler] there's this doctor who is being mentioned throughout the entire game. She's apparently very important. But we don't even know why she's important? Anyway - fast forward to like 2/3 of the game - you can understand from the very scarse information that she worked for the government or got kidnapped by the goverment or took part in some experimentation (WHO KNOWS?? It's not explained!) I'll spare you the details about the main plot twist, but just know that she basically becomes the main character of the game by the end of it. And we know like two things about her... That she's a doctor and that she's *blank*. [/spoiler] So yeah, that's the first red flag.

Second one - you don't get much information at all. All the notes are either ramblings of some mad people or are barely relevant to the story. And you know what - hey! If you want to make a very vague game it's fine to not explain things, but then why even bother with notes? Some even sound very funny, not on purpose I'm sure. There's this one note made by a member of the hospital's staff saying that she hates this other woman and curses her out and... she formally signed the note, with her whole job name and name and last name. Like wtf?

So if you expect to [spoiler] find out why the disease started, who ACTUALLY is The Pathfinder (like the human version, before he became what he is), what species we are, where we came from, did WE start the disease) - there's no answer to that.  [/spoiler] I will say though - this, I don't fully mind. Why? Because the game goes the philosophical route instead of giving people every answer possible. However, as I already mentioned - [spoiler] the lack of info on the doctor or what really happened to her is infuriating, cause the ending is like "oh you need to be really sad about this character" I DON'T KNOW HER. The immersion breaks, cause I didn't even get time to think like "ok, I feel bad for her", cause I don't even know what happened, or if that helps her or not... [/spoiler]

The two endings that come with the first time playthrough are nothing short of awful. They just [spoiler] show you two "different" outcomes that end up in the same way... basically the doctor gets supposedly saved or not by us, but it doesn't matter what you choose! She gets sick and presumably dies in both of those endings [/spoiler]
The saving grace comes in the form of the NG+ only ending. It's not perfect by any means, but it's way better than the ones you can get on your first try. It hints at [spoiler] Weronika being stuck in a loop and now resembling The Pathfinder as well/falling in love with her human version and starting the experience AGAIN??? [/spoiler] I don't know, that's my impression at least, but when you think about it it's really cool and it definitely gets that point across that [spoiler] no matter what you do, you can't change the human condition and that history is meant to repeat itself?  [/spoiler] , I guess? Or maybe that [spoiler] there's always a chance for things to get better [/spoiler] ? Honestly I don't know, but it's cool that's it's open to interpretation like that and whichever it is, it's good.

Anyway - now about the good stuff.

The gameplay itself is a stellar experience, I had a lot of fun. Some people complain about the lack of dodge, but I found that refreshing. The game is a little bit hard, but for me it was just the right amount. It doesn't punish the player like a soulslike would, all ammo you've lost, if you're not shooting the bullets just about everywhere with no care in the world - you'll be good, the ammo will be "given back" to you.

It brings back the classic survival horror experience of managing your inventory, choosing what weapon should be prioritized in use during a specific section, there's definitely some tactics you have to do against bosses. If you're an average gamer like myself, you will die a little bit during the game, but it's nothing to worry about and nothing that will drive you crazy. It might be too tough for not experienced players though, I'm sure.

The soundtrack is relatively simple, but it just fits the game, the vibes and the story.

I really liked the voice acting of the main character, The Traveler. It might seems trivial to even mention that and you might think nothing of it when you just started playing the game, but it [spoiler] changes overtime, she becomes more and more human like, even the interactions with cats change a little bit [/spoiler] and it's just so cool and in my opinion - perfectly executed, whoever played her deserves their flowers.

The cats are a nice touch and almost a comedic relief sometimes [spoiler] because of the lines of our character [/spoiler] and I loved that they were in the game.

Lastly - this game doesn't really tire you out, at least it didn't tire me out. Replay value is pretty decent (well, maybe not for 3+ playthroughs), I played through the entire game twice, one time on NG+ and one and a half time on the regular mode (half cause I ended up loading a save for an achievement that has to do with the ending of the game).
I like exploration and checked every nook and cranny - the first playthrough took me 21 hours and I died 18 times, but the time flies when you play this thing.

The NG+ is pretty cool, lets you keep your upgrades and weapons and everything you kept in your crate. I beat it on hard mode and it was alright. I only died once lol, the weapons become OP with the late game upgrades on from the start lol. The NG+ playthrough took me 10 hours. Got all of the achievements, however I needed to follow a guide for some (especially the upgrade all weapons to the max one, please, look it up because you can easily get it in just two playthroughs).

If you're worried about jumpscares - there's quite a few, enemies just pop out of closed doors destroying them, I wouldn't say this game is scary per se, but some jumpscares can get you for sure.

About the recycling of enviroments and bosses - yes, a certain section appears twice and certain bosses appear twice too (two of them, so 4 fights are kinda sameish), but personally I didn't mind it. The section that appears twice is changed the second time around and you have to go a different route and later do different things etc. so it's not EXACTLY the same. The "same" boss fights, they also differ enough for it to still be fun, because they happen in different places, the space is different, one more, one less cramped and you have to strategize a bit different to get them each time, so it's fine.

Overall I recommend this game. If this story had an underwhelming gameplay it would be one of the worst games of the year probably. But the gameplay is very very good and this way it's one of the best games I played this year lol, very thin line between best and worst apparently. So all in all - worth to play even if just for the gameplay alone. Just a fun time to be honest.

[h2] Cronos The New Dawn is Perfect [/h2] 

After completing 100% achievements and enjoying every single second of it I can happily say that Cronos the New Dawn is an incredible horror game. If you are a survival horror elitist you may say its not exactly survival horror but its closer to dead space as a resource management horror with incredible story telling and atmosphere. I am going to break the review down into a few sections that will be titled. 

 [h2] The Good [/h2] 

 [h3] Atmosphere [/h3] 

Cronos The New Dawn has some of the most oppressive atmosphere I have seen in a horror title to date. Every location every detail every room had me on edge in my first play through. My first play through took me around 12 hours as I took it very slow and found myself "E3 dev showcase walking" around, you know that walk they do in the trailers to show off the environments. Yeah not many games can make me do that. I was just taking in the grandness of some of these locations. As you enter areas like The Steelworks and The Abbey just as you arrive and the grandness of the location comes into view it will play some of the most beautiful music to score a game in a long time. This is one of the strongest points of the game, the atmosphere. 

 [h3] Sound Design [/h3] 

Along with atmosphere the sound design is incredible. I cannot quite call it perfect yet as the sounds for enemies left me desiring a little more. Its purely because sometimes the directional sound for them confused me a little bit. But outside of this the enemies sounds were good and the overall environmental sounds and general design for the sounds was incredible. This is all topped off with a great OST. I would recommend getting the OST if you are a fan of those. 

 [h3] Gameplay [/h3] 

The gameplay for Cronos is also very nice. Every footstep from the traveller feels heavy and bulky which to some is a down side but I would definitely disagree. This is very similar to Dead Space or Gears of War where you characters and their heavy hefty suits of armor feel the part rather than just looking the part. The guns feel like they truly pack a punch and have a hefty kick to boot. I did this a few times in my new game plus playthroughs and hard mode playthroughs just to move a bit quicker. 

 [h3] Story Telling [/h3] 

I will not spoil any story beats here.
Bloober team has done an incredible job in creating one of the most interesting horror stories with this title. It had me hooked and asking hundreds of questions from the very beginning and I found myself unable to put the game down just hoping to find more and more answers as I progressed and explored. I highly recommend anyone who plays this tries to experience all endings. I would personally recommend saving a lot on your first playthrough so you can just load a save before the final boss and then see one ending and reload to see the second so that you can move on to new game plus and see the true cannon ending. I had some issues getting the game to stop crashing but I have put out a guide for that for AMD GPU users. If you are going to check this game out I highly recommend making sure you meet the RECOMMENDED system specs not the minimum and if you have any crash issues please do check my guide. 

Aside from this the game is really a master piece and even with the small crashing issues that I was able to trouble shoot and work out I found that I can now play the game for up to 20 hours straight without a crash. I would still give this game a perfect score even with this. 

[h2] Final Verdict [/h2] 

I think this game is a must play for anyone that is a fan of Dead Space, RE2make, RE3make, Evil Within, or just cosmic horror in general. 

I give it a 10/10 I was not expecting much from this because I had heard absolutely no news about the game releasing ahead of time and then all of the sudden I found it on steam. I was truly blown away by this title.

Cronus: New Dawn - A Tale of Two Games (8/10)
Cronus: New Dawn delivers an exceptional experience for roughly 80% of its runtime, only to stumble dramatically at the finish line. What begins as a gripping survival horror mystery transforms into something far less compelling, leaving players with a bittersweet taste despite the journey's many strengths.
The Stellar Foundation
The game's opening act is nothing short of masterful. The central mystery surrounding a mysterious disease creates genuine intrigue, with environmental storytelling and personal accounts that had me genuinely invested in uncovering the truth. Playing as a well-equipped, resilient protagonist who embodies the game's "Such is Our Calling" ethos strikes the perfect balance—you're vulnerable enough to feel tension, but capable enough to push forward with determination.
The crafting system deserves special recognition. Being able to manufacture ammunition and equipment on-demand creates a satisfying gameplay loop that rewards resourcefulness and planning. There's a genuine learning curve that makes mastery feel earned rather than given.
Technically, the game largely excels. The graphics are impressive throughout most of the experience, and the sound design is absolutely phenomenal—every audio cue, ambient noise, and effect contributes to an immersive atmosphere. And yes, the cat-saving mechanic is a delightful touch that adds heart to an otherwise dark experience.
The Disappointing Conclusion
Unfortunately, the final 20% abandons nearly everything that made the earlier portions compelling. The narrative takes a jarring turn that feels disconnected from the carefully built mystery, introducing elements that seem to belong to an entirely different game.
The ending situation is particularly frustrating. Players are presented with three conclusions that range from unsatisfying to outright disappointing. The requirement to replay the entire game for the third ending adds insult to injury—it's not just narratively weak, but disrespectful of players' time investment.
Final Verdict
Despite its weak conclusion, Cronus: New Dawn succeeds where it matters most for the majority of its runtime. The strong foundation of gameplay, atmosphere, and storytelling carries enough weight to overcome its stumbling finale. It's a reminder that even flawed games can be worth experiencing when their strengths shine as brightly as they do here.
Rating: 8/10 - Exceptional until it isn't, but the journey is worth taking despite the destination.

A hauntingly beautiful survival horror experience. With visuals and sound design that rival the best in the industry, Cronos: New Dawn delivers stunning lighting effects and a chilling soundtrack that elevates every moment of gameplay. It also boasts a truly unique setting that may feel like a strange trip down memory lane for Polish people. I was fascinated by the story and the whole concept of the Travelers and the Collective. After beating the game once, I immediately started a New Game+ playthrough upon discovering that a 'true' ending is only available in NG+. 
Cronos merges (heh) mechanics and ideas from various survival horror games. While the gameplay isn't particularly original, it plays beautifully and introduces a few small mechanics of its own. I particularly enjoyed the Integrity Scanner, which displays an enemy's health level when aiming at them. It's especially useful for scanning bodies lying around to anticipate possible ambushes without wasting ammo by shooting every corpse you encounter.
The heavily advertised mechanic of merging enemies is very cool and forces you to prioritise threats effectively, adding an extra layer to resource management. You can deprive enemies of bodies to merge with by burning the dead using the flamethrower or other fire sources. Ending up in a situation where you run out of flamethrower fuel and get surrounded by a horde, while other enemies hang back and absorb the corpses you've already killed to strengthen themselves, can really ruin your day.
I wholeheartedly recommend Cronos: The New Dawn to any survival horror fan. It's an amazing game and another step on Bloober Team's road to greatness. I've always liked their games—even the early Layers of Fear series—but their recent output is all killer, no filler. I can't wait to see what new IP they come up with, and I'm especially excited for their remake of Silent Hill 1.

1. I start with a pistol? Why?
- Everything is made of goop and runs at you. Seems like the last option a highly secretive organization would want to give me. I don't find it, they strait up had it ready for me. Bad choice.

2. A shop? A storage bin? An upgrade system? Why?
- Seems taken strait out of Dead Space. Some places have these "Safe Zones" where all this is tucked away. Great, but this isn't the Ishumra. Why do I sell and buy things, to whom? I'm selling energy? Who wants this? Why do I need upgrades since I was sent out on this highly classified mission. Who prepped me so poorly I need to buy my own gear and weapons?

3. Inventory limits despite I form pockets of space? Why?
- I have to upgrade my pockets. Despite my TIME SHIFTING SPACE PISTOL forming into other weapons they all use different ammo types and each weapon my pistol can fuse into takes ANOTHER slot, which makes inventory management feel tacked on clearly pushing players to choose rather than make any lick of sense. Oh, and sometimes I get unlimited ammo "handed" to me just to solve puzzles. I don't like that. Sometimes I do have ammo, other times I have none. What gives? Is this the same guy who set up my pistol and my suit, because I hate them.

4. Enemies have no mind? Fusing is overpowered? Why?
- It's not really that fun when a swarm of them just walk up to you and pile on you. They really do nothing else. The "fusing" part is also very unfair. Given our limited ammo, very bulky controls, and useless punching mechanics things easily get out of hand fast locking players into running around in circles praying the fused creature takes pity on you as you flounder around like a fish desperate not to have to restart the mission for the 5th time.

So there you have it. 

There are plenty of good games that don't need combat mechanics thrown into them to be gripping or action packed. Portal, The Room, Amnesia, Stories Untold, and more do this with more focus.

Simpy put. Game mechanics should enhance the narrative, not deter from it.

While this is an interesting way for Bloober to go, especially since it's a departure from their prior works, it's attempting to be something that it cannot match. To me, it feels like it wants to have the writing of Returnal and still have overlaying metaphors and mysteries that involve collectivism and isolation. The monsters are a collective, so is the fictional society found within Cronos, and so is the mysterious company the main character "works" for. While I have played under two hours it falls short narratively for me and I wouldn't want to see more of it as it lacks the finesse that I had hoped for. 

Every few moments you get bland, but just rarely good, commentary from the main character. I don't need or want to have a friend narrate every moment of my life and the events in front of me, but unfortunately the main character here does exactly that. Returnal does this as well, but the writing is nigh always giving more than telling: The alien architecture, the weapons, the alien language are all talked about as they are seen, but reflect the character perfectly. In Cronos, the narration is blunt and matter-of-fact, but it does little than explore the surface level allegory of being a mindless drone for the hive mind/parent company. It's uninteresting after hearing just a few short snippets and doesn't give much at all to study and dissect.

The enemy design is interesting, but doesn't quite set itself apart from other titles—though the mechanic of monsters fusing with their fallen bretheren is neat. It all serves well for a metaphor and I think it's good enough. The music is fine, but feels a little out there when it comes to atmosphere-setting. Visuals are obviously good. I think Bloober Team did well with crafting different locations and settings, especially with making parts of it feel inhabited and lonely at the same time. 

Gameplay is where I decided to quit. The game is a Frankenstein's Monster of Resident Evil inventory management, Dead Space's fleshy abominations, and the time mechanic of swapping between present/past. The "puzzles" were dull as far as I experienced and don't have any depth as far as I saw—could have done without them honestly. When it came to inventory management I honestly think it's horrifically miserable. Lots of people complain about having to throw things away when they play too well and don't expend enough resources or having to backtrack for a long time to deposit items to then pick up a key/progression item and use it seconds later. It really is that bad. You can upgrade your inventory and I did so, but playing too well was still a punishing experience because I would have to throw or waste resources just to pick up a key item. It's miserable. Then the gunplay is fine, but didn't feel like there was much weight to it. Hitting enemies with melee attacks is optimal once you realize the enemies have some very easy attacks to just walk out of or around, but lord help you if you get so much as tapped just three times without a health upgrade. Dead Space and, sometimes, Resident Evil made feeling getting hit so much more dangerous than Cronos does. It just doesn't feel like some enemy attacks would really do as much damage as they show on your screen. I only died once and got hit a handful of times in my 2 hour run of this game and it felt more frustrating than fear or panic inducing. 

Overall, it wasn't an enjoyable experience and I don't want to spend $60 on a game that I know won't feel satisfying or enjoyable at the end of the day. I'd avoid it and recommend Returnal, which is close enough to the experience that Cronos wants to be but doesn't live up to.

No matter what I did and how much I played with gamemode, gamescope and some really handy tools baked into Bazzite - I could not get it above 60 fps and frametimes were as high as 120ms(!) at times.

The general negative things I felt are as follows:

- Lots of the negative reviews say the game is too hard, personally I felt the complete opposite. Game was really easy for me. Once you figure out that enemies take 3 charge shots to kill you pretty much have got the combat down.

- Really dislike the way the charge shots felt. I disliked how it would make me fire once fully charged instead of being able to hold and release the charge shot. 

- The game is VERY boring looking early on. Maybe it gets more interesting later, but if you're a real "grey and dust" fan, or you REALLY liked the other place thing in Stranger Things, this might be your cup of tea. 

- They'll probably explain why the characters talk like stiff robots eventually, but I just wasn't hooked by what was going on at all story-wise.

-  Exploration felt pretty hand-holdy and minimal. Typical "go slightly left or right then return to the main path" type of exploration. It could open up later, but I doubt it as there isn't a map in game or anything.

- They introduce a time power, but you pretty much get disappointed immediately upon getting it. It's just a typical "look for thing to use it on" type of power and didn't see any further expansion during the 2 hours I played. Might get more later though (no idea if so). 

- The enemies are REALLY boring and not scary. Lots of people are like "it's like Dead-Space" when it barely is at all. There is no limb cutting, you just shoot enemies till they're down. The only variations I ran into during the first two hours of play were "enemy that goes down in one shot," "enemy that takes more than 3 shots," and "guy that explodes if you get close." Though, tbh, that last one was more of an obstacle than an enemy. Maybe they get cooler later on, but I simply cannot imagine them being that varied or interesting to fight.

- Continuing the Dead Space comparisons - since many like to make them. All of the game's similarities to dead space start and end at "you're in a suit". There are no diegetic elements to the game, I literally forgot the stomp existed until writing this exact line, the first power you get seems to be unable to be used in combat, and the world/enemies simply aren't that interesting. A vastly closer comparison would be to the more recent Resident Evil remake games in terms of gameplay loop. 


Some things I did like:

- I did like the suit, minus the weird mouth thing it's got going on. 

- I did like the inventory management somewhat. The game kind of forces you to craft things so you don't horde materials, which I didn't hate. I immediately rushed inventory slots though, so inventory space literally wasn't an issue when I played. I imagine it could become something you consider later on in the game for things though.

- Sound was good. Liked the sounds. Bit squishy, bit ominous. Didn't blow me away, but they didn't do bad with it.

- I did like the VA gimmick of the main character and her faction/people she works with. Them talking like robots did have me mildly intruiged, though I can imagine I'd get tired of it after a bit.

- I liked the general design of actual game UI, suit, guns, and tech in the game.

That's about all I can think of at the moment. To be clear, don't hate the game or anything, just real "meh" on it. I'll probs pick it up on a sale in like a year.

I think the majority of the reviewers are either paid bots, or easily impressed children. This game seems like a mixed bag of Silent Hill, Resident Evil, and Dead space, and it has failed all three. Yes the game looks stunning, it also runs badly. Yet another Unreal Engine 5 game that trades functionality for art. My cpu is stronger than the reccommended settings, and my gpu is i'd say 10% weaker than what would be reccomended. 

I run it all on high speed RAM and the game itself is on an SSD, it stutters so.. so much. Framerate wil jump erratically between fluent 60+ down into the sluggish and laggy feeling of 30fps or below. Without much reason either, as it can happen when there's almost nothing on screen. Then there's character control, she's slow as a tank but has the HP of a fruitfly. Your 'sprint' is a disinterested jog. Now, i know for a fact that the more immature community on steam wil shoot this review down because it is inconceivable to them that someone can get a general feel for the core parts of gameplay rather quickly. That gameplay as far as i've noticed, is nothing special or interesting. The character is incredibly slow and bulky, which is already a major red flag.

 Movement in a game is critical, it must feel right, examples of this would be early call of duty or even unreal tournament, or the DOOM (2016) reboot or DOOM Eternal. All these games are fantastic due to a combination of the right feel of movement, plus visual art. This game only delivers on visuals, and wil tank performance as a result. Perfect for screenshots, not very practical in real life. And don't go saying "Lol just buy a 3000$ rig". If a piece of modern software cannot run even half decently on very modern and reasonably high end hardware, then the software has not been made correctly.

All in all, this is yet another case where steam would benefit from a point system. I don't want to give it a flat-out thumbs down, rather i'd rate it roughly 6/10. It matters not how great a story is or how interesting or quirky a character is.. Once you spend your own money on a product, and find it lacking, one should make a review detailing the how&why of why it didn't land properly. Prepare for a highly demanding graphical experience, unsteady FPS even if you are in the same area, frustratingly slow character movement, and overall prepare yourself for a game that took too many ideas from too many IP's and implemented them poorly. Yknow the whole meme where a child asks a parent and the parent says they got it at home? This is "We got deadspace, at home." 

I know many wil lose what little emotional control they have at the sight of this review, as any negative review these days somehow equals to "utter and complete hatred" But that is not the case here. The case here, is a person writing a review using freedom of speech to review a product that was found to be lacking in every aspect i could find. Any time a survival horror game introduces slow motion movement as your go-to standard move style, is a no-no. It's survival horror, survival, as in run away. Not a geriatric jog while a limb shredding monster wants you for dinner. Its old, silly, and annoying. 

TLDR: Looks like total eye candy, runs like shit, typical Unreal Engine 5 product designed to keep your money within the first 2 hours as it draws you in with stunning vista's and atmospheric effects, that ultimately do little to nothing as the game offers not much else, as per by other people's reviews as wel.
