From a Galaxy far-far away. Your dreams are becoming true. You’re about to touch them… just with a bit of money spent. Ah, those marketing divisions, if they learned anything about the gaming industry it’s how to sell the expectations. And it’s disgusting.

Cronos could have been taking the best parts of Dead Space and Callisto Protocol and advancing them further. But it didn’t.

No matter what people are saying about Callisto, it has very good things: animations and fluidity in their execution and blending, no stutter when moving and transitioning in between different states, no “stick in the ass” feeling like Dead Space has, but still a very good feeling of heavy armor, and also very good approach opening a road to a very good melee combat system with evade moves that make sense - you don't roll in an armor, you sidestep and you keep the control of your space.

Drawbacks of Callisto are (1) its textures which are a bit generic (and it’s my biggest reproach to the game) - Dead Space has a better atmosphere because in that game textures are organic, you can feel them, they’re alien, scary; (2) its UI which tries to mimic the one from Dead Space, but it’s not doing well enough; and (3) AI restrictions (due to animations processing and queuing) - only one enemy can attack you, others are waiting (I was against this initially, but I learned to like this approach).

In Cronos when you touch something your character is not using his hands, there’s no animation for grabbing. It’s AA, but you don’t need to be AAA to make good animations nowadays with UE5, so those kinds of excuses are just bullshit talks. Cronos UI doesn’t take example from Dead Space, devs probably looked at all the similar games and took the one from Alien Isolation as something easy to implement. But while that UI fits well into the world of Alien, in Cronos it’s disconnected, it makes no sense, there’s no coherence.

Cronos is supposed to be a horror, but it’s not scary at all: scripted sequences when you know exactly which of your actions will trigger enemy spawns, simplistic AI which can’t follow the player through passages in walls (though from their looks and animations it’s clear they could) and either stands still or runs in circles like crazy headless chicken when pathfinding fails. It’s hilarious, but not scary. It negates the difficulty making the game very easy (and it’s also happening with elevations, not just passages).

The best part is the traversal. Because it’s made in the easiest way for devs to implement. If you think you’ve got freedom of movement, it’s false. You won’t do a free jump, it’s a predefined sequence and a non-fluid one (opposite to Callisto). For example, you won’t be able to jump down the floor even if it looks like you can - you need to find a predefined interaction point to do it. And the same mechanic is everywhere. Temporal anomalies (a bit of Stalker here or Quantum Break) - you need to find a premade interaction point to create a passage. And then finally like in Dead Space - you’ve got gravity boots. But you won’t be able to move freely with them - it’s one point to another, premade travel from A to B. So traversal is a fully scripted movement. And here we are - stutters  [b] -- processing... AI bloober team investigating....[/b] Bah ... Probably because Bloober Team did not manage the async loading of resources the right way.

So what’s left for the player? A combat system which is not good: push your trigger to use your weapon, but before that you need to collect resources to upgrade your damage to a comfortable level, because the progression is all about numbers.

Now why I stopped playing and refunded the game: when I got outside into the city I saw a big road with a small fence in between, so small you could step over it… but in this game you can’t. The same way as you can destroy a wooden crate with your stomp, but you can’t destroy a small wooden chair blocking a door. No logic. Sorry, but it’s not possible.

Cronos: A Beautiful Shell in Search of a Soul


On the surface, Cronos has all the makings of a compelling survival horror experience. From the moment the game boots up, it's clear that a lot of care went into its presentation. Visually, the game is impressive, with detailed environments and a polished aesthetic that runs beautifully. The core mechanics are equally solid; the shooting feels tight, responsive, and impactful, providing a satisfying foundation for its combat encounters. 

However, this slick presentation is ultimately a facade, hiding a core experience that feels disappointingly hollow and derivative.

The game's most significant failing is its complete lack of a compelling narrative hook. You are unceremoniously plopped into its world with the barest minimum of context or motivation. The entire complexity of the story, at least in its opening hours, can be summarised as: "Poof. You're looking for someone who went before you." There's no world-building to sink your teeth into, no characters to connect with, and no central mystery that sparks any real curiosity. You're simply a vessel pushed forward with no emotional investment, a critical flaw for a genre that relies so heavily on atmosphere and suspense.

This narrative vacuum wouldn't be so damning if the gameplay loop offered something fresh, but it unfortunately doubles down on unoriginality. The level design is a checklist of "been there, done that" tropes. Progress is constantly halted by the most basic of obstacles: a door with a locked code here, a hunt for a specific key there. It feels less like an engaging puzzle and more like a chore designed to pad out the runtime.
More than anything, the gameplay feels like a reskin of classics like Silent Hill, and it really shows. From the environmental design to the core exploration loop, the inspiration is so heavy that it borders on imitation, but without the psychological depth or masterful storytelling that made those titles legendary. The only way games get away with such familiar mechanics is by wrapping them in a gripping and original story that keeps you desperate to see what's next. Cronos, so far, is completely empty of one.

Maybe the plot will pick up, and these early hours are just a slow burn. But as far as the beginning of a game goes, it has to do more to grab the player. Right now, Cronos is a technically proficient game that looks and feels great to play, but it's an experience utterly devoid of a compelling reason to keep pushing forward. It's a beautiful machine with no ghost in it.

[h1][i]"New breed of Survival Horror"[/i] ~ No. It's not.[/h1]
[h2]PSA: Disable Panini in Display Settings - Helps Cutscene crashes[/h2]

Gosh Bloober Team, I was rooting for you. I still am, the story to Cronos is.. intriguing albeit thin right now but their capacity with optimising UE5 is very concerning. 

[h2]Tldr on: [b]Not recommend[/b][/h2]
- Terrible performance (9800X3D x 4070ti @ 3440x1440)
- Poor UE5 optimisation ~ Consistent choppy drops below 60fps
- Crashing (Particularly during cutscenes)
- Update: About the half way point, incredibly underwhelmed.

[h2]First Impressions[/h2]
The story is thin at this stage, outside a plague that has seemingly wiped out humanity current day, there's not much detail as to what you're doing, what your importance is and the community of other travellers. However, the notion of time travel through rifts is certainly curious on how these events might uncover why the Earth is in the state that it is. So more to come and I'm at least invested to learn more. If the game actually works.. more on that later.

Gameplay is akin to Dead Space weight and combat, with early Resident Evil inventory management torture. You won't be shooting limbs but rather aiming for the head or the glowy fleshy bits. You're encouraged to prime your weapon with a charge before shooting for maximum damage which gives your enemy the chance to close the gap, get a range attack in or complete a wind-up within range. Picking to finish your charge can be tight sometimes to stagger them which is welcome intensity. Along with a flame stun emergency tool, you can also choose to stun and run instead which allows for more evasive play. 

Addressing the resource complaints - It's still early but honestly I've not felt any problems at all and you can opt to avoid combat since enemies don't know how to walk through doors or leave the areas they're clearly attuned to. Running back into the apartments and watching half a dozen enemies along with the big "merged" fatty decide "Welp. Never mind I guess" whilst the door is wide open is hilarious. It does allow for the notion of "Pick your battles" but at the same time, it's 2025 and this is kinda pathetic and ruins any sense of danger.

[h2]"Don't let them merge"[/h2]
Speaking of danger - the enemies are.. uninspired. 
The gimmick for this "New breed of Survival Horror" is a twist on Crimson Heads from Resident Evil 1. Back in 2002... Everything is an inspiration from something, it's tough to be original these days but.. this isn't strictly new guys, come on.

The tag line you'll see in the trailers "Don't let them merge" is the star mechanic here, cautiously choosing how to leave the battlefield: torched or littered. In RE with Crimson heads, you had an option to burn corpses since they could get up after meeting death a second time and come back meaner and faster than ever. The.. *googles* Orphans are closer to Necromorphs with their horrific transformations as previously expressed but if you want to see the real horrors of Cronos, it's almost to suggest.. not to play correctly? Huh?

Great idea on paper but so far, either the area is pimped out with explosive terrain to deal damage or even outright kill enemies (these explosions need more umpf) in the action set-pieces or you can just run. If you play conservatively (which is the whole point) you won't have problems stopping them from merging so..... mute marketing? I do hope more variety comes but so far I'm rather concerned that pressure comes from poor play, which is an odd choice. 

That said, I have chosen to reload an autosave if things aren't going in my favour or I know I could do better to save resources. However, I don't consider this penalising my experience to feel "the merged" since the nature of Survival Horror is coming out on top as best as you can. 

Reserving complete judgement but so far, consider me unimpressed.

[h2]The bad[/h2] 
You know the story for UE5, it's a gorgeous engine with horrendous performance. And the implementation here is no different at all. 

You'll experience frame drops in areas for seemingly no reason, the area doesn't change or events don't occur in the area and you'll consistently drop in the same places. I experienced this several times, the one I can recall is on the landing amongst one of the first buildings you enter and it's a warning sign for things to come. It's not a deal breaker as for where it counts, the drops are absent during combat, so there's that at least. 

Then there's hitching when things are dynamically loading (I assume). Silent Hill 2, Bloober Team's previous project, had this also which ruins the seamless worlds we've come to expect. I don't mind the elevator sequences or forced walking exposition if it means the world can load, 2018's God of War was the first game I truly appreciated this. When the game hitches for a second or two, it just breaks immersion and becomes a blemish rather than a refined work of art. Anything that brings the user out the experience is markedly a problem, an irrefutable fact.

You know what truly breaks immersion? And incites frustration? Crashing. 
In my time with the game so far, I've crashed 3 times. All during cutscenes:
1x when encountering [spoiler]Edward[/spoiler]
2x during the ascendance sequence, ironic and utterly hilarious.

There's no defence for this, when you're ejected from the experience, it takes effort and a desire to see it through to offer up more of my time for your product, giving it fair shake before condemning it. 

After it immediately crashed again initiating the first ascendance sequence in the same place, here I am with this first impression and opposition in a recommendation. I truly ascended as I'm no longer in your crafted world. [i]Ba dum tssssh![/i]

I'll be trying again without streaming to my friends in discord to see if that improves things but if that's a solution, that will only further display the poor experience on show here. 

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
Outside an obscure plot, there's not much innovation here and wouldn't recommend full retail. Even at £40 via Fanatical (great authorised retailer), I'm not impressed and only further frustrated with the performance issues. Take that away, Cronos The New Dawn early hours are nothing more than: okay. 

If you're into Survival Horror, yeah it's gonna be your bread and butter. We're not always in it for the plot and these games are typically more gameplay driven which is to say... it's more of the same. I don't know how Bloober can push this experience as a "new breed". Maybe its intention is to be frustrating and artificial as here comes an additional nitpick:

A key takes up a single inventory slot but so does my Boltcutters? 
If they were limited use, I'd understand but there's seemingly no end to these padlocked doors so it's more of an integral tool. So why the f*ck am I having to juggle this? I also notably have an empty carabiner on my belt. I couldn't use that in some capacity to carry my Boltcutters? I'm an old RE Veteran, this is not new but pushing it imo. 

After all this, pardon my gall here, but I can't help question Bloober Team's competency with the UE5 engine. 

I recently walked away from Virtuous's work on Metal Gear Solid Delta in UE5 and it was seamless. No stutters, hiccups or crashing for the 30 hours to 100% achievements and 4 playthroughs. Therefore I refuse to believe it's impossible to have a good UE5 experience. Especially since Delta is close to 30% cutscenes.

Being this was an in-house project with no outside partners interfering, they had complete control being their own product. Sorry guys, but this has made me doubt you yet again like I did with the Medium and will be choosing cautiously to investigate your projects with more scrutiny here on out. 

Here's to hoping more updates and actually able to progress. Do better.

I feel like it's important to note that I'm a huge fan of Dead Space, Resident Evil - OG and the more modern action focused entries, scifi in general, and Silent Hill.

Cronos draws inspiration from a bunch of different scifi and horror material, namely Twelve Monkeys and Dead Space. The soundtrack is pretty good and the story isn't bad. Every other aspect of the game is mediocre at best. The combat wants to be Dead Space but it's *so* slow and supremely predictable. Every combat encounter is punctuated with reusable explosive barrels that take away any potential surprise. "Reusable explosive barrels?" you ask.. due to time travel shenanigans you can reassemble barrels to blow them up again. You do this after running in circles with your last bullet because ammo is constantly a scarcity. You begin the game with what you think is going to be a really cool heavy handgun that can morph into brass knuckles.. and who knows what else?! I do, I know what else. It morphs into every generic firearm archetype you can imagine and that's about it. You have a flamethrower built into your wrist.. awesome! Not really, it consumes charges that you can only carry one of at a time for most of the game and it basically only serves to stun enemies even though they make it clear that fire is the ultimate weapon against the infected. Enemies are bullet sponges and the "don't let them merge" marketing is essentially moot, if you can hit the broadside of a barn from a few feet away they will never merge. I played for 5 hours and honestly I'm not sure what even happens when they do. The story unfolds as slowly as the combat, and after those 5 hours I had enough and watched the rest of the relevant cut scenes on Youtube. The scariest thing about the game is the unpredictable framerate, tried all sorts of settings and nothing could maintain a decent FPS during combat, and it doesn't even look that great. The enemies are really uninspired and so are the fleshy environments that just look blurry and generic - especially up close. 

All of that said, if you could pick it up on sale for $9.99 I'd recommend it.

Summary: Great visuals.  Amazing sound.  Interesting story.  Bland combat.  Tedious back tracking.  Awful upgrade/weapon balance.  

Great Visuals: The game has an amazing atmosphere, reminds me of Metro 2033 as it seems to take place in a post apocalyptic setting and the confines of an abandoned city therein.  The grim, gray mist and dusk like ambiance is wonderful.  Intermingled with this are heaps of biomass and the obvious presence of the Travelers via safe houses and other fortifications.   A bit like the Combine from Half Life in a way, if they existing in Silent Hill that was also populated by The Many from System Shock 2.

Amazing sound: The crunch of my boots on the cracked pavement.  The gurgling from the masses of flesh.  The sickly patter of creatures feet as they walk thru the apartments chasing me.  The guns sound great (what few of  them I had found) and the electronic clicks and beeps feel perfect.

Interesting story: I did not get very far in before I realized I hated the game, so I can not really comment on this more than it was intriguing and I would have loved to see more if I had decided to stick it out.  It reminds me of the STALKER series in that there are mutants and anomalies present in the area - and a group of folks set on researching or utilizing them for some possibly nebulous purpose.  The writing though was very... obvious in the propaganda.  It seemed to be designed to be unbelievable though.  

Bland Combat: You feel like Robocop but are less maneuverable than such a protag.  It should be that way from the giant helmet you wear and bulky suit.  But in the 5 hours I played combat did not really grab me.  The enemies did though a few times.  It involves mostly knowing where the explosives are and ensuring you are using them to conserve ammo.  In this regard it follows the same type of AI 'director' that Resident Evil 4 had - you receive very little ammo so you will be hard pressed to stock pile it as it prefers to keep you low on ammo to make the battles tougher.   The enemies remind me of a combination from The Thing and Dead Space, but have none of the feeling of dread that accompanies them.  Their attacks are easily dodged and you can run around them without feeling threatened.  Ironically it is when you aim at them to charge your gun that you are in the most danger.

Tedious Back Tracking: You are encouraged early on to burn bodies.  You can only carry 1 flame thrower fuel (2 if you take an incredibly situational and very lack luster upgrade that only allows you to carry a second if you craft it yourself) but can receive an infinite amount of it from dispensers in every base.  Bases are scattered everywhere - as are the bodies - so you will go and burn a corpse, run back and get fuel, burn another corpse, return and get fuel, etc.  The game even makes you do this for burnable walls early on so it is aware this is something it is going to force you to do.  After the 14th corpse I decided I hate this mechanic and began to resent my time in the game.  After the 20th corpse I realized the game is wasting my time.  Totally should have been on a cooldown instead of an item.

Awful upgrade/weapon balance.  There are clear winners and losers here and the %ages seem like they barely matter.  By far and large inventory, weapon stablization and magazine capacity are what I imagine everyone takes.  Then probably charge speed and/or damage.  Other things are useless.  Since your starting pistol is arguably the best weapon there's little reason to use the others aside from if you don't want to reload but instead switch to a different gun.   It is very... forgettable.  As opposed to the weapons in Dead Space or Resident Evil where the upgrades felt powerful, or had some utility to make them memorable. 

I wish I could give the game a 'not for me - wish I could refund it' instead of an upvote or downvote.  However I must give one, and a thumbs down is more appropriate for my limited experience.  If you must buy it wait until it goes on sale.

Graphics and sound are spot on. The atmosphere is excellent and the story is right up my alley; think the movie Twelve Monkeys meets Resident Evil/Dead Space.

The gameplay, on the other hand, isn't great. I could complain about the clunky handling, the limited inventory space, and the linear level layouts, but my main gripe is just how stingy this game is with ammunition. When I mean stingy, I mean ridiculously stingy. I'm no slouch when it comes to survival horror. I know conservation is key, but this borders on downright tedious. Even with fully charged shots (which I'll get to in a second), every enemy takes a pounding before going down, soaking up what precious few bullets you have while yielding diminishing returns, if any drop at all (shoot four bullets, get two back if you're lucky).

Which brings me to the gunplay. I despise charged shots, and you have to charge every shot if you want to stretch your measly ammo across encounters. Every gun I've found so far has charged shots, and while you can shoot enemies without charging, your bullets basically bounce off them; meaning not only does every bullet count but every charged bullet counts even more. It's downright obnoxious. 

My final complaint is with the upgrade system and how this one is just so uninspired. Upgrading weapons boils down to spend energy (game's currency) and purchase the next level of damage, reload speed, charge speed, stability, or capacity. Your suit, on the other hand, requires special items to upgrade, and these are far more scarce. Worse, upgrades are progression capped, meaning you can't save up and max your weapon's firepower first and then move to something else, not that you could really afford to do that anyway with how limited resources are.

All in all, Cronos has an intriguing enough story and atmosphere, but as far as gameplay and survival horror goes, it doesn't really bring anything new to the table or expand on existing concepts of the genre. Compared to something like Dead Space, for instance, which was made almost twenty years ago and from which Cronos clearly draws inspiration, it feels extremely bland and rudimentary in its design and mechanics. Even the enemies are just generic flesh nasties who lazily whack at you, pitting their predictable attacks against your sluggish movement. 

Cronos isn't a terrible game, it's just not all that great either; and when you slap a $60 price tag on your game, going toe to toe with a backlog of stellar classics in the genre, graphics alone just won't cut it. If you can grab this game on sale for $30-40, it's probably a fair deal.

Side thought, but I never understood why more games didn't try going down the 12 Monkeys route. Great movie, if you haven't seen it.

Cronos: The New Dawn opens with a promise—a hauntingly beautiful world steeped in mystery, where every corridor whispers of a forgotten catastrophe and every flicker of light feels earned. The narrative is a slow burn, expertly paced, drawing you deeper into its lore without ever resorting to exposition dumps. It respects your intelligence, letting environmental storytelling do the heavy lifting. From the eerie silence of the derelict observatory to the pulse-quickening descent into the geothermal vaults, the game delivers moments that feel truly epic—cinematic in scale, yet intimate in execution. These sequences, while spoiler-free here, are masterclasses in tension and atmosphere.

The immersion is near-total. Lighting, sound design, and environmental detail coalesce into a world that feels tactile and alive. The suit’s HUD flickers with believable glitches, the ambient hum of machinery feels oppressive, and the subtle shifts in tone as you traverse different biomes reinforce the sense of isolation. It’s clear the developers poured their hearts into crafting a world that’s not just seen, but felt.

But then you’re asked to fight in it.

Combat is where Cronos stumbles—hard. It’s evident the developers intended to convey the weight and restriction of the protagonist’s cumbersome suit, especially when pitted against agile, erratic enemies. That thematic choice could have worked, had it been paired with mechanics that respected the player’s need for agency. Instead, the absence of any block or parry system leaves you exposed, forced into sluggish dodges that feel more like guesswork than strategy.
Aiming—particularly with charged shots—is a chore. The reticle drifts like it’s underwater, and the delay between charge and release often results in wasted ammo, missed opportunities, and mounting frustration. And with ammunition being predictably scarce (as any survival horror fan would expect), the stakes of each encounter feel artificially inflated—not because of tension, but because of mechanical inadequacy.

As someone who’s lived and breathed survival horror, I understand the value of limited resources and vulnerability. But Cronos crosses the line from challenging to punishing, not through design but through oversight. The combat doesn’t complement the narrative or environment—it actively detracts from them. It’s a shame, because the story and setting deserve better.

Until the developers address these core issues—whether through a rework of the aiming system, the introduction of defensive mechanics, or even a rebalancing of enemy behavior—I cannot recommend Cronos: The New Dawn. It’s a beautiful, compelling experience shackled by gameplay that feels like it’s fighting against you.

PROS:

1.Performance, this is the main reason why I cannot recommend this game, from constant stutters, to frames freezing and sudden FPS drops, and not like 2-3 FPS, NO, it sometimes goes down even 25FPS.

I've tested on 2 system, an older i5 11th generation with RTX 4070 and a newer i7 with RTX 5070. 
On both systems in 1440p with DLLS balance + FG ON(not multiple frame generation, just DLSS regular), I get around 65-70ish FPS using also HIGH settings, as the game recommends.
Well, here start the issues, sometimes when using melee attacks your frames drop so bad the image stutters, sometimes when you come near a corner and there's a more bright light that reflects shadows you get again more frame drops. (RTX ON cuts like 35-40 frams, so I never used it)

It is really hard to like this game.
On one side, it's a very pretty and intriguing game, but on the other, the performance is bad, the combat is slow and repetitive, and the resource scarcity is punishing, to the point it makes it hard to win a scenario if you miss just a few shots.

Bloober team did an excellent job with the feel of the game, a lot of people saying the game is "clunky" but it really just feels like classic re4 with strafing instead of tank controls. The character designs are cool, the world and worldbuilding are fantastic, and the sound effects are like candy to the ear.

But to me the big issue is the combat. For something so slowly paced, there should be more options in the way you handle combat encounters. So far, half of the encounters are pretty resource demanding, revolving around shooting nearby explosives or trying to land as many charged headshots as possible. You could shoot them in the legs and stomp on them, but they can still hit you if not stunned, so there's not much reason to do that unless it's a one-on-one encounter. 

And the resource pay off is taxing, even if I do everything perfectly, It will result in missing a good chunk of ammo and not nearly getting enough back for another encounter. And there are moments in the game where there are two scenarios back to back, which is just draining.

The next big thing that annoys me is resource crafting - it was dumb in re4r, so why do it in this game? You never get enough to craft until you've fully explored an area, and for what? Five more bullets? 2 SHOTGUN SHELLS? A light medpen that I find EVERYWHERE!? The crafting system is redundant, there is no thinking behind it, I never have the moment where I need to consider what I should craft first before going into anything, since you rarely ever get enough chemicals anyway. 

Lastly the flame charge. It should not even be a resource since you get a technically "infinite" amount of them. It seriously should be just a recharging ability, that would punish you if you chose the wrong spot to use it, and would take some time to get back. It's very gimmicky and doesn't feel like an actual mechanic, save for the harder combat scenarios.

Underneath all of that the game is still pretty enjoyable, but I wouldn't recommend it. To me it's just a slower, more tedious iteration of dead space, without the cool dismemberment stuff.

Here is my list of cons with this game that are mostly focused on the melee combat:

1. MC is about 10-20% too slow running and recovering from melee attacks given most enemies are up in your face, making movement clunky inside combat.
2. Melee attacks don't do enough damage to balance with needing/wanting to use less ammo. It should be satisfying to stomp an enemy after you down it or as it's on fire, but it isn't.
3. There should probably be a strafe/dodge function in this game given the enemies can stay locked onto you while swinging at you, even at medium distance. (If movement was a bit faster I don't think this is necessary)
4. Many combat sections are in narrow corridors which makes keeping a safe distance frustrating, given the clunky movement makes it easy to get stuck on doors and corners of the terrain during combat.
Bonus. IMHO, I don't think the first weapon damage upgrades should be 3000 energy.

Everything else I've encountered I like. Weapons, upgrades, resource management, time oddities, and the aesthetics.

Dead Space meets Evil Within during the Covid pandemic. That's pretty much this game. If you didn't like either one of those mentioned titles, you most likely will not enjoy this game. I am barely two hours in, as you can tell, and I'm not too thrilled that I invested the full $59.99 price tag. In fact, I was going to refund the game, but alas, I was 2.2hrs into the game by the time I made that choice. In my honest opinion, you're better off waiting for a 30% discount, at a minimum. 

What's wrong with the game? Well, if you're looking for a scary horror game like I was, this isn't it. In fact, I have only played this in the black of night, windows shut, no lights on, and not even a peep came out of me. So, despite having clear inspiration from Dead Space, it does not deliver in the fear department. You may get spooked, of course. However, I didn't grow up playing horror games, I was always too scared. Hell, I couldn't even get myself to play the OG Tomb Raider games because I feared the water sections having sharks. If I am that easily spooked from horror games and this game does not even do anything to me, it surely won't for you. 

The game has very interesting vibes. I don't want to say indie vibes, because Hollow Knight and Silksong are indie, yet they don't give off the vibes this game does. If you ever played the Lords of the Fallen remake, it gives me the exact vibes. I can't tell you what that means, but perhaps it's the feeling of a game that is made by adequate developers who have vision, yet fail to meet that vision in their execution. I don't know what else to tell you. Not a lot of games I've played give me that vibe, but everyone that did, I ended up not liking at all. And I guess these are the same developers who made The Medium? That too was a generic game that has the exact same vibes. You feel me? We ain't vibing, this game and I. And I fear it's them and not me.

Graphics are solid, but again, it seems like low budget. Game-play is very linear. Too linear, if you ask me. And a lot of the time, you jump down obvious paths that the developers want you to go and can't go back. There's not a lot of exploration, so the little backtracking you end up doing is silly. The enemy's are generic looking and easy to dodge. The only thing that I like about this game is the world building you discover as you listen to audio recordings and read letters left over from citizens. But if that's all I'm enjoying out of the game, that's pretty lame. It's not a bad game by any means, but it's not worth the price they're asking for. If nothing else, it's nice to support the developer for making a new I.P when we're constantly getting sequels or remakes. But do we settle for a generic game and call it a win simply because it's a new I.P? Tough call. 

Ultimately, the game is interesting enough to keep you invested, but it's not doing anything new. It's not pushing the genre forward. It's not blazing its own path. It's playing it safe, while taking inspiration from other games that are far greater than it in every aspect.

Given Bloober Team’s previous track record and initial showings of Cronos: The New Dawn, I was considering ignoring it entirely as it looked extremely mediocre at best. Yet, at release, the game started getting a lot of positive reviews from everywhere. It can’t be that so many people are praising a poor game, right? Wrong, apparently. Cronos turned out to be not just mediocre in ways that I predicted, but it also somehow managed to do poorly things, that Bloober Team usually does really well.

Cronos: The New Dawn claims to be a “survival horror” game, though for the initial 3 to 4 hours of my playtime I was fully willing to accept that it was yet another example of marketing gaslighting people into thinking linear third person shooters can be considered “survival horror”. However, as the game goes on, it does become a survival action, of sorts, with even some sections that indeed work as they would in a survival horror game. Which, unfortunately for Cronos, puts it into direct comparison with representatives of several genres, at all of which it is quite average at best.

As mentioned, the game functions as something that could be considered a survival action – think Resident Evil 4, – so it’s an action focused action adventure with horror theme for the story and setting and a mix of fully linear sections with some interconnected locations you get to explore and unlock more of. The team has previously attempted a similar approach in the quite adequate Silent Hill 2 remake last year, though this time around the “more linear” sections are extremely linear. Not that it’s a bad thing if the combat and locations are good, but sadly both are quite poor. The combat is far from the worst I’ve ever played – it functions and there are some nuances to it, like the ability to charge shots or the fact that enemies try to merge with other enemies to get stronger, which can be prevented. But it is exceedingly dull most of the time, except when it’s very poorly thought out and frustrating instead. There’s no real “difficulty” in the latter moments, nor does the game do what The Evil Within did – it doesn’t kill you for “playing wrong”, it’s just so messy that sometimes you get unlucky and start to slowly lose a battle of attrition. Boss fights are especially poorly designed, which is odd, since that was the only genuine combat highlight in Silent Hill 2 remake.

The biggest surprise, though, is in the visuals. I often said about Bloober Team’s games – they don’t know how to design a fun game, but their tech art and level art team are top notch. Their environments always looked interesting, transitions creatively used the Unreal Engine tech, they did a lot of genuinely impressive visual trickery all the time. But Cronos: The New Dawn is easily the ugliest Unreal Engine 5 game I’ve seen. Everything looks dull and boring and very reminiscent of the Unreal Engine 3 era at the end of 2000s, where games often looked hideous and you couldn’t tell one location from another. I feel like they were banking on the whole “alternate reality 1980s Poland after apocalyptic event” atmosphere being weird and unfamiliar to a lot of more English-speaking audience and maybe it is (it’s certainly not weird to me). But I do feel like if you want an interesting take on this whole “vibe”, there are far more visually interesting titles like You are EMPTY, STALKER or, heck, another Polish attempt at creating a Resident Evil 4 clone – Afterfall: Insanity. I can’t believe I am saying that Afterfall is more interesting than anything, but it is actually true.

Storytelling and the plot start very strongly, at least. There’s an interesting mystery and curious events that hook you in and make you wish to learn more. But even by the middle of the game it becomes clear that the most interesting ideas are never developed or followed up, some of the genuinely interesting mysteries are left hanging and the game, in typical Bloober Team fashion, is far less interesting in sci-fi, and more in “what if this was a metaphor about something” plot development that is, at the same time, so non-commital or surprising, that I can’t imagine anyone being interested in it. It’s told very poorly too, with utterly stupid dialogues and cutscenes, wild mood swings between moment to moment and plot points never organically developing or leading from one to another. Things just happen when the developers want them to happen, so there’s no flow to anything narrative or gameplay-related. All while somehow lasting for about 14-16 hours of playtime it absolutely does not deserve.

I’m surprised at this game. Cronos: The New Dawn is extremely mediocre at best, and poorly designed and put together as a game or a story at worst. Yet it is getting far better reception than, say, Post Trauma, which lands in the same range of quality overall. For some reason, people keep giving Bloober a pass and the clout from releasing a decent remake of a fantastic game probably didn’t hurt either. But really – just ignore this one. It’s not good at all and even the already mentioned Afterfall: Insanity is a more interesting project than this. At least it’s often unintentionally funny. This, however, is just boring and frustrating.

[h1]Review after game completion[/h1]
After completing the game, I can say the story absolutely picks up. But it does so too little, too late. I can't concisely summarize the plot, because it's overly complex and the main driving forces behind the characters are ignored in favor of the twist. Unfortunately, this means a lot of basic questions, like "What are the collective?", "Where did the virus come from?", "Why are these specific people being extracted?" and "Are Travelers even human?" are never answered or even really hinted at, and most of the plot only occurs in the last third of the game. There's no real hook to get you into the game, so if you want something more than the strange aesthetic and post-apocalyptic Poland, you won't get it until near the end of the game.

You get more weapon variety later, and the enemy variety does increase, but not significantly. I think there's less than 7 enemy types, with 2 others used and reused as bosses later on. My biggest gripe is that the game FEELS like a total conversion mod of the original Dead Space, with almost every gameplay feature lifted from that, even when it doesn't really make sense (the counter-gravity device is basically the zero gravity system from the original Dead Space). 

At the end of the day, I'm not saying this is a bad game, just that they've made better (with >observer_ and Silent Hill 2 Remake) and if someone were to ask me to recommend them a modern survival horror game, I'd struggle to recommend Cronos over the Dead Space Remake or Silent Hill 2 remake, as the former streamlines a lot of the quirks that Dead Space had which Cronos still has, and the latter is just... well, I doubt I have to tell you anything about Silent Hill 2.

[h1]Original Review[/h1]
I was pretty hyped for Cronos, but I'm afraid it doesn't quite do what I want. It apes Dead Space and Resident Evil, but the whole "mysterious traveler who you don't know and don't understand why you are doing what you are doing" bit puts a massive wrench in the formula. 

I don't care about what happened in Poland (in this game), because it's pretty obvious the resulting zombie apocalypse killed everything. The zombie variety is way, way less interesting than Dead Space. There's almost no characters in the game, what with the protagonist and the single other character I've met being essentially brainwashed zombies by whatever the driving force is that sent them back in time in the first place is. Which leaves you with a survival horror game in a pretty setting that you don't care about, and only two characters; the only actual characterization for either of which is "they like cats."

Combat is... sorta dull. It's not interesting, there's not great feedback on headshots, of the three weapons I've used  so far, the SMG seems to be just straight better than the pistol, since it doesn't have to charge bullets but does about the same damage as 3 charged shots from the pistol. Inventory is really tight, upgrades are dull and outside a few areas it isn't remotely challenging or scary. 

The game isn't bad, the vibes are cool, but like... if i'm not scared, why am I playing this?

What do I dislike about this game?

The game frequently crashes during cutscenes, especially during ascensions, forcing me to skip them entirely. Thankfully, it doesn’t seem like you miss much, but it really breaks immersion.

Resources are incredibly scarce. You spend most of the game scraping by, surrounded by upgrade options but rarely able to afford any of them.

Any time you manage to gather a decent amount of supplies, a swarm of enemies shows up and drains them immediately.

The inventory space is far too limited, making resource management more frustrating than challenging.

I spent a lot of time running back and forth to the safe room to grab my “free” fire capsule (or whatever it’s called) just to clear bodies off the floor so low-level enemies didn’t turn into super beasts.

The church boss fight was incredibly annoying, constantly getting the boss to a sliver of health only to die because I ran out of heals was more exhausting than fun. It wasn't hard on the face of it, it was just awkward and poorly implemented.

[spoiler]Immediately after that fight, you’re thrown into another section where you’re basically forced to run from enemies with one arm, trying not to get hit, which felt cheap and poorly paced.[/spoiler]

Then it crashed again during the cutscene after escaping the church, meaning I had to redo the whole sequence and skip more cutscenes out of fear it would happen again.

By that point, I was done. The church segment drained any enjoyment I had left, and being tossed into more fights with barely any ammo felt like the game had overstayed its welcome.

I did make it to the final boss, but honestly, I had no motivation left to finish it. The fight’s move set includes some seemingly unavoidable attacks, and it’s a complete bullet sponge. Watching a video of someone else beating it was enough to confirm I wasn’t missing anything fun.

Conclusion:
The game clearly wants to be a modern-day Dead Space, but it just doesn’t get there. It feels more like a rough imitation than a tribute. I play games to enjoy myself, not to feel like I’m being trolled by poor design choices.

[h2]Should You Buy [i]Cronos[/i]?[/h2]
If you enjoyed the gameplay of [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/2124490/SILENT_HILL_2/][i]Silent Hill 2 Remake (SH2R)[/i][/url], you might like [i]Cronos[/i] for its similar mechanics. However, its plot, character development, and narrative delivery are weak, making it a hard recommendation for those who value story or expect a true survival horror experience.

[h2]My Experience with [i]Cronos[/i][/h2]
I was frustrated playing [i]Cronos[/i], feeling my time and money were poorly spent. I gave [i]SH2R[/i] a positive review because it exceeded my expectations, despite being a somewhat bloated downgrade from the original [i]Silent Hill 2[/i]. I hoped Bloober Team would excel with an original, action-oriented game like [i]Cronos[/i], but I was disappointed. Here’s why
1) [b]Bloated Length[/b]: The game stretches to 15 hours when it could have been a tighter 7 hours, feeling unnecessarily padded.
2) [b]Underused Mechanics[/b]: A gravity control mechanic, letting you walk on walls or ceilings, is reduced to basic “press X” sections that feel underdeveloped. Other mechanics are also promising but repetitive and underused. 
3) [b]Weak Storytelling[/b]: The story relies on numerous notes that fail to make you care about the world or characters. Only two characters matter; the rest are forgettable and unlikable.
4) [b]Unclear Plot[/b]: The main plot idea is interesting but poorly explained, with time travel elements that lack clarity or meaningful use, leaving the narrative confusing.
5) [b]Repetitive Gameplay[/b]: After the first 40%, no new enemies or mechanics appear. For example, a “wall-sticking” enemy, that appears early in the game, is encountered everywhere until the end, turning combat into repetitive “whac-a-mole”.
6) [b]Not Survival Horror[/b]: Unlike [i]SH2R[/i], which had some non-linearity and exploration, [i]Cronos[/i] lacks these and meaningful backtracking, missing the survival horror genre’s essence.

[h2]What Worked?[/h2]
The main plot idea is compelling, though poorly executed. The combat, crafting ammo, and weapon upgrades are good, though not exceptional.
[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]
[i]Cronos[/i] has a promising main plot idea and decent mechanics, but its long runtime, weak narrative, and repetitive gameplay make it hard to recommend. If you want a gripping story like [i]SH2R[/i]’s or a true survival horror experience, [i]Cronos[/i] will likely disappoint.

So Cronos New Dawn is such a mixed bag, In some areas it excels while other areas it really drops the ball.

In regards to the gameplay it is fairly solid. The shooting mechanics are not too bad however to really do any kind of real damage to enemies you have to charge your gun which really can become frustrating if many swarm you at once, which will happen. Also the bosses are a mixed bag as well. Most are annoying/not fun in regards to how to defeat them and the final boss is such an annoying fight that I quit at the end after several BS attempts. I was mixed on this one, but nah $60 is way too much for what this game is. First things first, yes this is a blatant rip-off of Dead Space without the fun mechanics that made that game interesting. 

 -The combat is serviceable enough but kind of mindless and repetitive, shoot the thing until it dies, the most complex it gets is using fire to stun them momentarily or hit explosive tanks to blow up a bunch of them at once, almost every enemy attacks the same way: “swing around big floompy arm to hit you” or “spits venom”. It doesn’t take too long to get used to every encounter.

-Lack of laser and no shoulder swap. Might sound like a minor complaint but there were many times when my shoots kept hitting the edges of walls even when the crosshair were pointing directly at my target. Also the inability to swap shoulders exposed me to traps that, if you are inside enough to their field of vision, they’ll catch you almost immediately.

-The weapon variety is kind of underwhelming. The game says there are 7 weapons but in reality, there are only 4, with 3 main weapons each with an alternate version, and a special weapon. All alternate versions feel almost the same as the main ones, with some minor tweaks. But the reality is that you don’t even need that many weapons, not only because the combat is so standard, but because there’s an obvious better weapon: the main handgun. You can carry and upgrade the handgun through the whole game and you’ll rarely need any other weapon, it does decent damage, its charged shot is almost as powerful as that of a shotgun, you can carry a decent amount of ammo in each inventory slot and they’re the cheapest to make. I had so much extra ammo for my other weapons that I practically never ran out.

-The story. Knowing this was a Bloober Team game I was already expecting 4 things: Cool visuals, cool atmosphere, bad dialogue, and mid writing, and oh boy they do deliver. Not spoiling anything, the lore and the mystery behind what is happening in the world, who you are and what is your mission are interesting enough to tolerate the poor way some of the pieces of story were delivered. But all goes downhill at the end when all the interesting mystery gets dropped for some relationship drama with some of the most cliché dialogue and on the nose allegories, you can’t help but roll your eyes. Is this really strange tug of war the writers have between having characters say “theme” related stuff and things that make sense, and is really weird to watch. 

I didn't hate the game, in fact this is definitely my favorite Bloober Team game so far, but it's a bit too disappointing and I don't think is worth that price.

Tried to like it and I was enjoying it to an extent for the first 10 hours but the gunplay overstays it's welcome very quickly and the game becomes a slog.

I guess the game is "difficult" but I wouldn't call it a selling point like it is for souls likes and other similar games in the survival horror genre. A lot of the larger encounters can lead to trial and error to progress. For me the difficulty comes from having to dig deep within yourself to muster up the effort required to actively engage with the games combat to overcome the challenging encounters the developers place in front of you.

 If you enjoy the gunplay and are fully engaged, I would say the game is fairly easy. The combat really revolves around understanding what attacks the enemies will perform based on their startup animation, and taking the necessary maneuvers to evade them. Then you start shooting them during an opening with whatever gun you choose, and repeat. There are other systems that allow you to stun multiple enemies and control the chaos, but the basic gunplay is dodge, shoot, repeat. This game feels like it wants you to find out how to cheese every encounter, which doesn't take long.

Now this might sound fun, but you aren't really given many tools to interact with this loop. Unlike the developers previous game, Silent Hill 2, there is no dodge mechanic with I-frames, and the melee is reserved for desperate situations when your ammo runs dry. When you aim your gun, your movement is severely limited, which reminded me of Resident Evil 5 where you could not move at all while aiming (that game is amazing though). Ammo can be sparse, similar to other survival horrors. Your movement is pretty clunky as it is, so when you engage enemies within the gameplay loop I described above, it turns into this weird strategy of running around in circles for evasive maneuvers in between openings where you can punish the enemies.

As much as I disliked the combat in Silent Hill 2, I feel that Cronos really needed another movement tool like a dedicated evade button to make the combat make some sense. It really feels like there's a mechanic or two that's missing from making the combat feel natural and fluid. Going back to the difficulty aspect, because I found this combat loop to quickly become repetive and boring, my patience ran out and I think that's where the "difficulty" comes in. Because the combat is relatively unforgiving, if you are reckless and impatient, you will have a difficult time getting through large encounters. 

I was expecting puzzles, but I would argue they are largely absent from this game. Most "puzzles" just require you to continue along the mostly linear level designs, find some item that acts as a key, loop back to the local hub of the area you're in, and unlock a doorway that continues progression. There is a gameplay mechanic where you can manipulate the environment by interacting with magical sci fi spheres to open up new pathways or help with combat, but aside from the couple that are lazily hidden behind something, they are right in your face and come off as more of a gimmick than anything. Rarely do these result in you finding optional content, most of it is required to progress. Later in the game you get the ability to jump around in what can be described as a zero g environment similar to the 2008 Dead Space gravity boot mechanic, but this too is largely linear in level deisgn, requiring you to move around your camera to find the one platform you're able to jump to.

What kept me going in this game was the interesting world building and mysterious plot. I won't spoil anything, but everything, from the state of the world to who your character is and how they fit in the world was very interesting to me. I thought this would be enough to will myself through the slog of a gameplay loop, but the pacing and dialogue were so slow and plodding that eventually the whole game turned into a complete chore. 

Major characters in the game, including yourself, talk in a slow monotonous robotic tone. I understand that there may be reasons for this in the lore, but after a while I found myself completely tuning out all the cutscenes because of h o w   s l o w   t h e   c h a r a c t e r s   s p o k e. I found myself staring at the armors and details of the characters, studying the background of the scenes, and before I knew it the cutscenes were over and I had learned nothing. Maybe for others this is not an issue, but I could not care less about the cutscenes.

But even with all those issues, is the game actually scary? I would say not really. It's more of a mysterious and atmospheric game than a full on horror experience. Even moreso that SH2. And this aspect I think is done very well. The only times I felt myself engrossed in this game were when my curiosity was fully piqued. I would walk down the corridors taking in the details, big and small, that painted a picture of what happened in this world. Then I'd encounter combat and quickly lose interest.

A lot of comparisons to Dead Space have been made. This is purely an aesthetic similarity; the gameplay is nothing like it. The combat is much more in line with Silent Hill 2 remake for obvious reasons, though I think it might be a step down (I hated SH2 combat). 

All this is disappointing because the game looks amazing, the trailers got me excited even after I found SH2 remake to not be my cup of tea. But when I really got into the meat of the game I just found I had to convince myself to not quit and play literally anything else from my Steam library. Even though I mentioned this game is nothing like Dead Space, it really did make me want to play that game instead. 

I'm aware a lot of people have performance issues with this game, same as SH2. I will say the games runs very well for me, without the constant stuttering that I experienced in SH2, but I do have a relatively beefy rig.

Before I arrived at this idiotically-conceived fight, there was much to enjoy about this game:

GOOD:
- The atmosphere, sound, and overall visuals were good (with some odd choices here and there, like lightning that looked like it had been drawn by a child).
- The gameplay flow was interesting and satisfying, and not as difficult as early reviews led me to fear. If you pay attention to cues and your environment, you'll do all right. However, this is not a typical shooter. If you waste ammo or try to dodge your way out of combat, you're dead.
- The various missions and environments were interesting, and the gravity elements were creatively handled.
- I don't know if this is a good or bad point—you'll need to decide that for yourself—but the game is not scary. It's creepy and sometimes sad, but not once was did I glance behind my gaming chair in apprehension. I mean, once you've seen one or two fleshly abomination, everything similar is just a variation on that theme.

BAD:
- Upgrades are expensive but never seem to make much difference. That is a true crime in games like this. You make me suffer and scrounge; you'd better give me some bang for my heard-earned buck,
- There is no difficulty setting. So basically, because I'm not good enough or, in the end, patient enough, I literally can't finish this game. That is a deplorable, anti-gamer approach to game design.
- There are typos in some of the text logs, and some awkwardly-translated sections. Come on. Be better than that.
- I actually came to enjoy the clunky movement and limited weapons, but the lack of a dodge mechanic was a deplorable omission in a game that demands you to constantly evade melee attacks.
- The story completely falls apart at the end. Whether it was laziness or a lack of sufficient time or some other factors, I don't know. But I have no idea what they were trying to say, and many questions remained (for me) unanswered). The "big revelation" fell utterly flat, buried beneath the plodding, incomprehensible delivery of the Warden. I spent twenty-plus hours following a story, and it just fizzled out. So, so bad.
- It was an absolutely ridiculous plot point to so strongly evoke Covid. Whether or not that was the intent, I don't know or care. But a virus that ravages an entire population, despite isolation and feverish attempts at a cure...didn't we all just live and suffer through that?! What in the world would make anyone think that's appropriate game fodder?

UNFORGIVABLE:
- Non-specific spoilers from this point on.
- By the time you reach the last boss fight, you have spent all your resources on ammo and upgrades. You can swap weapons, but you have no way to buy more ammo or even switch out your upgrades. You're stuck with what you have, with absolutely no warning that that will be the case. Horribly unfair.
- Even if you could equip yourself well, it doesn't matter when that hateful enemy can kill you without warning with one swipe or blast.
- When you die (and you will), you must skip through two cutscenes and climb a ladder (which is a long, tedious process in its own right), in order to get back to the battle. Thanks for making a tedious level that much more unbearable.
- The boss fight is one we've seen too many times before: level one is survivable with practice. Level two is survivable with more practice. Level three is utterly unforgiving but survivable after you learn the patterns. Level four is simply impossible for me, and I've been gaming since the dawn of the internet. You have to get through the first three long levels to get to that last one, and when you do, you die too quickly to really learn anything. The polar opposite of an enjoyable, satisfying experience.

WHEN will game developers learn that games should be FUN before they're anything else? I can put up with just about any flaw as long as I'm enjoying myself. Instead, they layer on such brutal frustration that I never want to play another game by this developer and I can't even experience the ending of this one...an ending I feel I've more than earned the right to see.

What a crushingly disappointing end to a game that I would otherwise have recommended (with the caveats I've already mentioned).

With [i]Silent Hill 2[/i], the narrative, gameplay loop and enemy designs were already in place. Bloober elevated that with their strengths (atmosphere, sound design and overall gameplay feeling) which are also great here. The problem is that, without the borrowed framework, everything else falls flat.

So ultimately,
Do you want a really good survival horror experience? [spoiler]Buy [i]Resident Evil 4R[/i][/spoiler]
Do you want a neat atmospheric survival horror game in space? [spoiler]Buy [i]Dead Space[/i] or [i]Alien: Isolation[/i][/spoiler]

This is a hard game to review because I love almost everything about it. While conflicted, I was ready to end on an overall recommend, until I reached the final stage of the game. The visuals are stunning. The story is interesting, and the game play is overall very engaging. It genuinely feels like a perfectly crafted game. The one failing trait is that I don't think the developers actually care if players enjoy the experience. 

Don't get me wrong, there are players who want this level of challenge, so there is an audience for it. The enjoyment of everyone else is just unimportant, or so it feels. What sucks is that it just seems utterly unnecessary as you could easily enable different difficulties, or even build in options to remove certain mechanics of the resource management--a component I generally enjoyed engaging with, but only up to a point.

While I am marking it as *not recommended*, the truth is I just want to see the developers release an update that offers more accessible difficulty levels. It took me a solid 10 hours to learn the basic game play techniques needed to thrive in this game.  While I recognize part of that is on me, I also think there needs to be much better tutorials. We can punch or smash gas barrels without using ammo--except when they are red. You can evade most attacks by walking away as the enemy charges up, and you don't always need to shoot--in fact its best to assume you don't until you know you have to given the limited resources. Then there are enemies who only take damage on glowing boils--sometimes only after being burnt (details that are just left to figure out on your own). These are essential things that you learn playing, but the lack of sufficient guides by the game makes you learn by experience--which it is hard to get joy out of failing just because I've not been told basic mechanics for the game play. 

After my first 7 hrs or so I decided to max out my equipment upgrades with Cheat Engine, but I left the resources limited. This works out well because equipment upgrades are limited by how far you are in the game (even if you have the right ingredients to otherwise upgrade). This, coupled with learning the basic techniques, made for a generally great experience for me. That is, again, until we reach the final set of boss fights (the church fight specifically), where I spend an hour and a half trying to defeat the boss, literally up to the last strike needed, only to go down given the increasingly limited resources and area to maneuver. I can't tell you how unsatisfying that is. I don't even mean losing. I knew how close I was, and even if succeeded, that was a level of difficulty I just got little enjoyment from. I promptly proceeded to use Cheat Engine for unlimited ammo, because I had no interest in repeating that a single time. This is where I am at now.
 
I will finish the game. I don't know if I will keep the unlimited ammo, but i do know this game needs to be better accessible if I am going to just mass recommend it. If you are up for the challenge or are ready and able to utilize cheats, then I say 100% go for it. To be clear, I loved this game in almost every way. I wish more people could enjoy it, so why not let them Blooper?

This game is about 15 hours long on a first playthrough if you're competent at survival horror games.

The game is not particularly scary. There's a couple of flashing image + audio jumpscares, but otherwise you're fighting spaghetti people for most of the game. 

There isn't a lot of enemy variety. If we don't count variants of the same enemy, there's 3 enemy types in the game, and 5 boss types in the game.

The charged shot mechanic is fun to play with, and the gunplay is satisfying. Just the starting pistol feels like a pocket railgun which is great. But the movement is clunky, which is on purpose so you can't avoid damage easily, and there's no additional mechanics to the combat gameplay loop. Shoot enemy, throw explosive at enemy, shoot explosive barrel next to enemy. That's it.

The merging mechanic is easy to ignore since any merging enemy can be stunned out of merging with a charged headshot. Burning bodies is not a viable strategy most of the time because of the limited ammo on your personal flamer, and the fact having flamer ammo on you takes inventory space when you have such limited inventory.

There's melee buttons but I don't think you're meant to use them. Outside of when you're in NG+ or late in your first playthrough, if you've figured out enemy health breakpoints there's -sometimes- you can use it safely, but most of the time the melee button might as well not exist.

No dodge, no parry, no Stasis, no Kinesis, nothing. Its a survival horror game from the mid 2010s. It does nothing particularly new.

And I know what some people are going to say. If you give the player more ways to fight back you make the game less scary. Taking away player agency, player options, and making the player feel weak is how you build tension and make a good horror game.

I'd agree with you if I wasn't 1-shotting every basic enemy with the starting handgun once I fully upgraded its firepower.

I'd agree with you if I wasn't 2-shotting wall crawlers, which ambush you in large numbers and from odd angles and are clearly meant to be an actual scary enemy with it too.

The game doesn't give you the power fantasy but it doesn't do enough to be scary either.

And more frustrating than all of that, is that it leaves too many questions unanswered to instead focus on a personal drama storyline. All the parts of the game that are interesting to me, are left vague. Who/what are the collective? Who made them? Who made the tech we're using? How does the time travel work? What started the change?

We can only speculate with vague snipets of information left on notes and audio logs. There is no concrete evidence, which means the game's biggest most interesting misteries never go answered.

Buy it for half price.

It is a real shame I have to lean toward the not recommend on this one, because the game has some pretty good combat direction and the balancing act between a rather limited resource economy made for a strategic angle I haven't seen in while. The problem ultimately comes down to the story elements, particularly abandoning the most interesting aspects of the plot for a rather predictable time loop story that doesn't have any direct pay off, even when you make it to the end of new game +. I enjoy leaving things up to interpretation as much as the next person, but when you basically bog down the entire third act (which is thankfully very short) with something far less interesting with no hope of getting a resolution in the main plot that sparked the interest to play the game to begin with, it comes off as a major disappointment. Then you have the voice acting, limited character scope, unskippable cutscenes (not all of them, but anything with a unimpactful dialog choice will force you to rewatch it), overall model movement in cutscenes, very rough environmental design (engine issues most likely), and a slew of annoying clipping issues that force the need to load a previous save. I wanted to love this game, and normally a good foundation for combat can carry a weak story, but I at least expected something in the form of a conclusion (I guess B ending, but C barely gives anything for the length I pushed through to see it).

Performance:
The performance is the biggest issue. Stuttering and severe FPS drops happen in some areas, even though I’m running the game on a 4090 with 7800x3d. With this kind of hardware, I shouldn’t have performance problems, but unfortunately, it suffers from the same issues as Silent Hill 2—it's a mix of Unreal Engine 5 struggles and poor optimization from the developers, and that’s unacceptable.

Story & Presentation:
I actually enjoyed the story, the level design, and the voice acting. Those aspects were well done and kept me invested.

Gameplay:
The gameplay, however, was disappointing. The beginning is strong—you need to be careful with your shots, conserve ammo, and manage inventory. But in the second half, the pacing falls apart. The game just throws waves of enemies at you, one after another, purely for the sake of difficulty. That isn’t good design. On top of that, recycled boss fights make the experience feel repetitive, boring, and lazy.

It tries to channel the kind of intensity and polish that Dead Space had , but Dead Space actually delivered and still stands as an incredible experience. The end completely turned the tables for me and I cannot recommend the game simply due to how it shapes when you get to the end. It's ass.

The first 3/4 of the game is very good, and I really hate to give it a thumbs down. But there are just too many things I disliked here that prevent me from recommending it. No, it wasn't too hard. I have played [i] lots [/i] of horror games over the years, and it mostly ran fine on my system.

Let's start with what I liked. It attempts to be a survival horror game, and mostly succeeds. It has limited inventory and fairly slow, deliberate combat in claustrophobic environments. The gameplay is solid and has some unique quirks that I haven't seen in the genre. Taking cues from RE1make, you need to burn the corpses of enemies - otherwise, living ones will come along and absorb them, making them stronger. Combat is more frantic as a result, as you need to make split second decisions on which enemies to burn with your precious incendiary resources. Moreover, the combat largely revolves around charged shots. You hold down your trigger to charge, but once you start, you are committed to the shot. As such, you need to be confident in your ability to make a hit before you pull the trigger. If you rely too heavily on quick, uncharged shots, you will rapidly run out of ammo. I found the challenge to be just right - I rarely felt too comfortable, but I wasn't constantly scraping by, either. 
There are also lots of collectables, which is always a big plus for me. Bonus weapons, hidden areas, and [spoiler] cats that drop upgrades [/spoiler] are fun to discover. 
Voice acting and graphics are mostly excellent. Lots of neat visual effects, and the performances are full of emotion.
Finally, the setup to the story is unique and intriguing. The setting of Communist Poland was a neat choice, and a great setting for a story about a disease outbreak. More than anything, the mystery of The Change, who The Collective & The Traveller are, and picking up on thematic elements kept me wanting to proceed through gameplay that was mostly fun.

Unfortunately, I noticed early on that the environments are quite bland and linear. You spend a lot of time traversing through half-collapsed apartment buildings that all blend together. It really becomes a problem about 3/4 through. After the third main area, I was ready for the game to start winding down and have the mystery solved. Unfortunately, I was stuck traversing more ruined apartment blocks, fighting waves of the same enemies, solving the same type of basic puzzle, and reading more expository notes that really didn't add much. At this point, when you need to [spoiler] start a generator to activate a tram - which you've already done between areas 1 and 2 [/spoiler] The Traveller says "this is getting tedious". Okay, then. If the devs [i]know[/i] it's tedious, why include the padding? And why give me a sly little wink about it? Just get rid of the sequence altogether.
It became especially frustrating right before the final boss [spoiler] when you fight gauntlets of enemies and go through a looping hallway, only to end up back in the room you entered from [/spoiler]. Why? What's the point? There's a the trite saying of "less is more", and in this case, it's certainly true. By the end of the game, I didn't care much any more. I was just ready for it to be done. 

And then...[spoiler] You're treated to an ending that doesn't really explain anything. All of the interesting themes and plot points that were set up are just...unresolved, in favour of something much more simple and much less interesting.[/spoiler]
Now, maybe it's one of those games that you need to play twice to fully understand, or get another ending. Which I'm okay with, in theory. But Cronos' biggest issue is that it's repetitive, and overly long to boot. The results screen said my runtime was 16 hours. And with how much I disliked the last 3 or 4 hours of the game, I don't see myself ever playing it again. There are many sequences that could have been cut that wouldn't have detracted from the story at all, and would have shortened the runtime by 2-4 hours. In this instance, the game would have benefited greatly.

It's a shame. I thought Cronos was fantastic for the first half or so, and I thought many of the criticisms were unfounded. It wasn't too hard - I liked the "clunky" combat and limited inventory, and resources were fairly generous. I was drawn in by the somewhat confusing nature of the story that invited me to piece it together. I didn't have (many) performance issues.**

But it just doesn't know when to stop, and really fumbled the ending.

Given that the current horror landscape is largely dominated by legacy franchises, I was hoping for something to really shake things up. And for a while, it looked like Cronos was it. I hate to give it a thumbs down.

Full breakdown

This game has so many great ideas that it refuses to explore more than on a surface level. It's not terrible just so very mediocre and by the numbers. You walk around reading a stack of notes and audio logs left behind by people while also gathering resources. You do one or two smaller enemy encounters to whittle down those resources you just collected. You visit a safe room right before a bigger fight so you can use currency and points to upgrade your equipment. Unfortunately the weapon upgrades don't have branching paths or any interesting bonuses to them, it's the "number goes up" type of a deal.

The game draws heavy inspiration from action focused survival horror games like Dead Space and Resident Evil 4. It however doesn't include fun or useful quality of life features like quickturning or a map. There is no separate inventory for quest items. There were multiple times where I had to backtrack to a safe room to store some items or simply waste some bullets so I could pick up the next mcguffin required to proceed. Inventory is very limited and needs to be upgraded with points for more space.
You only have one gun that transforms between different types so why is it that all the different forms take up one more inventory slot? This resulted in me not experimenting with the different variations simply because there wasn't enough space to carry them around.

You can charge your weapons up for more damage but this causes the crosshair to start shaking around violently while the enemy is barreling towards you. This adds a nice risk&reward mechanic that forces you to risk getting hit by the enemy. Character movement is deliberately slow and slightly clunky. Enemies are rather slow so it balances out decently enough.

Enemies aren't very interesting. It's the very trope biomass that deforms people into hideous monstrosities. This type of body horror loses all scare factor when used too much. Almost every area is just goopy flesh walls so it trivializes the horrid nature of the sickness that wiped out the world.

Game includes minor environmental puzzles where you have to route electricity by shooting spikes into a wall. I wish you could charge up these spikes so you could use them to stun enemies during combat or to create electrical traps during fights. The spikes are used on puzzles only and nothing else.
You can also rewind time at certain points of the game. Usually this means uncollapsing a structure so you can walk forward. It also allows you to rewind exploded barrels so you can reuse them during combat. This makes some enemy encounters trivially easy.
There is also gravity defying platforming similar to Dead Space remake but those are at very set points and usually just a way to get the player across longer distances. The gravity shenanigans aren't used in any interesting way, simply to get player across floating platforms in a boring void. Towards the end of the game there is a glimpse of what could have been when you get to fight upside down against some enemies.

The enemies themselves can merge with dead bodies becoming more powerful but this was rarely an issue. It did put nice pressure on the player during some of the early fights in the game when guns aren't as powerful and ammo is scarce. Later on this whole thing is trivialized by your powerful guns and the abundance of explosive canisters in nearly every big arena you fight in. You can also reuse the explosive canisters by rewinding time to reconstruct them.

WHOEVER WAS IN CHARGE OF APPROVING THE FOLLOWING ENEMY DESIGNS NEEDS TO BE PUT IN THE NAUGHTY CORNER! It is as if they tried to take the worst types of enemies from other games. Exploding acid blisters that are hidden behind corners or on walls. They can be shot to pop them or triggered by going near them for a second and running away. They spew acid on the floor forcing you to wait for a moment before proceeding. There are also tiny crawling explosive acid enemies that crawl towards you, explode if you get too close and jump at you exploding at contact. Worst ones are the wall enemies that quickly grab you forcing you to complete a quick time event to break free. Very often they are placed in very cheap spots or trigger when you pick up resources from a certain spot. Did they not listen to any of the playtesters since I can't fathom anyone enjoying these miserable time wasting traps.

The game has a poor balance between resource gathering and combat. There is too much snooping around for ammo and not enough situations to use said ammo. Whenever the game showed me a hallucination of a massive enemy horde I was ecstatic "FINALLY A BIG FIGHT!" only to make all the enemies vanish.

Boss fights early on are alright and those types become standard enemies later as is typical. Closer to the end of the game there are two boss fights almost back to back and both are such annoying ordeals to slog through. Acid spitting one liner repeating flesh totem with wall blisters that need to be popped and a teleporting bastard that has nearly unavoidable attacks. The final boss has two cutscenes right before you encounter him and thankfully you can skip those.

The performance of the game was all over the place. Lots of moments where it was stuttering and dropping FPS. I haven't tried the game on the Steam Deck yet but I'm very sceptical about them getting it Verified when it runs this poorly on a gaming PC on medium graphics (with DLSS on ultra performance setting).

I would recommend picking this up from a 50-75% sale if you're really thirsty for some third person shooting. Just don't expect to do that much shooting.
