[h1] Cronos: The New Dawn is a technical disaster [/h1]

After spending over an hour tweaking settings, I came to the conclusion that this game is simply unplayable for me. GPU memory usage is constantly maxed out at 100%, causing the game to run out of VRAM and throttle nonstop. Frame rates swing wildly — jumping up to 80 FPS, then dropping to as low as 20 in an instant. Traveling between areas causes constant stuttering, even after shaders have supposedly finished compiling. No matter what settings I use, performance remains awful across the board.

It’s a shame, because the game itself looks genuinely interesting. However, some design choices completely kill immersion. Having to press a button just to jump or squeeze through tight spaces feels clunky. The bright yellow paint marking breakable crates look ridiculous and break the atmosphere. And for some reason, the flashlight turns on and off automatically — you can’t control it yourself. It even flickers to “warn” you of nearby danger. Hard to believe this is the same studio behind last year’s Silent Hill 2 Remake.

It’s clear that Cronos: The New Dawn takes a lot of inspiration from Dead Space, and I’ve heard the story is actually really good. Unfortunately, the technical performance is so bad that I can’t even experience it properly. Until the developers fix these issues, I can’t recommend this game in its current state.

A No with a caveat.

Cronos does nothing new with its survival horror roots. If you're a seasoned vet of the genre all the good and bad you'll remember from earlier titles is here. That is it's downfall. Outside of its setting, a Cronenbergian Soviet apocalypse, everything feels very familiar. As you march forward through the grey wasteland you'll find yourself wondering if you've played this game before. In another place, another time, you played this game to death and now returning to it you know all its tricks by heart. None of the ambushes will ever surprise or scare you, you've seen them all and their telegraphing before. No enemy will phase you as you revert to skills learnt over a decade ago. The sight of an explosive barrel or a time anomaly will come to cause a sigh of frustration, a desire for this nostalgic experience to be over already.

Then you'll find the game wants to be played a second time, not explored a second time of course, as this is a linear game, there's nothing new to explore here. No you'll be asked to march through the whole thing again with some minor tweaks, just for the chance to see another ending, because again you played this game 10 or more years ago and we have learned nothing about game design in the intervening time.

So what's the caveat? Well if you're newish to the survival horror genre this might still be a fresh enough experience for you to get something out of it. It'll be an uphill struggle in places as the game doesn't care deeply about making sure you don't screw yourself over and by the end of it you'll be very aware of the genres enduring flaws, but if you're still exploring the survival horror genre, Cronos would make a great second or third game.

The inventory system might be the worst in gaming history; it feels like it was put there just to make things harder for the player. Also, upgrades don’t seem to affect the weapons, it felt like the upgraded and non-upgraded versions hit with the same effect. The character’s movements are very clunky, and the lack of a dodge feature basically turns you into a sitting duck.

Even though the atmosphere and story of the game are overall quite good, you can’t really enjoy it because of the inventory system, and after a certain point you just get bored of the game. At some point, I stopped following the story and started going back constantly just to look for resources.

The variety of enemies is nice, but dealing with them is very difficult because of the constant ammo shortage. Instead of making the gameplay itself challenging, they’ve tried to keep the game difficult through these unnecessary restrictions, which I think is a very wrong approach. At the very least, they should have added a dodge mechanic. Unfortunately, I have to give it a negative review.

This game has so many great ideas that it refuses to explore more than on a surface level. It's not terrible just so very mediocre and by the numbers. You walk around reading a stack of notes and audio logs left behind by people while also gathering resources. You do one or two smaller enemy encounters to whittle down those resources you just collected. You visit a safe room right before a bigger fight so you can use currency and points to upgrade your equipment. Unfortunately the weapon upgrades don't have branching paths or any interesting bonuses to them, it's the "number goes up" type of a deal.

The game draws heavy inspiration from action focused survival horror games like Dead Space and Resident Evil 4. It however doesn't include fun or useful quality of life features like quickturning or a map. There is no separate inventory for quest items. There were multiple times where I had to backtrack to a safe room to store some items or simply waste some bullets so I could pick up the next mcguffin required to proceed. Inventory is very limited and needs to be upgraded with points for more space. 
You only have one gun that transforms between different types so why is it that all the different forms take up one more inventory slot? This resulted in me not experimenting with the different variations simply because there wasn't enough space to carry them around. 

You can charge your weapons up for more damage but this causes the crosshair to start shaking around violently while the enemy is barreling towards you. This adds a nice risk&reward mechanic that forces you to risk getting hit by the enemy. Character movement is deliberately slow and slightly clunky. Enemies are rather slow so it balances out decently enough.

Enemies aren't very interesting. It's the very trope biomass that deforms people into hideous monstrosities. This type of body horror loses all scare factor when used too much. Almost every area is just goopy flesh walls so it trivializes the horrid nature of the sickness that wiped out the world.

Game includes minor environmental puzzles where you have to route electricity by shooting spikes into a wall. I wish you could charge up these spikes so you could use them to stun enemies during combat or to create electrical traps during fights. The spikes are used on puzzles only and nothing else.
You can also rewind time at certain points of the game. Usually this means uncollapsing a structure so you can walk forward. It also allows you to rewind exploded barrels so you can reuse them during combat. This makes some enemy encounters trivially easy.
There is also gravity defying platforming similar to Dead Space remake but those are at very set points and usually just a way to get the player across longer distances. The gravity shenanigans aren't used in any interesting way, simply to get player across floating platforms in a boring void. Towards the end of the game there is a glimpse of what could have been when you get to fight upside down against some enemies. 

The enemies themselves can merge with dead bodies becoming more powerful but this was rarely an issue. It did put nice pressure on the player during some of the early fights in the game when guns aren't as powerful and ammo is scarce. Later on this whole thing is trivialized by your powerful guns and the abundance of explosive canisters in nearly every big arena you fight in. You can also reuse the explosive canisters by rewinding time to reconstruct them. 

WHOEVER WAS IN CHARGE OF APPROVING THE FOLLOWING ENEMY DESIGNS NEEDS TO BE PUT IN THE NAUGHTY CORNER! It is as if they tried to take the worst types of enemies from other games. Exploding acid blisters that are hidden behind corners or on walls. They can be shot to pop them or triggered by going near them for a second and running away. They spew acid on the floor forcing you to wait for a moment before proceeding. There are also tiny crawling explosive acid enemies that crawl towards you, explode if you get too close and jump at you exploding at contact. Worst ones are the wall enemies that quickly grab you forcing you to complete a quick time event to break free. Very often they are placed in very cheap spots or trigger when you pick up resources from a certain spot. Did they not listen to any of the playtesters since I can't fathom anyone enjoying these miserable time wasting traps.

The game has a poor balance between resource gathering and combat. There is too much snooping around for ammo and not enough situations to use said ammo. Whenever the game showed me a hallucination of a massive enemy horde I was ecstatic "FINALLY A BIG FIGHT!" only to make all the enemies vanish. 

Boss fights early on are alright and those types become standard enemies later as is typical. Closer to the end of the game there are two boss fights almost back to back and both are such annoying ordeals to slog through. Acid spitting one liner repeating flesh totem with wall blisters that need to be popped and a teleporting bastard that has nearly unavoidable attacks. The final boss has two cutscenes right before you encounter him and thankfully you can skip those. 

The performance of the game was all over the place. Lots of moments where it was stuttering and dropping FPS. I haven't tried the game on the Steam Deck yet but I'm very sceptical about them getting it Verified when it runs this poorly on a gaming PC on medium graphics (with DLSS on ultra performance setting).

I would recommend picking this up from a 50-75% sale if you're really thirsty for some third person shooting. Just don't expect to do that much shooting.

[b]What it did well:[/b]
- Graphics: one of the best looking games I've played
- Level Design: Very detailed settings, very well designed environments that don't really force you to backtrack (but the inventory system does), very well designed and placed props.
- Voice acting: Very good.
- Music/Audio: Perfect, it really helps set the atmosphere. Both audio effects and music are really well made.

[b]What it didn't do well[/b]:
- The inventory and storage system - tries to emulate RE, but ends up as constant, unfun juggling.
- Overused cheap jump scares. Towards the end it's just annoying, since the game keeps doing the same thing over and over again.
- The Story: Feels like it was written by multiple people. Someone started a very good, compelling story. And someone else, not so talented, finished it.
I felt let down at the end. Even though I liked playing it, the second half was so frustrating, with the ending and the constant inventory frustration, that I felt cheated of my time somewhat.

Initially this game was a recommend for me, until the last boss fight. One of the absolute worst implementations of a final boss fight I've ever seen. I thought this was going to be the first time I gave a bloober game a positive review. They were SO close and had to just mess it up at the end. 

The game is designed that you need to run when enemies get close, create a little distance, and then hit them with charged shots. There is no dodge mechanic. This works completely fine once you get used to playing this way, until the final boss where everything changes. Now running just equals death and you also have to try and hit him for enough damage fast enough to stop attacks. Otherwise he is far faster and has a few attacks that are going to almost always hit unless you get lucky and move just the right way he might miss. One of the attacks you can't ever get away from. Have to shoot him to stop him and that's if you are lucky enough to not need to reload. 

I only died a few times prior to that fight, then I died a bunch until I got the perfect roll of the dice. 

a few other cons worth noting that are annoying but not end of the world. 

- Inventory is ridiculously small and ends up promoting back tracking. You can't drop anything and pick it up later, only discard, so once you pick something up you have to keep it until you get to storage/sell it or use it. I focused 100% on upgrading inventory slots because of this and as the game goes on it keeps giving you more and more items you might want to have (multiple weapon types, useful items like keys, ammo, health, etc.) I focused on inventory slots because I hate backtracking for no purpose other than to make games feel grindy. I did not rush my play through, but you can tell just how bad the back tracking is by how people who play that way have nearly double the playtime I do. 

- Raised black levels. There is a 3rd party mod you can install to fix this, but typical bloober fashion they must design all their games on a washed out LCD panel as the game looks horrible by default on an OLED. If you enjoy grey blacks, the default version of this game is for you. They could have fixed this, but they seem to love this as previous games from them always have this issue. 

- It's more old school that if you die you go back to your previous save as if you hadn't played past that save at all. This means that if you die after searching around and finding a bunch of notes/collectibles/etc you have to redo all of that. Most games that even implement this now, at least save this kind of stuff. Still have to get useful items and stuff, but having to reread all the notes/comics/etc again every single time is frustrating and serves no purpose other than to be grindy. This isn't the end of the word for me as I don't care about achievements past being curious how many people have completed the game, but if you are you are in for some frustrating times if you die. 

As mentioned, none of these last three would have caused me to not recommend this game, it's 100% that last boss fight. I don't think that is something they'll ever fix either so I imagine this will always be a do not recommend.

Edit: I finished the game now, about 30 hours for a first play through. Despite positives, it is very annoying, and I cannot recommend it. There is about 20 hours of content, but you will spend hours retracing paths, cleaning areas, and loading saves, or just dying constantly.

Performance is horrible. Even at very low settings, motion blur disabled, and low resolution it is hard to play. Upscaling works really poorly. And this is with pretty modern hardware (RX 6900 XT, which was higher end just few years ago, and now is still good mid-range compared to current offering). You look at one point, and perf is nice, 140 fps (at very low settings), but then you turn your camera few degrees, and it suddenly drops to 30 fps, with a lot of chop. Linux version is even slower at same setting, while Proton one is ok.

There are also some bugs. Keyboard navigation in some menus (like save) is broken. Some textures and meshes fail to load or are black, especially at higher visual settings. Some distant objects like trees in background are pixelated mess. Plus you are limited to 9 save slots, and you can only save in specific places on map. Only last save is saves in Steam cloud, which is a very easy way to get softlocked.

On the game play, it has interesting visuals and environments, and story, especially as I am from Poland, and lived in Kraków for many years, so I appreciate it. I also like that it is inspired by "The Thing" movie, with art, direction and music, and obviously monsters.

But progression and level design are meh. They are very linear. Constant lack of resources, poor aiming, sloppy movement, are all annoying. Enemies attacks, especially in enclosed spaces, are essentially impossible to dodge, parry, cancel or avoid. Even if you are visually out of range, if they started an attack, the attack will connect, no matter what you do. Some of your attacks are hard to cancel, or auto-retrigger, you need to stop and restart the attack to actually do anything, this includes melee, and gun charge shots. Ammo reloads add to this. The worst one is the last boss fight, which I needed to do about 30 times, despite me hitting all the shots. Low ammo and heals at the end did not help.

There are times there game closes your path back, and if you do not have enough ammo, or right weapons, you basically soft lock. So better have saves from various points in the past to unlock. Similarly there are points, where you are out of area, and will not able to go back - I was able to only get 9/10 cat collected, because of this.

I would say stay away. Not worth it at the moment. Even with better hardware in few years, it will still be meh and not worth the trouble.

I don’t know who tested the controls (keyboard/mouse and gamepad), but I haven’t seen anything this buggy and inconsistent in a long time. Want auto-aim because your aim is bad but you still want to play through the story? Sure, here you go. Except in combat it will never actually lock onto enemies — only supply crates, or sometimes enemies, but never their weak spots. For example, the fight in the church against the multi-armed monster: try turning on aim support and beating this boss. You won’t be able to target the weak points (those glowing growths), only the still-invulnerable parts. Okay. Forget the devs’ advice, let’s switch to keyboard and mouse. And right away it’s obvious why the developers push the gamepad. It feels like the input handling was written in Python. It feels like 500–700 ms of delay, though Nvidia overlay shows only 50 ms. I suspect the issue is “object magnetism” and penalty timeouts between actions (animations). But then the question is — why the hell add magnetism/animations for keyboard and mouse if you can’t consistently process my input? On gamepad I can run and reload at the same time. On keyboard/mouse — only if I get lucky and there’s no conflict between the sprint-start and reload animations. You’ll get sprayed with green goo long before the game responds to a basic combo like Shift + turn + W. I get it when edge cases aren’t tested, but skipping testing for core story fights is just shameful. I don’t recommend buying the game until they rework the input handling.

P.S.: The story and atmosphere are fantastic. Haven’t seen that in a while. But again — the controls really ruin the experience.

There is so much good squirreled away in this game, sandwiched between game design choices that just feel annoying and malicious. Not scary, not tension inducing--just annoying. Everything just feels like the devs needed to be right, at the expense of being enjoyable. 

And it is so, so close to being great. The atmosphere is fantastic, the sound design is fantastic, the world building is provocative and thoughtful. I wanted to wander everywhere, see everything, read everything.  But it is an absolute chore to play, because being right is more important than being enjoyable. And, technically, the game is difficult, in the same way that performing your own colonoscopy might be. Towards the Church, I just found myself dreading the next combat encounter. Not because it was scary, or tense, or difficult, but because it was so tedious and remarkably unenjoyable. I saw a bunch of explodable shit everywhere and just decided, nope, I am not sludging through another half-baked 'all doors lock until you kill every enemy' shooting gallery with the most unmaneuverable character since the tank control days of old. Running in circles charging my shots and trying to craft ammo while dodging enemies with attacks that seem wholly undeterred by walls or doors or any other obstacles. And there was no way I was going to do yet another boss fight where I have to play ring-around-the-rosie with pillars while its projectile attacks clip through and still damage me anyways. 

And, by *god* was I not going to spend another full 72 seconds (yes I counted, because it was just so goddamn slow) climbing a ladder like a geriatric riddled with arthritis. 

I love slow burns. I love atmosphere. I love difficulty. But I also love my time, and respect it more than anything else. And Cronos really wanted you to die in dumb ways just to be right about being able to kill you. And even mostly failed at that as I only died about 7 or 8 times total by the time I reached the Church. Even when the game threw cheap unavoidable hits at me (again, the favorite in this game is enemies that smash through a wall at random places and stun you into damage, with the trigger being directly where the enemy bursts out into). It felt like getting together with friends for some D&D and having a DM who makes up new rules to hamstring you every time you're doing too well, or like going on a date with someone who is angry at you for agreeing to go out so they keep sticking their fingers in your food and drink and farting loudly to try and get you to leave so they don't have to 'be the bad guy' and end the date themselves. 

Again, a dipshit. 

Cronos has so much to love, and there was so much I did love. But by god did Bloober want me to really know it didn't want me there and didn't want to end the date themselves.

I’ve always had a complicated relationship with [b]Bloober Team[/b] games. Usually, I notice the quality of their form, interesting visual design, strong art direction and good presentation. But when it comes to the substance, things get more complicated. Perhaps I have the fewest complaints about [b]Observer[/b], but this game was released eight years ago. My expectations from “[b]Cronos: The New Dawn[/b]” were low enough from the start, but aesthetics and potentially intriguing setting interested me. Well… The studio Bloober Team did not disappoint and made a very typical game for them. In a bad sense.

Cronos was developed in parallel with [b]Silent Hill 2 Remake[/b] as another project that actually focuses on gameplay, full-fledged mechanics, a combat system, and complex actions beyond just walking around and opening doors. The sources of inspiration are instantly recognizable and developers never concealed them. The problem is that all these borrowed elements are made much better in the games that inspired Cronos than in Cronos itself. “Great, let’s do a combat system like in [b]Dead Space[/b].” But we’re gonna ruin impact and make close combat absolutely useless. “How about an inventory like in [b]Resident Evil[/b]?” But we’re gonna reduce it to absurdity and it will be ridiculously modest even with a maximum upgrade. There are even dalliances with gravity here, that don’t offer really any interesting situations and only serve to extend the walkthrough (like many other things in Cronos). By the way, where is the diegetic interface like in Dead Space and the map like in Resident Evil? Probably there was not inspiring enough. As “interesting situations” you are offered “time rewind” the individual level elements and fuel tanks like in [b]Singularity[/b]. In the first case this should be used to unlock the inaccessible areas (in fact hide the laziness of developers, lack of ideas or money — underline as needed — and extend the game again), in the second case make battles with mobs and bosses more exciting (if you like blow up the barrels, restore and blow up again, and this process never gets boring you, you will approve it).

The most defiant problems of game design are found with non-standard player’s actions. In my case that player was me, of course. For example, soon after the start, when I picked up the key from a locked door, the monster appeared (in Cronos they are known as “Orphans”). Rather than killing it, I ran away to a breach in the wall (one of the favorite features in SH2R) that I used to get in and out. It turned out that skinny Orphan can’t get through places that our bulky suit wearing Traveler can. The Orphan will just think that I disappeared from its view until I get back into the room. I made another wonderful discovery in the hospital: monsters can’t climb over dividers. I witnessed a fun scene: a waist-high divider was between Traveler and Orphan, and the helpless Orphan could not do anything. These creatures of  biomass spread around the world and destroyed all living things. Should I take it seriously after that? In general the AI of monsters is really stupid: they can stop seeing the protagonist after she hides behind a specific pillar (in this case the distance will be only about a few meters), or they can spit acid furiously at the same pillar. Or they can try to hit with a huge curved arm right through the room geometry without hitting the player by some miracle.

But the most amazing thing was yet to come. At a later stage the Traveler’s route will pass through the previously closed room, the doors of which will be broken by a large monster pack. I had an interesting situation where I’m almost out of ammo, running circles around enemies. I got into the room with an obstacle, under which I have to pass. But there was no interaction button. To say that it was a total surprise for me would be to say nothing. Happy monsters are roaring behind my back and it seems like here is it, my escape route. But I can’t escape. There is no interaction button. To figure out what it is, bug or game design feature, I loaded my save game before then, somehow procured ammo and went there again after killing all enemies. And you know what? The interaction button for the obstacle appeared and I could pass under it. That is, the button will not appear until you destroy all monsters from this room. It will be impossible to describe the whole range of emotions that flashed from the depths of my brain to facial muscles. It was not a bug. It was a conscious solution of game design. That’s exactly how the game works.

You could argue: “so, you did not act as intended by a game designer”. And you’re right. But I’m sure that a game designer should think about the possible situation in this section of level, when the player can’t kill all monsters. And don’t link such an element like passing under the obstacle to neutralizing all enemies. Either you make a game rule that works perfectly the entire game or you don’t make it at all.

I would write a lot more, but the character limit is relentless. As such my final comment will be something about the plot and setting. The plot is sinking into a weak and unconvincing drama and the further, the more. The Cronos lore is not revealed in any way. Playing the game, you will find tons of notes, most of which have no value for the main story, and none of them explain to you where time-travel technologies, gravity platforms and other magic things come from. It seems to me that Traveler could take all these notes to the nearest paper collection point and make good money. A cats’ presence in the world where all animals went extinct is not explained in any way either. They are here just because it’s cute. And there is nothing that would sympathize with characters in any way. All the setting’s potential is just not used as superfluous.

In total, “Cronos: The New Dawn” feels more like a kit of disjointed exhibits, not a solid game in which the body of different gears provides a coordinated work. Or it’s like another “exhibition of achievements” of Bloober Team, which is obtained from their previous games, and Silent Hill 2 Remake is no exception (but let’s talk about that another time). “Hey, dude, check out how we can! And like this! It’s cool! Oh yeah!” One could call it “the summing up of sci-fi horrors’ experience” in all seriousness. It’s been so many years, the studio already has eight horror games in their portfolio, and Bloober Team still looks like an ambitious young upstart desperately trying to make games “like the grown-ups do”, but never has enough either talent, time, money or all of those together. The genre titan, Resident Evil, can rest easy.

At the same time, I do welcome their attempts to create new original IPs instead of just working on other people’s franchises. Sadly, the quality of form in Cronos does not solve problems with the quality of its content. And familiar mechanics are executed infinitely better in the same Resident Evil and Dead Space. However, this did not really affect the game’s success: it gathers positive gamer reviews and seems to be selling fairly well. Everything is going according to plan. If you still really want to try it, wait for a sale.

P.S. Despite all of the above, I can say that Cronos is definitely better than [b]Silent Hill f[/b]. Because in Cronos you have firearms and no stamina bar. Thank you for that.

I may be the minority here with this take, but I genuinely didn't enjoy the game as much as I hoped. 

It's such an unoriginal, uninspiring gameplay design. This game takes the ideas of Dead Space & RE4 and makes them horrendous.

It's the same copypaste survival-action formula from every modern RE title ever.
The only difference being how terribly implemented it is.

Significantly worse inventory system.
Awful balancing.
Limited "upgrade" system.
Boring and overused enemies.
Clunky movement & combat.
An overused trope of body morphing.. done terribly.

The inventory system racks my brain. I cannot fathom why you'd want such a frustrating system in your game.
Imagine needing to collect a progression item and having no room for it. Why not have a quest-item inventory like every other game in this genre does? I'm sure people are just jumping for joy having to use up their spare meds / ammo in order to free up ONE slot to move on with the game. I feel bad for those that have to back track through everything just to clear 1-2 slots for quest-progression items. Speaking of, why is it that the main weapon of the game is a singular pistol that can change forms, but takes up a slot for each form? You're just making the already-terrible inventory system worse by default with this decision. 

I can't tell if this is a chronic skill-issue on my part, or the RNG is absolutely horrendous. Anytime I break open a yellow-tape box (yes, those stupid things are littered in this game too), I get.. absolutely nothing! That's right, nothing! Break open 3-4 crates and receive completely nothing in return. No ammo, no meds, nothing. When I DO on the off-chance actually get SOMETHING from the crates, it's just energy.. and the smallest amount possible at that (energy is this game's "currency" for the shop). Due to the poor distribution of supplies, I find myself being LUCKY to have 10 bullets to use at any given time. If you're not using the charge shot ability on the pistol at all times, you're literally wasting ammo. 

Upgrading your suit & weapons is as bare bones as it can get. Nothing gives you a special skill, ability, or perk. It is quite simply "number go up" and that's it. Wanna upgrade the duration of burning enemies? Spend a core to make it burn from 1 second, to 1.33 seconds! Wow!!

The enemies are so overused & limited it hurts. I dunno why they do the Dead Space method of "Black skin = strong." Somehow a darker version of the same enemy just has more health. Not only that, but why the worst kinda of enemies? Why slugging pus-balls? Why Spitters? Why wall-attached enemies that just trigger QTE events constantly? These aren't fun, they're annoying. Couple this with the jank movement and you've got boring, clunky combat. I can't lie, I had more fun running up to them & slugging a mean right hook and stomping them than actually trying to shoot. I wish melee was actually usable because the animations are clean. I assumed it was supposed to be a replacement for the utter drought of ammunition, but a loading tip says "Don't rely on your fists, only a last resort." TL;DR melee does absolutely no damage, and no.. you can't upgrade your melee strength / force whatsoever. Which begs the question; why even add the ability to melee, knowing it does nothing and you can't upgrade it? Especially considering the vast majority of enemies spit acid puddles everywhere forbidding you from getting within 20 feet of them. 

All in all, I expected better. It takes existing ideas from other popular titles and.. that's it. It doesn't expand upon any of them, nor does it explore anything deeper than face value. It genuinely just doesn't feel original, new, or fun.

The game is advertised as a mix or homage to a few classic survival horror games, but doesn't really deliver on any of the things that made those games exceptional. The survival part of the game is weakly fleshed out, being of a very basic "craft this thing when you need it and be economical" skein. There's some light RPG upgrade systems that are *very very basic* to the point of it just being raw numbers. It does make the difference when it comes to playing the game, but is so boring/uninteresting I felt cheated given the games they reference.

The gameplay is very weak though. It's THE MOST basic kind of survival horror that is more reminiscent of PS2 games than any kind of modern riff on them. Headshot the enemy or shoot the glowy spot, dodge enemy attacks by literally walking out of the way. You can inflate your gameplay to 20+ hours if you want by melee juking things to death if you really want. Not a fan of the basic nature of this, especially when other titles have already set a better standard. Then there's the fire/merge mechanic, severely limited in it's execution that it's seemingly pointless except on boss fights, and even then it's...the same as everything else.

The Setting is absolutely great though, a lot of mystery and questions, a lot of beautiful settings, a lot of visual horror - a visually great and interesting world...

...which is a shame because the story is so BASIC it's insulting. They hint at things bigger than we are, and then proceeds to NEVER explore them and instead focuses the story around a completely uninteresting *nothing* that doesn't even make sense in terms of the story they DO tell us.

Skip, wait for sale, your choice.

UPDATE AFTER BEATING THE GAME: My original review remains pretty much spot on, in fact, the game gets slightly worse as you progress further like most games these days where they dump most of their development time on the first part of the game to get people "hooked".

Added annoyances in addition to previous review:

1. Third person shooter with significant offset, there is no way to switch aim shoulders. Have fun making blind right hand turns.
2. The levels get so dark towards the end that the flashlight is almost literally useless, on top of it's hilariously short and unrealistic range already.
3. Every single boss in the game, sans the last one, are basically the same (some are literally the same, just in a slightly different arena).
3a. In fact: In the entire game there are less than half a dozen unique monsters.
4. You won't stop constantly fighting with the inventory until like four fifths of the way into the game when you finally max it out... on the second to last level.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:

Story is unique, game is visually acceptable, and that's largely what's carrying the reviews. Gamers these days are extremely shallow.

Otherwise the game is a mashup of various different horror games that have come in the past, but does not replicate any portion of what they did well below surface level.

In fact in some cases it borrows the concept but completely disregards the pieces that made it good.

We have Dead Space enemies, but no limbing system, just shoot them in the head. Shooting them in the leg will cause the smaller ones to fall over temporarily, but melee damage (Stomp, just like DS) does so little damage that spamming it on something won't kill it, and due to animation locking, doing it with more than one mob around is a death sentence.

We have brutal inventory management (as if anyone ever actually liked that), just so that "increasing inventory space" has value as an RPG mechanic, you will be forced repeatedly to drop at least one or two pieces of your gear just to carry story items that have zero value. As an example that means potentially having to drop your shotgun just so you can pick up a door key (they take the same space), dropping requires backtracking to the last checkpoint to put it in a box, and then running all the way back to the key, once you've used the key, you need to run all the way back to the previous checkpoint to pick up the gear you had to drop for the story item.

A lot of people complain about the slow character movements, this doesn't bother me, your basically stuck in a Big Daddy suit so it makes sense that the character is just going to be slow. What does bother me is the fact that collision modeling and movement in this game can be pretty bad. Your big character will get stuck on a whole bunch of stuff it shouldn't. Your character is also treated like it has no momentum. To give you an example, running away from something that hits you in the back, you will not keep moving in the direction you were going in and will "stun" in place instantly, monsters that are visually "less dense" than the player will flinch the player far more than seems believable.

Finally, the game designers seem to be in love with the completely cheese of just locking the player in an arena with a ton of mobs when you pick up a story item. "...and here we have the player pick up the key, which magically makes a dozen monsters angry, and the doors autolock until all the monsters are dead."

All in all it boils down to a game that is surface level unique, but actually extremely generic mechanically.

Cronos is a straight up arena shooter with a horror paint job and inventory management tacked on.

Would it be worth it? Yes, if it was maybe half of what it currently costs. Blame steam for the thumbs down because their system is binary, in reality it would probably be something like 6 or 7 out of 10.

Getting tired of these art house style games that are basically solely carried on the story and graphics and then just throw in game play mechanics they've seen other games do so they can call them games.

...actually Cronos could make a pretty decent movie.

Will update this review if my opinion appreciably changes the further I get, but I doubt it.

[h1][b] DISCLAIMER: THIS IS A NEUTRAL REVIEW. NOT A NEGATIVE REVIEW [/b][/h1] 

Cronos: The New Dawn has been one the game's I have been looking forward to playing since October 2024. It generally looked like the next "Dead Space" (although it's NOT Dead Space, if you get me). It's made by Bloober Team which, done an excellent job on Silent Hill 2 recently. So, because of this, I had really, really high hopes/standards for Cronos: The New Dawn.

After playing the game (almost) to 100% completion in 10 hours, I am going to write a review that is honest about the game in every way. So, let's get to it!

[h1][b] A personal opinion [/b][/h1] 
Before the game came out, it looked like the next "Dead Space" (or the next sort of game like it) Pretty heavily too. From the looks of the trailers, gameplay we got shown and other sorts, the big reviewers were comparing it HEAVILY to Dead Space. So it wasn't just me with that take.

My thought's when I started the game was something along the lines of - Aim for the limbs. Good horror. Good Action. Stomping on monsters to make them drop loot. Y'know, the Dead Space in me, but sadly... it wasn't like that and I will explain all of this in pro's and con's. 

I just wanted to make this abundantly clear because I was going into this thinking it was HEAVILY inspired by Dead Space. I know my opinion is probably going to upset some people going forward.

[h1][b] Pro's [/b][/h1] 
⚫The graphics are just... gorgeous. Each area is heavily detailed. From flickering lights to a gargantuan clock-tower looming over the sky. Interiors are also heavily detailed. Not only that, they are visually stunning to the eyes also!
⚫The story is phenomenal so far. In my opinion. Not going to spoil anything, sorry.
⚫If you adapt the "RUN" and not fight mindset, you can run past the majority of enemies without feeling pressured. Like in the hospital when you can reach a fallen over cupboard, go to it, hold in "A", while being chased by 2 big guys and several smaller enemies and boom, you don't need to fight them at all! Smashing! True survival right there.
⚫Performance/Optimisation. To be clear, I am on a very good PC. A 5090 (PC SPECS ARE LISTED ON ACCOUNT). I had no stuttering. No lagging. No FPS drops. Nothing. I am absolutely amazed at how good this game runs. (especially in 2025).
⚫The exploration was on point. The game doesn't really FULLY hold your hand and you can loot, run around like a headless nutcase and find collectables. Guns. Upgrade materials and more. I really enjoyed looking around each area for new guns.
⚫The music really suited the game! I like the soundtrack for this one!

[h1][b] Con's [/b][/h1] 
⚫The melee combat. If you are like me, came from Dead Space, the melee combat is atrocious in this game. It takes you 10-15 hits to melee kill an enemy. You have "METAL" or some type of "METAL" knuckle dusters and it deals piss-poor damage to anything you hit. You do get an essence later on that increases melee damage.. but why choose that over the others, especially so late into the game too.
⚫Another note about melee, you don't stun the enemies when you hit them. You swing once and then again... that's it. Then you go into a cooldown before you do the same combo. Meanwhile the enemy just stands there, takes it and then does it's attacks towards you. The enemy is VERY static when you melee them. Compared to Dead Space, this is a step backwards in my opinion. Even Silent Hill 2's melee was better, also IMO.
⚫To kill enemies. Again, I thought it was going to be like Dead Space. I was aiming for the limbs. Turns out, the best way to kill (so far) is by FULLY CHARGING a shot from your pistol (starting weapon) and aiming for the head. Limb damage is basically non existent. 
⚫It tries to hard to be "Dead Space". The stomping animation and mechanic - Dead Space. The blood written on the walls - Dead Space. The "Gravity boot" sections - Dead Space. The enemies "absorbing" other enemies to get stronger - DEAD SPACE. Heck... one could say the Traveller's outfit is an Issac Clark unlocked outfit?!?! 
⚫The guns. There was not really any difference in the guns. When you found a gun mid-way through the game, it's not even slightly upgraded to match your gun. What is the point in giving me other guns whereas my already upgraded 5+x gun slaps? 
⚫At the start of the game you see your gun transform into knuckles and back into a gun. My question is this, why does every gun need it's own inventory slot? If you had one gun that could "shapeshift" into the other guns, it might make them more use-able. I left my spare guns in my chest almost constantly because my inventory was always full.
⚫The price of the game. Personally, it's not worth £50, or £60 for deluxe. I think it should have been more around the £30 mark. 

[h1][b] My (VERY HONEST) Verdict [/b][/h1] 
Again, it's not Dead Space. It should never have been made to look like Dead Space and because the game "tries" or "takes way to much influence" from Dead Space, it feels like it lacks its own identity. Especially if you go into this as a massive fan of Dead Space expecting it to be something that it's not, remember, we were shown lots of clips, trailers and gameplay showcasing all this "DEAD SPACE" type combat and such. 

I'm not going to lie or sugarcoat my words to make this game look better. Just because Bloober Team made an excellent Remake last year. I'm going to be brutally honest about it.

Please, PLEASE don't get me wrong. Cronos: The New Dawn is a good game. It really is, but I would not recommend it based on what I've played, based on the combat and not for that price anyway. 

If you want a game like this, cheaper, I'd recommend the Dead Space, Resident Evil 4 or Silent Hill 2 Remake. More bang for your buck, BUT, at the end of the day, it's your choice to buy the game or not. After all, this is MY opinion. My thoughts. My review. Your might absolutely love this. This might be YOUR GOTY. 

Please don't let me sway you from buying and playing the game. I am just here to give my two cents on the game and, I have done just that!
